#6296. The Best Airbnbs in Colorado, Including a Ski-In Chalet and a Cliffside Cabin

I’ve always found Colorado a little hard to resist. After a handful of trips, I’ve explored everything from Aspen’s glitzy streets to Denver’s spirited food and cocktail scene to the many smaller towns in between—and somehow, there’s still more to discover. With four national parks; miles of hiking and biking trails; world-class ski resorts; and cities brimming with independent shops, restaurants, and bars, Colorado is a year-round playground with plenty to keep you busy (and plenty of reasons to come back).

Finding the right Colorado Airbnb is part of the fun. Think tucked-away mountain cabins with front-row seats to the snow, sprawling homes made for group getaways, and character-filled apartments that put you right in the middle of the action. While there are plenty of gorgeous Colorado hotels, there's something pretty wonderful about having your own Airbnb to return to after a day of chasing fresh powder, hiking, or exploring a new town. Whether you're plotting a winter ski escape, a summer adventure, or a fall foliage getaway, these are the 13 best Airbnbs in Colorado to add to your wish list.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 9Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: In-ground pool, firepit, outdoor shower, dedicated office space, rooftop with mountain views

Don’t let the university neighborhood fool you—this south-of-downtown oasis is ideal for a quieter, family-friendly stay. It's close to the light rail, making it easy to get around when you so choose. With succulent-filled rooms, large paintings, five cozy bedrooms, and two-story windows, there’s lots to love about this space.

Any kids you're traveling with will favor the foosball and ping-pong tables in the basement, while adults will enjoy lounging in the sunken family room. But perhaps the most lovable feature is the private backyard, which has a pool, firepit, and full dining table, all surrounded by lush greenery and sleek appliances.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Observatory Park, The Robert and Judi Newman Center for the Performing Arts, University Hills Farmers Market, University of Denver

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: California king bed, flat-screen TV, immersive sound system, disco ball, LED lighting, faux-fire Malm fireplace, skyline views

Get groovy at this nostalgic studio apartment, which features an authentic disco ball and skyline views (including a peek at Coors Field, where the Colorado Rockies play) in the heart of Denver's Lower Downtown (LoDo) neighborhood. Lucky for its guests, this spot is within walking distance of downtown Denver’s hottest entertainment, shopping, and dining outposts for a day or night out on the town. Plus, it’s equipped with all the amenities of your dreams, including a spacious California king bed, a 13-foot vintage couch, and a fully equipped kitchen for whipping up meals.

City: DenverThings to do nearby: Coors Field, Commons Park, Little Man Ice Cream shop, Ball Arena, 16th Street Mall, Larimer Square, McGregor Square, Denver Union Station

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Central location, fully equipped kitchen, private backyard, in-unit washer and dryer, kid-friendly amenities

You and your crew are in for a treat when staying at this charming, historic Boulder home. With original woodwork, colorful wallpaper, a fenced backyard, and three spacious bedrooms, guests here will enjoy a stylish stay.

Its location is the true star of the show: Right off Pearl Street, Boulder's happening hub of art, food, and entertainment venues, you'll be within walking distance from it all. Previous guests have raved about not having to rent a car when booking this base; even the airport bus takes you within three blocks of the address.

City: BoulderThings to do nearby: The Museum of Boulder, Pearl Street Mall, Boulder Theater, Pearl Street

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Rocky Mountain views, hot tub, outdoor kitchen with gas grill, firepit, Dobsonian telescope

Tucked on five private acres, this is a true mountain retreat in Bailey—a Colorado town less than an hour outside Denver, known for its quirky roadside attractions, outdoor recreation, and historic mountain charm. Dubbed “Skytrail Lodge,” this cabin fits right into the neighborhood.

The main living area is bright and welcoming, with floor-to-ceiling windows that bring the outside in. A big, comfy sofa anchors the living room, complemented by green and black accents that create an upscale, modern feel. Outside, lounge about on the deck and take in the incredible view of the Rocky Mountains. What better place to sip on your morning cup of joe, read a book, or indulge in an evening glass of wine?

City: BaileyThings to do nearby: Mount Bailey, Pine Valley Ranch Park, Brookside-McCurdy Trailhead, Crooked Top Mountain, Shawnee

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Walkable to ski resort, private hot tub, chef's kitchen, spacious design, smart TVs

Tucked in the storybook town of Cascade Village, you'll find a stay that exudes real mountain charm, with creature comforts to write home about. This Vail house is just a five-minute walk to Vail Ski Resort, with a free shuttle to Lionshead and Vail Village nearby. Meaning no matter the season—whether skiing or hiking—guests will have a convenient stay accompanied by the amenities that make an Airbnb great: a private, six-person hot tub; a fully equipped kitchen; en suite soaking tubs; private balcony access; and a laundry area.

Folks who stay here can cook up dinner on the grill or in the spacious kitchen, enjoy their meals in the eight-person dining area, play some groovy tunes on the Sonos speaker, and sip on a cup of coffee while looking out over the city and mountains. If you needed a sign to book a fun group adventure, consider this it.

City: VailThings to do nearby: Eagle Bahn Gondola, Lionshead Village, Vail Village, Ford Park, Betty Ford Alpine Gardens

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Central location, wood-burning fireplace, shared hot tubs and heated pool, private patio

If you're looking for a stay in a mountain city that's as convenient as it is cozy, this Breckenridge condo is your solution. The renovated two-bedroom town house is designed for folks interested in exploring the downtown pubs, restaurants, and art-filled spaces—as well as the mountain trails, ski resorts, and beautiful natural surroundings.

Back at the rental, use the space to “ski, stroll, soak, and repeat,” as stated in the listing. Unwind around the crackling wood-burning fireplace, enjoy a home-cooked meal around the big dining table, stay in for a round of board games, or indulge in one of the condo's shared amenities: the heated pool, sauna, or one of the four hot tubs.

City: BreckenridgeThings to do nearby: Illinois Creek Trailhead, Carter Park and Pavilion, Breckenridge Brewery & Pub, South Main Street, QuickSilver SuperChair

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, wraparound deck, wood-burning fireplace, mountain views

Say hello to your next base for that upcoming group trip. This three-story timber lodge is all about space, convenience, and mountain fun. With a light-filled, open-concept kitchen and living room, you'll have some room to breathe. The floor-to-ceiling windows with sprawling mountain views and a wraparound deck make it even better. The home sits only 12 miles from Breckenridge, so it's drivable to the city's best hubs—from nature to dining—while also being tucked away enough to sprawl out and frolic.

Aside from the four queen bedrooms, there's a game room complete with a foosball table, vintage arcade games, table tennis, and more, making it a truly kid-friendly base.

City: AlmaThings to do nearby: Peaceful Valley Lodge, Wheeler Lake Winter Trailhead, Downtown Breckenridge, Montgomery Reservoir

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Slopeside location, heated pool, hot tub, private balcony

With its ski-in/ski-out location and proximity to one of the lifts on Aspen Mountain, this is a stellar booking for snow chasers. But it's also a fantastic base for those heading to Aspen in the warmer months, thanks to its swanky year-round amenities, like a sprawling pool and hot tub with lounge chairs for relaxing or soaking up the sun.

City: AspenThings to do nearby: Aspen Mountain Ski Resort (one block to Lift 1A), Aspen Art Museum, Main Street, John Denver Sanctuary, White House Tavern

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bedsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, sauna, mountain views, wood-burning stove, design-forward interiors

This swanky cabin is ideal for those in need of a restorative nature trip. The cool cabin aesthetic extends throughout the open-concept kitchen, big windows, hot tub, and sauna—and the view of the sprawling mountain range is well appreciated.

The biggest peak you can see from the living room is the region's iconic La Plata, which is the fifth-highest in the Rockies. Mount Elbert, Colorado's highest peak, is at the back of the home, with one of its trailheads a few minutes down the road. Another big plus? The home sits just over a two-hour drive from Denver—making it a sweet weekend trip for Mile High City locals and a good road trip stop for those heading onward.

City: Twin LakesThings to do nearby: Rinker Peak, Independence Pass, Mount Elbert, Twin Lakes Village, Colorado Trail, Continental Divide Trail, Leadville

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Sauna, firepit, hot tub, tasteful interior design, barbecue grill with outdoor seating

The lush Glenwood Springs is an underrated gem compared to its more frequented neighbors, Grand Junction and Moab. At this one-of-a-kind cabin, though, you'll likely question why it's taken you so long to plan a trip here in the first place.

Awe-inspiring canyon views await in every room through expansive windows, adding to the spot's light and airy feel. Each bedroom features a Tempur-Pedic bed and private deck access for true comfort and solitude. Indulge in the outdoor perks, too—there's a six-person hot tub, a firepit on the patio, and a four-person barrel sauna ready for post-adventure restoration. You'll also have prime access to the village's downtown square and its iconic hot springs.

City: Glenwood SpringsThings to do nearby: Colorado River, No Name Trailhead, Lookout Mountain, South Canyon Hot Springs, Horse Mountain, Hanging Lake Trailhead

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Mountain and forest views, private patio, bathtub, indoor fireplace, Wi-Fi

As one of Airbnb's most wishlisted properties, find this spruced-up, octagon-shaped tree house tucked away in the small mountain community of Cascade. It’s a scenic 15-minute drive from Colorado Springs, but you’ll find serenity easily among the tree house's natural surroundings. With floor-to-ceiling windows that look out to a little forest paradise, a wood-burning stove, a coffee and waffle maker, puzzles, games, and a smart TV, you'll never want to leave.

If you do plan to go out, you’re just five minutes away from Pikes Peak Highway, dotted with loads of gorgeous hiking trails, but you don’t have to leave your property to catch a glimpse of hummingbirds and other wildlife.

City: Cascade-Chipita ParkThings to do nearby: Ski and/or trails, scenic drives, Woodland Park, restaurants, reservoirs

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Pikes Peak views, convenient location, fully equipped kitchen, opt-in grocery delivery

This lofty town house—positioned (basically) right next to Garden of the Gods public park—is all about the views. The kitchen, living, and dining room all face the iconic Pikes Peak through a glass garage door. When open, it transforms the space into a picture-perfect indoor-outdoor area, complete with an overhanging balcony for taking it all in.

Two of the three spacious bedrooms sit on the home's ground level with shared bathroom space. There's also a separate “kids room,” complete with two twin beds—plus a trundle and space to hang out with a television (and a game system). You might not want to spend too much time at home, though: The home sits just a few blocks from Manitou Springs and Old Colorado City for sightseeing, restaurant trips, outdoor adventures, and more.

City: Colorado SpringsThings to do nearby: Manitou, Red Rocks, Garden of the Gods, Old Colorado City, Academy Riding Stables, The Incline, The Cog Railway

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Quirky design, infrared sauna, firepit, mountain and valley views

Just a one-hour drive from Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve, this otherworldly home deserves a spot on your Colorado bucket list. It sits at the base of the Sangre de Cristo range, with mountain views by day and dark skies for stargazing at night. As one of the quirkiest picks on this list, this hobbit home has more creature comforts than appear at first glance. There's a kitchenette for meals at home, a dining table that seats four, and an in-unit washer and dryer. You'll also find an infrared sauna to relax in, as well as a firepit to cozy up around. Do note, the home is most ideal for duos or small families, with its one queen bedroom and a double bed in the loft.

City: CrestoneThings to do nearby: Great Sand Dunes National Park, Blueberry Peak, Duncan, Eureka Mountain, Sangre de Cristo Mountain Range

Amazon has a new restaurant delivery partner for its Prime members: Uber Eats, which replaces the Grubhub+ benefit Prime members had until today.

To celebrate the new partnership, Amazon Prime members can get $20 off each of their first two eligible Uber Eats orders of $25 or more on linked accounts made via Amazon, as long as those orders are for U.S. restaurants and placed by Nov. 18.

Beyond the limited-time launch promotion, Prime members will get $0 delivery fees on eligible Uber Eats orders of $25 or more placed through the Amazon app or website. Interestingly, this appears to work separately from any existing Uber Eats account or benefits you may already have.

Related: Which is the best food delivery app?

There's no need to download another app or create a separate Uber Eats account to use this perk. When you opt in through Amazon, you can use your existing Prime account information, including linked payment methods.

Think of it almost like ordering a box of paper towels from Amazon with free Prime delivery, only this time it's a salad, burger, breakfast tacos or fries. You place the order via Uber Eats in your Amazon account, almost as you would any other Prime delivery, but this time it is fulfilled by Uber Eats instead of your friendly neighborhood Amazon delivery truck.

Amazon has also said that there will be additional Prime-exclusive offers available only on Amazon that could save you more than $175 per year, so we'll be sure to keep an eye out for those.

TPG tip: Amazon Prime Visa cardmembers earn 5% back on all Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5, 2026 with eligible Prime membership.

The information for the Prime Visa has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

This $20 introductory promo seems to apply whether you use pickup or delivery, which isn't always the case with Uber Eats promos. So, it is possible to truly save $20 on a $25 order if you select pickup. If you opt for delivery, you will likely have some service fees and a tip to factor into the equation.

One thing to remember: After the introductory promotion ends, you may want to compare the total cost of ordering through the Amazon-linked version of Uber Eats with any promotions, credit card benefits or discounts available through your regular Uber Eats account. The best deal may depend on which version of Uber Eats you're using.

#6294. Qatar Launches Two South American Destinations

Qatar Airways added two South American destinations on Wednesday, becoming the first Gulf carrier to serve Venezuela.

The new service flies from Doha to Bogotá, Colombia, then continues to Caracas, Venezuela, before returning nonstop to Doha. Qatar Airways will operate the route on Wednesdays and Sundays using a Boeing 777-200LR.

Flights are scheduled to leave Doha at 7:35 a.m. and reach Bogotá at 4:25 p.m. After a 90-minute stop, the aircraft continues to Caracas, arriving at 9 p.m. The return flight leaves Caracas at 11:30 p.m. and reaches Doha at 8:35 p.m. the following day. All times are local.

The airline originally planned to start flying the route in July but postponed the launch following an earthquake in Venezuela, according to Aviation Week.

Qatar Airways is also expanding its codeshare with LATAM to include domestic flights from Bogotá. The agreement will put Qatar’s code on LATAM flights to destinations including Medellín, Cartagena and Cali.

The additions bring Qatar Airways’ network in the Americas to 17 destinations. The carrier began serving South America in 2010 with flights to São Paulo.

#6293. The 50 Best Restaurants For 2026 Have Been Announced—With a Remote European Spot in First Place

The 50 Best Restaurants for 2026 have just been announced as part of a prestigious awards ceremony in Lima on Wednesday, November 5, 2026. As with every year, we wait for the release—an indicator of which restaurants will be topping travelers' lists in the year ahead, and the trends that will shape the experiences they offer. Below, we cover which restaurant snagged the top spot, which restaurant led on every continent, and the industry stars celebrated with individual awards like Best Pastry Chef, Best Sommelier, and more.

Read on for the full list, and notable takeaways from the winners. (For more on the trends revealed at the Lima event, read our reporter's conversation with winning chefs here.)

The Best Restaurant in the World for 2026 is hidden away in sleepy Basque village, Axpe.

Climbing up from its number two spot in last year's list, this year’s winner is Asador Etxebarri in Atxondo, in Spain's Basque Country.

Basque wood-fired cooking is at the heart of this rustic fine-dining restaurant. Chef-owner Víctor Arguinzoniz (also known as Bittor Arginzoniz) is considered a pioneer of grilling and live-fire cooking. At Asador Etxebarri, every course of Bittor Arginzoniz's €300 euro (about $337 USD) tasting menu touches the wood and charcoal grills—from Palamós red prawns to smoked milk ice cream.

Hidden away in the sleepy mountain village of Axpe, about 45 minutes by car from Bilbao, foodies have been making the pilgrimage to try Arguinzoniz's signature grilled dishes since the restaurant opened in 1990. It's been an 18-year journey to the top, as Asador Etxebarri has been a mainstay on The World's 50 Best Restaurants list since 2008, starting at number 44.

Once a restaurant gets the coveted number-one trophy, it is ineligible for nomination in forthcoming years—with the intention of allowing other restaurants a chance to earn top billing. Top-placing restaurants are then inducted into a new list, called the Best of the Best. This list includes such legendary eateries as Chef Thomas Keller's The French Laundry in Yountville, California, and Disfrutar in Barcelona, Spain. Last year’s winner, Maido in Lima, Peru, is the most recent inductee to this prestigious list.

It’s tempting to imagine the enviable job held by a panel of judges that sample every restaurant in the world. But that’s not quite how the 50 Best works. Rather, the 50 is an international media company that taps the expertise of over a thousand hospitality experts from around the world to weigh in on the industry that they know best. Chefs, restaurateurs, food journalists, and well-traveled gourmets all anonymously nominate restaurants that they have dined at within the last 18 months. (Members can’t vote for a restaurant they have a financial interest in.) Professional services consultancy Deloitte has access to the voting data to ensure the validity and fairness of the process.

Because of the voting-style nature of the awards, a restaurant might fall off the list one year only to return later. This year, previous entries to the list such as The Ledbury—a fine-dining beauty in London, United Kingdom where chef Brett Graham marries British produce, Japanese flavours, and French culinary techniques—returns to the list in the number 83 spot. Similarly, Luxe Mosu in Seoul, South Korea—home to chef Sung Anh's elevated interpretations of traditional Korean fare—returns to the list at number 78.

“Every year The 50 Best Restaurants list gives us a snapshot of where more than 1,100 individuals who live and breathe this industry have had their most memorable restaurant experiences over the previous 18 months," explains Rikki Tidball, managing director of awards and rankings for The 50. “And I think that’s what makes it so special. Each Academy member votes independently, so nobody at The 50 or any of our partners has a say in who makes the list, and restaurants can’t nominate themselves. This means every restaurant on the list has genuinely earned it.”

Gaggan in Bangkok climbed up to Number 2 after placing at Number 6 the year prior.

As always, the highest-ranking restaurants on each continent have been given a special mention during tonight's awards—and there are a few repeats from last year. Gaggan in Bangkok (this year's number 2) won the best restaurant in Asia again. Mexico City's Quintonil (4) was the best restaurant in Latin America again, while New York City's Atomix (11) was the best restaurant in North America. Dubai's Trèsind Studio (28) was named the best restaurant in the Middle East for another year. The best restaurant in Africa was Cape Town's La Colombe (35). Sydney's Saint Peter (50) was the best restaurant in Oceania, while top spot Asador Etxebarri took the best restaurant in Europe award.

Every year, the panel awards special prizes to chefs, front-of-house staff, and activists who are leading the charge in hospitality. In 2026, the Best Female Chef Award went to Jessica Rosval, head chef of Al Gatto Verde. Bangkok’s Dej Kewkacha won Best Pastry Chef Award, and Lesley Liu of Odette in Singapore won the Best Sommelier Award while the Estrella Damm Chefs' Choice Award went to Junghyun ‘JP’ Park from Atomix in New York City. Doris Lam won The 50 Best Restaurants Scholarship. Spanish chef Ferran Adrià of El Bulli won the SevenRooms Icon Award.

Restaurants given a special mention during the 2026 ceremony included Tuju in São Paulo, which earned the Highest New Entry Award. Copenhagen's Kadeau won the Highest Climber Award after soaring 33 places this year, and Naar in Kasauli, India, won the Sustainable Restaurant Award.

This year, only one US restaurant made the top 50: Atomix, in New York. It came in 11th place, rising one place from 2025, when it ranked 12.

#6292. The Food Trends We’ll See in 2027, According to the World’s 50 Best Chefs

On November 4, Lima, Peru, was a playground for global palates. Star chefs from across the world flocked to the culinary hotspot for the 50 Best Restaurants 2026, a prestigious awards ceremony that crowns the top restaurants around the globe based on anonymous nominations from over a thousand industry experts. Restaurant Asador Etxebarri, which is located in Spain's Basque Country, won top billing as the World’s Best Restaurant 2026 at the event held at the ornate Teatro Municipal de Lima. And before the winners took the stage, we were on the ground as Lima and its top restaurants buzzed with excitement all week.

In addition to knowing which spots came out on top, we also wanted to understand what these results signaled about dining in the year ahead—so we asked chefs for their hot takes. After the plates, tastings, and pisco sours (so many pisco sours), these the top dining trends and places to look for in 2027, according to the world's best chefs.

Read the full list of the 50 Best Restaurants in 2026 here.

Lobster from Kjolle in Lima, which was just named No.7 on the World's 50 Best Restaurants list.

Chef-owner Pía León of Kjolle in Lima—a fine-dining wonder that showcases the megadiversity of the host nation with startlingly beautiful tasting odysseys—snagged the number seven spot this year, making it the top restaurant in the host country. With the global spotlight on her, León looks to the growing importance of knowing specifically where your food comes from, beyond just a vague sense of ‘local.’ “To me, traceability means understanding where each ingredient comes from, who produces it, and the knowledge behind it,” she told Condé Nast Traveler. “Many of the products we work with come from local producers and communities who have kept their techniques alive for many years. As cooks, we have a responsibility to recognize their work and the value of what they grow.”

It’s a feeling that chef and co-owner Josh Niland of Sydney's Saint Peter (which also appeared on our 2025 Hot List of the best new restaurants in the world) emphasizes even further. The restaurant, founded by chef-owner Niland and his wife Julie Niland, focuses on whole-fish cookery and placed at number 50 this year, also earning the title of Best Restaurant in Oceania. “I think it [will be] ridiculous,” he says, if, in 10 years, restaurants are not telling us exactly on paper where things are from. “Like I think it's non-negotiable,” he said. “If you're writing a menu right now, let alone 10 years from now, I want to know why I'm paying $60, $70 for this chicken. Where is it from? That's how I feel about it. You know, we've got QR codes on the menu that you can scan and watch a fisherman pull a fish out of the water. Like, that's probably a very drastic leap, but I feel like that's where, to a degree, the premium end of dining needs to be. We need to be incredibly transparent about our labor, how we're paying people, like where things are from, all that.”

Saint Peter in Sydney came in at No. 50 on the list, and was named the Best Restaurant in Oceania.

At New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen—number eight on the list and also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June—head chef and co-owner Nicolai Nørregaard plays with time, drawing on both seasonal, hyper-local fresh produce, and preserved beauties from seasons past. Kadeau—where the team includes chef Francisco “Pancho” Cardenas supervising the kitchen, and Kyumin Hahn serving as partner—also won the Highest Climber award for jumping from number 41 in 2025 to its placement this year.

La Colombe in Cape Town debuted a Secret Cellar in 2024, an intimate subterranean enclave where guests hand over their phones before the meal begins. While chef James Gaag understands that some people want to take photos of their food—and certainly that Instagram traffic helps restaurants—he hopes for, but isn't counting on, more phone-free restaurant experiences.

So what, exactly, does “seasonality” mean when the seasons seem so different lately? Condé Nast Traveler asked Nørregaard just how climate change is impacting the menu, and what adjustments the team is making: “Some meals are shit,” Nørregaard said, “or some ingredients that we are relying on [are], so we need to change plans. But then maybe something else is in abundance, and then we just switch to that direction.” During Kadeau’s growing season, when it relies on produce from its garden on the Danish island of Bornholm and from what can be foraged nearby, adding more nutrients and water to the soil allows them to step in and give Mother Nature a helping hand, ensuring a better product. During the preservation season, in the colder months, the team showcases products like preserved onion that have been stored since spring and summer—but even that process is changing. Take the pine cone: A dry year might produce very few of the beauties, while a wet year will see abundance. “We sometimes need to think ahead and plan two years in advance,” he continued. “So we have to preserve something for more than one season because it might not come the next season.”

Around the globe, more nimble menus—shifting ingredients, planning well ahead of time—are on the way to account for increasingly unpredictable weather. This is a further expression of adaptations already underway, including a reduced focus on meat, due to its environmental impacts, and broadened waste-reduction efforts. For diners, this means that no two tasting menus, even at the same restaurant, may be exactly the same; that talked-about dish may be swapped out for something else when the seasons or weather requires. But this commitment to the best, and the possibility for newness on menus, presents an arguably more interesting fine dining experience. Each menu, and dish, may represent a singular moment in time.

The Sardine Pie at New Nordic gem Kadeau in Copenhagen, which placed number eight on the list.

Kadeau was also recently awarded three Michelin stars this past June.

Sprawling menus as an indicator of abundance; dozens of items on a single plate—foams, sauces, sprigs of herbs placed with tweezers; narrative-driven tasting menus that span six or seven hours. These used to scream luxury. Now? Simplicity speaks louder. It’s a trend noted by executive chef James Gaag of La Colombe in the Constantia Valley near Cape Town, owned by chef-proprietor Scot Kirton. La Colombe landed at number 35 and also took home the title of Best Restaurant in Africa.

La Colombe in South Africa placed No. 35 on the list.

At La Colombe and elsewhere, Gaag is energized by “less courses, fresher courses, lighter courses, less time at the table.” His innovative menus might be inspired by both his German upbringing and world travels, but that doesn’t mean trying to fit the entire globe in one menu. “We used to put 100 ingredients on each plate, and I think the longer I run the restaurant, the more confident I am in putting less on the plate,” he continued.

Chef Jeremy Chan, who owns Michelin-starred Ikoyi in London with co-founder Iré Hassan-Odukale, continues to rise. Ikoyi landed at number 48 this year, owing to its contemporary global menu that is inspired by both British microseasonality and meticulously sourced global spices. For Chan, though, fine dining doesn’t mean frigid. “Fine dining is about creating a refined experience, rather than a sense of preciousness or formality,” he told Condé Nast Traveler. “For me, it is about the refinement and technique of the craft, alongside the responsibility and precision in what we do to make people feel special.”

Odette, the Singapore restaurant founded by chef Julien Royer, placed at number 15 this year—one of the many high-ranking spots across Asia, including Gaggan in Bangkok (number 2, and also the Best Restaurant in Asia), Wing in Hong Kong (number 5), and the Chairman (number 6), also in Hong Kong. Condé Nast Traveler asked Chef de Cuisine Sheng Xiong—who blends his Asian heritage with French training for Odette’s menus—if there’s a fine dining trend he’d be happy to see vanish. “You mean we’re going to lose our jobs?” He joked. After his laughter subsided, the chef at the Three Michelin-starred restaurant echoed Chan’s sentiments: “I think moving forward, maybe the white-glove service [will go], because in our restaurant we treat everyone coming in like [they are] coming back home as a family member. It can be a bit too casual sometimes, and at the same time, it makes them feel comfortable. Guests are happy. At the start, Singaporeans, the older generation couldn't understand what we are doing, but as time goes by, they actually prefer that to a very stiff kind of environment.”

A Bluefin Tuna Rhubarb dish at London's Ikoyi, which landed at No. 48 on the list this year.

Chef Niko Romito of the lauded, three Michelin-starred Reale—which placed at number 27 this year—is seeing a difference in the way travelers experience his restaurant. Reale, which he co-owns with his sister Cristiana Romito, sits within a 16th-century monastery nestled in a remote medieval town in Abruzzo, Italy. As Niko Romito explained to Condé Nast Traveler, because of Reale’s remote location, tourists would often get there at the tail-end of a food tour of Italy—a tough situation to be in, when perhaps a meal at the end of a trip might feel less memorable after a string of stellar meals. “Today, it’s the exact opposite,” Romito said. “The location—tucked away in the provinces—was once a major limitation. Yet, this very constraint pushed me to create a style of cooking that transcends the distance, making the journey—the hours spent in the car—fully justified. I could say that the region where I live, Abruzzo, is beginning to emerge as a top destination for tourists. A territory rich in nature, parks, and hidden gems.”

At Singapore's Odette, number 15 on the list, Kampot Pepper Crusted Pigeon is served.

Inside Odette, the Singapore restaurant founded by chef Julien Roye

Many restaurants within this year’s list support the growing trend that rurally set tasting menus are sometimes more interesting than their big-city counterparts, luring an increasing number of diners. This year’s number one restaurant and also the Best Restaurant in Europe is Asador Etxebarri, which calls Atxondo, a village of less than 1,500 inhabitants in Spain’s Basque Country, home. Vyn, the number 23 restaurant, is located within a pastoral fishing village of about 7,000 people in southern Sweden. While Naar, number 50 and also the winner for this year’s Sustainable Restaurant Award, sees diners traveling deep into the foothills of the Himalayas for its open-flame-cooked dishes. As food tourism continues to boom, expect even more meteoric restaurants to shine from beyond bustling metropolitan areas.

#6291. How Boeing Losing To Lockheed's C-5 Galaxy Gave The World The 747

Chris earned a Master’s degree in Defense and Strategic Studies (Highest Honors) from the University of Texas at El Paso.

His graduate work concentrated on Global and National Security, Low-Intensity Conflict, Modern Warfare, and US grand strategy. He also undertook extensive regional studies, analyzing how key regions integrate into the broader US security architecture.

This rigorous program provided him with a comprehensive understanding of U.S. military operations, global strategy, and weapons systems. Additionally, he gained a strong appreciation for great power competition.—an increasingly central force shaping international relations and conflict for the foreseeable future.

Born in an era of Cold War competition and growing military airlift needs, the Boeing 747 became one of the most recognizable and influential aircraft in aviation history. Since entering commercial service in 1970, the jumbo jet has transformed passenger and cargo transport worldwide.

Spanning five generations, the 747 evolved alongside the aviation industry, culminating in the technologically advanced 747-8. Yet, its arrival coincided with a shift toward smaller, more fuel-efficient twin-engine aircraft, signaling the beginning of the end for the iconic four-engine airliner.

As a doctrine, Flexible Response was initiated by the Kennedy administration to confront the challenges posed by the Soviet Union on various fronts. As opposed to the doctrine of Massive Retaliation, which relied heavily on the threat of massive nuclear counterstrikes, Flexible Response, introduced in 1961, provided the president with enhanced options when confronting a crisis, ranging from greater nonmilitary to military responses. These options included diplomatic, political, and economic measures, as well as strengthening the military's ability to respond quickly wherever Soviet pressure emerged.

Regarded as the architect of Flexible Response, General Maxwell Taylor advocated for five central pillars concerning the military aspect of the new doctrine. According to the US Army War College Quarterly, Parameters, the second pillar called for the military to be revitalized to conduct warfare at levels below general or all-out war. The third pillar emphasized the need for a continental US-based, active-duty force in a high state of readiness. These personnel would be ready at a moment's notice for rapid deployment overseas to support forward-operating US military forces or allies.

Crucially, for the development of what would become the 747 was the fourth pillar, which highlighted the need to "...modernize and increase the size of air and sealift forces to provide a major capability for the rapid deployment of the active duty forces in the United States, and for resupply of all committed forces."

Moving the required military personnel to a contested region requires speed. If this were done solely by sea, a critical opportunity to halt a Soviet or Soviet-sponsored force could be missed. To this point, the United States Air Force (USAF) stated that "President John F. Kennedy, in his first defense message to Congress in March 1961, announced the buildup of the airlift forces to support flexible response..."

Following this announcement, President Kennedy endorsed the immediate development of the Cargo Experimental-Heavy Logistics System (CX-HLS) program. The five competitors were Lockheed-Georgia Company, Boeing, Douglas Aircraft Company, General Dynamics, and Martin Marietta.

Some of the best military designs emerged during the Cold War.

The future of providing the USAF and, by extension, the US military with timely logistics and surge capacity in a geographic region under Soviet duress was a major priority. On December 22, 1964, Secretary of Defense Robert S. McNamara announced approval of the plan to develop a new outsized logistics aircraft, moving the CX-HLS competition forward.

By May of that year, proposals for the aircraft had been received from the competing companies. After a down-select, Boeing, Douglas, and Lockheed Martin each received one-year study contracts for their airframe designs, while General Electric and Pratt & Whitney received contracts for engine development.

According to a December 1964 issue of Boeing Magazine, the company said competitive subcontracting for the project could total more than $1 billion (£745.7 million), equivalent to about $10.87 billion (£8.1 billion) today. Furthermore, the magazine explained, "The airplane could be the largest ever built. More than 11,000 suppliers in the United States and Canada will participate in the program if Boeing wins the contract."

The Journal of Aircraft and Spacecraft Technology summarized the competition.

"The Air Force considered Boeing's design better than the Lockheed design, although Lockheed's proposal was the lowest total cost bid. Lockheed was selected the winner in September 1965, then awarded a contract in December 1965. General Electric's engine design was selected in August 1965 for the new transport..."

On December 17, 1969, the first C-5A Galaxy was delivered to the 443d Military Airlift Wing, located at Altus Air Force Base, Oklahoma. Today, the USAF maintains a fleet of 52 C-5s. The aircraft has a maximum payload of 281,001 lb (127,460 kg) and an unrefueled range of 5,524 statute miles (8,890 km), according to the USAF. The aircraft would remain a mainstay of America's strategic airlift capability until the Lockheed Martin C-17 entered service in 1995.

The story behind America's flying colossus.

Although Boeing suffered a stinging loss in its bid for the major Air Force contract, the company bounced back at a critical juncture in commercial aviation. According to R. A. Davis, a former Chief Project Engineer for the Boeing 747, "Revenue passenger-miles (less than 50 billion in 1955) had more than tripled by 1965 on a rapidly rising trend. Air travel was forecast to reach at least 500 billion passenger-miles by the mid-1970s, and almost a tenfold increase in air cargo was predicted for the same period."

Furthermore, at the time, passenger traffic was expected to approximately double every five years. With airports already congested, adding more aircraft to accommodate traffic growth would only compound the problem.

Elaborating on this issue, Davis explained that if the congestion problem went unresolved, "By 1975, about 20 million departures of 707-sized aircraft would have to be scheduled each year to meet the predicted world demand. By contrast, if airplanes of 350-400 passenger capability were phased into the long-haul routes, it was estimated that annual departures could be reduced to about 12 million." Clearly, manufacturing larger aircraft appeared to be a promising way forward.

Tony Douglas of startup Riyadh Air says paper boarding passes will not even be an option with the airline.

Taking on the challenge, in 1965, Boeing tasked its Chief Engineer, Joe Sutter — widely known as the Father of the 747 — with reviewing the aircraft's design and reconfiguring it for commercial use. In doing so, the Northwest Airlines History Center states that the "...rear ramp and high wing were traded for a conventional layout, but the option for nose loading was retained — pushing the cockpit above the main deck and creating the distinctive “hump” and upper-deck cabin."

Incredibly, the aircraft went from the drawing board to a completed aircraft in a remarkably short period. In a piece by Airline Reporter, Mr. Sutter stated that "...Pan Am placed its first order in 1966, and we rolled out the first aircraft in 1968, with the first flight in 1969, followed by entry into service in early 1970.” During its first year of service, the 747-100 ushered in a new era of wide-body transportation. Within that short period of time, Mr. Davis stated that the 747 fleet carried over 7 million passengers, demonstrating the aircraft's immediate demand and success as a trusted passenger carrier.

Nearly 15 years after entering service, Davis stated that the 747 fleet expanded to more than 670 airframes. Together, these aircraft had flown more than 19 million revenue hours, traveled over 9.5 billion miles, and transported more than 670 million passengers. Furthermore, by around 1986, Boeing was preparing to continue its remarkable commercial success with the introduction of the 747-400. At the time, the aircraft was expected to deliver greater range, improved fuel economy, and lower operating costs, with projected fuel consumption reductions of 11 to 15%.

The impact of the 737-300, and how the 737's role within Boeing'slineup and the market evolved.

Spanning five generations and 25 manufactured variants, the 747 has been flying domestic and international routes for 56 years, an incredible run. The final passenger model in this iconic aircraft family is the 747-8i, which is optimized for comfortable passenger travel; it entered commercial service on June 1, 2012.

Boeing says the 48-aircraft variant can accommodate a total of 467 passengers. The upper deck can seat 50 Business Class passengers, while First Class accommodates 24 passengers on the main deck, alongside a second Business Class section with seating for 37. The large Economy Class section seats 356 passengers. The 747-8i can also accommodate up to 38 LD-1 cargo containers across its lower-deck cargo holds.

The 747-8i also incorporates several significant technological improvements over the 747-400. Its fuselage was extended by 18.3 feet, adding passenger capacity, while a redesigned wing, improved aerodynamics, and four General Electric GEnx-2B engines improved fuel efficiency and performance. The aircraft also featured a more modern passenger cabin, with larger windows, LED lighting, and an updated interior design. Despite retaining the distinctive appearance and four-engine configuration of its predecessors, the 747-8i represented the most technologically advanced passenger version of the iconic jumbo jet.

Lufthansa was the first airline to purchase the 747-8i and ultimately operated 19 of the aircraft, making it the largest operator of the passenger variant worldwide. Korean Air and Air China also acquired smaller numbers. While the 747-8i was an incredible aircraft, it entered the market as airlines increasingly turned toward smaller, twin-engine aircraft offering greater fuel efficiency and range, such as the Boeing 777. These aircraft could operate many of the same routes without requiring airlines to fill more than 400 seats to make each flight profitable.

The MAX 8-200 is a special edition of the MAX 8 developed for ultra-low-cost carriers that seek to maximize the workhorse's seating capacity.

From its origins in an era of Cold War strategic competition to its role in transforming global aviation, the 747 has enjoyed an extraordinary legacy. The aircraft helped redefine long-haul passenger travel, expanded the possibilities of commercial air cargo, and demonstrated the advantages of moving more people and freight in a single flight.

Although changing economics and advances in twin-engine aircraft ultimately ended production, the 747 remains an enduring symbol of engineering ambition. Its influence on commercial aviation, military logistics, and aircraft design ensures that the Queen of the Skies will remain an important part of aviation history.

One of my favorite things about World of Hyatt points is how much flexibility they offer. You could redeem just a few thousand points for a night at a Category 1 Hyatt hotel or use a larger stash to book a higher-category hotel or all-inclusive resort.

Since Hyatt still uses award charts for most of its properties, you can sometimes get outsize value by redeeming points when cash rates are high. But free nights aren't the only way to use your points. From room upgrades and dining experiences to airline miles and rental cars, here's how you can redeem World of Hyatt points, including which options offer the best value.

The best way to redeem Hyatt points is usually for free hotel nights. Hyatt has award charts for most free night awards, though some are dynamically priced. There are also ways to combine points with cash and free night certificates.

Hyatt publishes award charts for free night awards at Hyatt hotels and resorts, participating resorts within the Hyatt Inclusive Collection brands and Miraval resorts. Each of these charts has five award pricing tiers — Lowest, Low, Moderate, Upper and Top — for each category.

Here's the award chart for standard room award nights at Hyatt hotels and resorts.

Hyatt publishes separate award charts for Hyatt Inclusive Collection brands and Miraval resorts, as well as for club rooms, standard suites and premium suites. Check out our guide to the Hyatt award charts for all the charts.

You can click on "Points Calendar" on the results page for any particular property when searching for award stays to see how many points each night costs.

However, free night awards at Mr & Mrs Smith hotels and Homes & Hideaways by World of Hyatt are priced dynamically based on paid rates. For example, this night at a Homes & Hideaways property in Florida would cost 16,011 points or $192.13. This means you'd get 1.2 cents per point when redeeming Hyatt points for this night.

And this night at a Mr & Mrs Smith property in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, would cost 8,750 points or $58.91. This means you'd only get 0.67 cents per point when redeeming Hyatt points for this night.

TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Hyatt points at 1.65 cents each. As such, you'll generally want to get at least this much value when redeeming your Hyatt points.

Related: Best Hyatt hotels in the world to book with points

You can also book Points + Cash rates for some stays. When these rates are available for your chosen room type and property, you'll redeem 50% of the points required for a free night and get 50% to 70% off the standard rate (which may be higher than the best available rate).

For example, I could redeem 12,000 points, book a Points + Cash rate of 6,000 points plus $156.50 or book a paid rate of $220.16 for this night at the Hyatt Centric Rittenhouse Square Philadelphia.

When redeeming points, I'd get 1.83 cents per point. And when booking a Points + Cash rate, I'd get 1.06 cents per point.

Related: Which credit card should you use for Hyatt stays?

You can also combine Hyatt points with paid nights and even free night certificates when booking with the Hyatt Pay My Way feature. To use this feature, sign in to your Hyatt account, search for a paid stay, click on the property and room type of your choice and then click on rates until you see one with a Pay My Way option.

Click on the Pay My Way box, and then you can choose whether to use points, cash, Points + Cash or free night certificates for each night.

I often use Pay My Way when redeeming free night certificates, as this lets me book a multinight stay even if I only have one free night certificate. I've also used Pay My Way to redeem points for a stay with one particularly expensive night.

Related: The best Hyatt Category 4 hotels to maximize your free night award certificates

You can redeem points to upgrade eligible paid stays at many Hyatt hotels and resorts. Here's a look at the upgrade rate per night:

You can sometimes redeem points for an upgrade at the time of booking. In the following example, you could redeem 9,500 points for a premium suite free night, 4,750 points plus $158 for a premium suite Points + Cash booking or 9,000 points plus $152 to upgrade a paid night to a premium suite.

If you don't upgrade at the time of booking, you can call (800) 544-9288 in the U.S. and Canada or contact a Global Care Center to see if your existing stay is eligible for an upgrade with points.

Related: Your ultimate guide to Hyatt hotel brands

You can redeem Hyatt points for dining and spa experiences at participating locations even if you aren't spending the night. Plus, you can redeem points during stays at participating locations to pay for in-room movies, parking, transportation and more.

To redeem points, simply request to use Hyatt points at checkout and choose how many points to redeem. You should be able to redeem points at participating locations based on the following chart:

As you can see, the redemption rate you'll get ranges from 1 to 1.54 cents per point, which is below TPG's November 2026 valuation of 1.65 cents per point for Hyatt points. As such, you'll usually want to find higher-value ways to redeem your Hyatt points.

You can redeem Hyatt points for Find experiences. For example, you could pay $60 plus taxes or redeem 4,286 points for this one-hour aerial yoga and meditation class.

Or, you could redeem 5,357 points or pay $75 plus taxes for an e-bike tour of San Diego.

It's worth taking a look at Find experiences, especially if you select Find experience credits as Hyatt Milestone Rewards. But you usually won't get outsize value when redeeming points for these experiences.

Related: Why bidding on a Hyatt Find experience auction might be the most valuable way to redeem your World of Hyatt points

You can convert Hyatt points into airline miles with the following programs:

For most of the airline programs, you'll get 1 mile for every 2.5 Hyatt points you convert. However, Hyatt uses different conversion rates for Aeromexico Rewards, Air China PhoenixMiles, China Eastern Miles, Qantas Frequent Flyer, Southwest Rapid Rewards and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

You must convert at least 5,000 points at a time but can convert additional points in increments of 1,250. If you convert 50,000 points or more, you'll usually get an extra 5,000 bonus miles.

However, converting Hyatt points to airline miles will rarely make sense. Conversions can take six to eight weeks. Plus, at the usual 2.5:1 conversion ratio, transferring 5,000 Hyatt points yields 2,000 airline miles. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, you'd be giving up approximately $82.50 in Hyatt points for those 2,000 miles.

You can redeem Hyatt points for Avis free day awards, which are valid at participating locations in the U.S. and Canada, by calling (800) 544-9288. When available, you can redeem 6,000 points per day for an intermediate-size car. However, there are blackout periods that you'll see on the redemption certificate once you redeem your points. Avis free day awards usually expire one year after they're issued.

World of Hyatt members can redeem points for an Aeroplan flight reward certificate valid on Air Canada flights. The 30,000-point certificate costs 50,000 Hyatt points, and you can apply it toward the base fare in points of an Aeroplan flight reward.

Given that TPG's November 2026 valuations peg Hyatt points at 1.65 cents each and Aeroplan points at 1.45 cents each, this won't be a good-value redemption for most travelers. However, if you were planning to convert Hyatt points to Aeroplan points, the flight reward certificate might provide better value.

Related: How to redeem Aeroplan points for maximum value

World of Hyatt and American Airlines AAdvantage are winding down their partnership. But eligible Explorist and Globalist members can redeem Hyatt points for AAdvantage Status for a Day until 1 a.m. EST on Nov. 16.

You can redeem 5,000 Hyatt points to get AAdvantage Gold status for a day, 8,000 points to get AAdvantage Platinum status for a day and 12,000 points to get AAdvantage Platinum Pro status for a day.

However, you can only use these awards on your own travel itineraries, and some fares aren't eligible.

Related: Why I rely on credit cards to earn American Airlines elite status

Finally, you can redeem Hyatt points for a future meeting credit to use for meetings and catered events at participating Hyatt hotels and resorts based on the following chart:

As you can see, the redemption rate is 1.33 cents per point regardless of how many points you redeem toward a future meeting credit. You must call a Hyatt Global Care Center to redeem points for a future meeting credit. You can't use future meeting credits at Hyatt Vacation Club, Bahia Principe and Destination by Hyatt Residences locations.

Redeeming World of Hyatt points for free nights is usually the best way to get good value from your points. I particularly like redeeming Hyatt points at hotels where cash rates are high, as I can often get outsize value. But I'll also redeem points on stays with resort fees, as Hyatt waives resort fees on free night awards.

Other redemption options, including room upgrades, Find experiences and airline miles, can make sense in certain situations. But I generally recommend saving your Hyatt points for free night awards, especially if you can be flexible about where and when you stay.

#6289. Ask a Local: Where to Go in Nairobi According to Runner Emily Chepkor

"Nairobi is a city best understood in motion," says Emily Chepkor, founder of We Run Nairobi, the city's biggest and most popular run club. She's from a small town in Kenya, Kapsabet, that has produced more world-class runners per square mile than anywhere else on earth. While the country is known worldwide for its running heritage, Nairobi hadn't quite caught up to the hype until Chepkor came along.

She runs as a hobby, and is a 12-time marathoner (and two-time Boston qualifier) who felt that, though Kenya's running reputation was unmatched internationally, the runner lifestyle itself wasn't accessible to everyday Kenyans—elite athletes only. She set out to change that and bring running closer to all Nairobians, starting with a weekly run club that began with just her and three friends. It slowly grew through word of mouth and especially TikTok, into something bigger, built on a simple idea: no registration, no fees, you just show up and run alongside Emily.

That run has become a defining weekly ritual for Nairobians, drawing over 1,200 people every Saturday morning. It's now etched into the city's identity. The same way New York is known for its bagels, Nairobi is known for the We Run Nairobi neighborhood runs, a cultural landmark for locals and tourists alike.

Below, Emily tells us about some of her favorite things to do in the city she calls home.

Karura Forest is “without a doubt” the best place to run in Nairobi, if you ask Emily.

"Karura Forest, without a doubt, is the most scenic route in the city”, she says. “I run the Sigiria side, through Gate F; it's quieter, more canopied. My dog Biscuit and I do the 10-kilometer loop most Sundays, crossing little rivers every kilometer. If you want something gentler, the 5-kilometer route is just as lovely." Her Saturday club runs the same way: "We're completely pace-agnostic. First-timers run next to marathoners".

Karura is the second largest urban forest in the world after the Tijuca Forest in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, and provides the perfect place for an outdoor run.

“Kengele's is always a safe bet whatever's on, whether it's World Cup, rugby, athletics, you'll find a good crowd," says Chepkor. "What I love is how the embassies get involved: around big sporting events, they'll partner with venues across the city to host public watch parties. I'll never forget the British High Commission's watch party in Karura Forest, the day Sebastian Sawe broke the two-hour marathon barrier. The whole country was locked in, and experiencing that moment surrounded by hundreds of people felt incredibly special.”

The McMillan Memorial Library is one of her favorite places for some peace and quiet, and some history.

“The McMillan Memorial Library is a perfect little time capsule of Nairobi, architecturally and literally—it's currently being renovated by Book Bunk, founded by two Kenyan women committed to restoring our public libraries," she says. "I also love the Nairobi Gallery, home to Point Zero, the spot from which all distances in Kenya are measured.”

“Tigoni is a small town only 30 to 40 minutes from Nairobi, but it feels much farther away. The city gives way to rolling tea plantations and narrow country roads. I start at Brackenhurst with coffee from Muna Tree Cafe on the terrace, then rent a bicycle and ride through the plantations, stopping wherever the view is too good to pass.” Back at Brackenhurst, she'll spread a blanket on the lawn to read, maybe doze off, then finish with tennis or a walk through the Indigenous forest. "It's the itinerary I'm proudest to take an out-of-towner on," Chepkor says.

"Sigiria Coffee House is my default—small, intimate, and full of dogs on Sunday mornings. On tennis mornings it's Waitabit, same easy vibe." For souvenirs, she sends visitors to two spots near each other: "Spinners Web has beautiful rugs, a café, and a used-books library. Just up the road, Tribal Gallery has grander pieces—restored Swahili doors, oversized mirrors—alongside smaller suitcase-friendly finds like ceramics and jewelry."

"Fig & Olive in Tigoni is part bodega, part restaurant, with a lawn where no one blinks if you swap your chair for the grass. In the city, it's the Tin Roof Café in Karen—moving from table to grass and back, especially post-run, and the salad bar is iconic. For something dressier that still softens outdoors, Matteo's: white tablecloths, al fresco seating, and little intimate corners I'm still discovering."

The Talisman Restaurant is a Nairobi stalwart.

Scoring a place by the fireplace is a coup.

"The Talisman Restaurant is a Nairobi stalwart. Scoring a corner table by the fireplace on a chilly evening is a date-night dream. For something more stylish, Inti has skyline views in every direction—some Friday nights it turns into an intimate DJ set." For the rest of the evening, she splits the city in two: “If you're after energy, Geco, alive with Nairobi's music scene, especially on Wednesdays. For actual conversation, Cave-à-Manger has an expansive wine list and keeps the music in the background.”

"Toi Market, with one caveat: Nairobi isn't really a vintage city in the curated, boutique sense— we're much more of an open-air, flea market vibe, with thousands of stalls. Toi is sprawling, busy, and a little chaotic. You'll need patience and a willingness to dig, but if you put in the time, you'll almost always come away with something great for a fraction of what you'd pay elsewhere."

“Nai Nami is properly off the beaten track; it's a walking tour of Nairobi's CBD led by former street children. You see downtown Nairobi through the eyes of people who know it intimately, and leave with a completely different understanding of the city. The Alliance Française is an unexpected answer, but it's one of Nairobi's great cultural hubs—plays, concerts, exhibitions, most of which are free, and the original stomping ground of Sauti Sol, our biggest boy band.”

A view of the city from Nairobi National Park

"Nairobi is the only city in the world with a national park so if you’ve only got one day, make it a wildlife day. I’d go for a game drive through Nairobi National Park at sunrise, then the elephant feeding at Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, and the Giraffe Centre to finish. Afterwards, a slow lunch nearby at either Cultiva, Talisman, or Matteo's. "

"I'd highly recommend coming to a We Run Nairobi Saturday. One of my favorite traditions is that we 'brand' every first-timer with a little sticker, so everyone knows it's your first Saturday. I'll encourage people to say hello, ask where you're visiting from, and recommend a coffee spot. You're moving together with actual Nairobians, in neighborhoods where we actually live. You're not being shown the city, you get to experience it alongside the people who call it home.”

#6288. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

#6287. The Parking Spot Promo Code: Save 10%

As a New Yorker without a car, I don’t often put much thought into airport parking. However, a few years ago, my mom texted me raving about The Parking Spot, a service available near Connecticut's Bradley International Airport that allows you to park your car near (but not directly at) the airport in a secure lot, then shuttle over to the terminal. She effusively recommended the process for its ease and convenience, and has continued to rave about it since. Its reach extends far beyond Bradley—with more than 70 locations at 45+ airports, it’s a service that’s available across the US for fliers looking to reduce some of the hassle that comes with travel.

Here’s how it works: You can reserve a spot ahead of time on the company’s website or app, securing your place to park and sorting out the cost up front. Once you arrive at the airport and park your car (avoiding the dreaded terminal traffic), you’ll hop in the bright yellow, polka dot-covered shuttle (whimsical!) and head over. While you’re traveling, you can get your car washed or detailed if you so wish, a nice added value. Then, when you return, you can track the shuttle in real-time using the app to get back to your car quickly.

If all of that sounds appealing—or you’re a regular to the service and are just looking for the latest promo codes—read on for ways to save on your next booking.

(Looking to rent a car instead? Take a look at active promo codes for Budget, Avis, and Hertz first.)

Fall is a great time to squeeze in a long weekend getaway—or even a full week to yourself, if you've got the PTO days to spare—ahead of the holiday busyness. If you're headed off on a trip, know that for reservations that begin by November 15, you can save 10% or more on your airport parking with promo code FALL10.

An easy way to score The Parking Spot discounts: Sign up for the company's mailing list. New users will automatically receive 10% off their first reservation. You’ll also gain access to 10–20% off promo codes on parking reservations for select cities—right now, that includes Austin, Denver, Columbus, Houston, and Salt Lake City.

Like many brands, The Parking Spot offers a military discount for active duty military and veterans. A less common, though fitting, discount is available for airline crew members. Both groups can get 25% off a reservation with a Spot Club account. As for the fine print, discounts don’t apply to Basic parking reservations and can’t be combined with other offers. Airline crew will need to submit a photo of their work badge; similarly, proof of military affiliation must be submitted to receive the discount.

If a Parking Spot promo code isn’t working at checkout, there are a few things you can do to troubleshoot. First double-check the basics—typos, extra spaces, or incorrect capitalization can all prevent a code from working correctly. You'll also want to confirm that the code is still valid, as expiration dates and location exclusions may apply.

#6286. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite program. We want to ensure we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; even at the new rate, no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

#6285. Qantas Reaches Deal to Sell 44 Boeing 737s

Qantas has agreed to sell 44 Boeing 737-800s to British aviation aftermarket specialist AerFin as the Australian carrier prepares to retire most of its 737 fleet.

The deal includes the aircraft’s 88 CFM56-7B engines. AerFin said Wednesday it expects to receive the first jet before the end of 2026, with the rest transferring over the next seven years as Qantas retires them.

Qantas Domestic CEO Markus Svensson said the agreement gives the airline “flexibility to adjust the timing as new aircraft arrive,” in a news release.

Qantas operates nearly 80 Boeing 737-800s, according to data from planespotters.net. The carrier ordered 28 Airbus A321XLRs in 2022 to begin replacing the Boeing jets and later ordered another 20. Seven A321XLRs have joined the fleet, with 41 still on order.

AerFin, which supplies parts and engines to airlines and maintenance providers, said the acquisition is the largest in its history. The company said the deal would help it supply aircraft and engine parts to customers worldwide.
