The Star Alliance carrier's extensive US domestic network helps support these long-haul services by connecting passengers from cities across the country to its international gateways. San Francisco offers convenient access for West Coast travelers, while Los Angeles provides another major departure point and Houston expands the network into Texas. The airline's San Francisco to Adelaide Airport (ADL) connection is particularly noteworthy because it extends the available Australian destination choices beyond the country's more established eastern gateways.

It is the largest unserved market between Australia & the US. Find out more here!

Los Angeles to Sydney stands out as one of the defining routes in the US to Australia market, with American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Qantas, and United Airlines all represented. Their individual schedules show 365, 418, 353, and 362 flights, respectively, giving a combined total of 1,498 flights across these four carriers in 2026. Delta Air Lines records the highest individual flight count, although all four airlines contribute substantial capacity. The route's importance reflects the strong connections between Southern California and Australia's largest city, supported by tourism, business travel, education, and visiting friends and relatives.

Los Angeles is also a major connecting hub for passengers arriving from elsewhere in the US, while Sydney offers onward connections to destinations throughout Australia and the wider region. The combination makes the route attractive to both travelers beginning their journeys in either city and those connecting through the respective airline networks. Competition between four major carriers gives passengers a broader choice of schedules, loyalty programs, onboard products, and connecting itineraries.

A total of 110,960 seats are due to be operated by American Airlines throughout the year, with 114,981 by Delta Air Lines, 170,458 by Qantas, and 93,034 by United Airlines on their respective Los Angeles to Sydney services. These figures should be read alongside the flight counts, since aircraft capacity and scheduling patterns can influence the number of seats available. The four airlines operate a mix of Boeing 787-9, Airbus A350-900, and Airbus A380 aircraft on this route, and collectively, the services underline the route's central position in transpacific aviation.

United Airlines' San Francisco to Adelaide connection is a noteworthy addition to the range of routes linking the US with Australia, as Adelaide has traditionally received less direct transpacific service than Sydney or Melbourne. The carrier will operate a total of 44 flights and 11,308 seats on this route throughout 2026. Although considerably smaller than the established Los Angeles - Sydney operation, the service offers a direct link to South Australia rather than requiring passengers to arrive at another Australian city first. Adelaide provides access to a different side of Australia, with attractions including its central market, nearby wine regions, coastal scenery, and cultural festivals. The city is also an important gateway for visitors exploring South Australia, including the Barossa Valley and the Fleurieu Peninsula. For US travelers, a nonstop connection can also reduce the need for an additional domestic flight within Australia, although recent reports suggest the services are far from full, leading to a reduction in flights for the rest of 2026.

This route broadens United Airlines' Australian network by adding another destination beyond the country's largest eastern cities. Its relatively limited capacity suggests a smaller operation than the airline's established Sydney and Melbourne services, but the connection provides another option for travelers with business, family, or leisure interests in South Australia. The route's longer-term significance will depend on passenger demand, operating frequency, and how effectively United Airlines connects Adelaide with its wider US network.

#6264. Amex Gold Card Review: Benefits & Points For Those Who Like To Eat

The American Express® Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there if you’re looking to earn Amex Membership Rewards points.

The Amex Gold Card is an absolute powerhouse if you spend a lot on food, whether it’s at restaurants or supermarkets (or a combination of both). While the card has a somewhat steep annual fee, the good news is that it offers credits that can largely help offset it. We’re also currently seeing an exceptional welcome offer, making it the ideal time to pick up this card. Anyway, enough of an intro, let’s get into my in-depth Amex Gold Card review.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Gold Card

Before I get into my full Amex Gold Card review, let me summarize some of the most important features:

Here are my thoughts on the major pros and cons of the Amex Gold Card:

For someone looking to earn Membership Rewards points, the Amex Gold Card is one of the most rewarding cards out there. To start, let’s take a look at the welcome offer on the card, along with the eligibility requirements and fees. After all, these are important factors people consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Gold Card has an improved welcome offer: You may be eligible for as high as 100,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $8,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

The way this works, you can apply for the card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard credit pull unless you accept the offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each. So if you are eligible for a bonus of 100,000 points, those are worth $1,700, by my valuation.

This is a huge bonus, and on top of that, you have a full six months to complete the minimum spending requirement, which should be easy enough for many people to accomplish, as that translates to roughly $1,333 per month in required spending. Personally I’d only apply for the card if I got a welcome offer of at least 60,000 points (or ideally 80,000 points), but everyone has to decide for themselves what they’re willing to “settle” for.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Gold Card isn’t available to those who have or have had the card, or those who have had the Premier Rewards Gold Card in the past. Furthermore, those who have or have had an American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) may also not be eligible for the welcome offer on the card.

However, if you have had one of these cards before, you’re still eligible for the card, but you’re just not eligible for the welcome offer (which is “once in a lifetime”). In some circumstances, it could still be worth getting the card in those situations, if you’d benefit from it on an ongoing basis.

Let me emphasize that you’ll want to apply for the Amex Gold before you apply for the Amex Platinum. That’s because if you have the Amex Gold, you’re still eligible for the Amex Platinum offer, while the inverse isn’t true.

See this post for all the rules on applying for Amex cards, and see this post for details on getting approved for the Amex Gold Card.

The Amex Gold Card has a $325 annual fee. There is no annual fee for up to five additional cards. Meanwhile, the annual fee for six or more additional cards is $35 for each card (Rates & Fees).

Note that Amex Gold Card authorized users don’t receive some of the same benefits as the primary cardmember, but their spending does count toward the rewards that the primary cardmember earns.

The Amex Gold Card has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees), so you can use it for purchases globally. That’s especially useful when you consider that you can earn 4x points on dining abroad, all with no foreign transaction fees.

What makes the Amex Gold Card so valuable is the bonus categories it offers, in the form of Membership Rewards points. The bonus categories include the following:

This is an outstanding return on spending. Based on my valuation of Amex points at 1.7 cents each, that’s like an 8.5% return on eligible prepaid hotel stays, a 6.8% return at restaurants and at U.S. supermarkets, and a 5.1% return on eligible flights.

Now let’s take a closer look at just how those bonus categories are defined.

The Amex Gold Card offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

With the Amex Gold Card you’ll earn 4x points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year at restaurants worldwide, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar spent.

Generally speaking, restaurants are defined pretty broadly, and the category includes everything from fast food to cafes to fine dining. This even includes delivery and takeout, given the popularity of that nowadays.

Just note that convenience stores, nightclubs, and restaurants located within other establishments won’t typically qualify for bonus points. Furthermore, eligibility for bonus points is determined based on how the merchant chooses to be categorized. There’s a chance that some merchants may not be categorized as a restaurant, even though you might consider them a restaurant.

For dining, this card even beats the 3x points that the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) offer — this is one of the best rewards cards for dining purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 4x points on the first $25,000 spent every calendar year at U.S. supermarkets, and after that you’ll earn a single point per dollar. This excludes superstores and warehouse clubs, so don’t expect you’ll be able to earn those bonus points at Sam’s Club, for example. This is one of the best rewards cards for grocery store purchases.

The Amex Gold Card offers 3x points on airfare, with no limits on how many bonus points you can earn. This only applies when booking directly with an airline, through the Amex Travel App™ or through amextravel.com. Furthermore, charter flights and private jet flights are excluded.

Officially, booking through online travel agencies (except Amex Travel) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice, it may still sometimes code for 3x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them. This is one of the best rewards cards for airfare purchases.

The Amex Gold Card also offers 2x points on prepaid car rentals and cruises booked through Amex Travel. This bonus category doesn’t make or break the card, but it’s a nice extra, especially if you already make these bookings occasionally.

The Amex Gold Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to about 20 partners, consisting primarily of airline loyalty programs, but also of some hotel loyalty programs.

The reason this represents such a good deal is that you can get outsized value toward first and business class travel. These tickets are often disproportionately expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal on points. On top of that, Amex often has transfer bonuses, which can stretch your points even further.

While you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than 1.0 cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

In general, I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Gold Card offers a variety of benefits that can help offset the annual fee of the card. In particular, the Amex Gold offers statement credits for eligible purchases, which could save you up to $424 per year, more than offsetting the annual fee. Let’s take a closer look at how these work (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

The first perk is that the Amex Gold Card offers a dining credit of up to $120 per year. There are some restrictions to be aware of with this credit:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually:

This is a fantastic benefit and should be worth face value for anyone who uses Uber at least once a month. Even if you don’t use Uber, this can be useful for getting food delivery through Uber Eats.

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $100 in Resy credits annually:

The Amex Gold Card offers up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually:

One thing I’d mention is that anecdotally this also works for Dunkin’ reloads, so you can always get the Dunkin’ app, and then load $7 onto your account each month, and that should trigger the credit. That’s a great way to use this to “bank” credit with Dunkin’ toward a future purchase.

One of the great features of Amex cards is access to Amex Offers, which offers savings or bonus points on purchases with all kinds of retailers. There’s huge value to be had in getting as many Amex cards as possible, so that you can get these offers on multiple cards. Amex Offers could save you hundreds of dollars per year — just note that enrollment is required to take advantage of individual offers.

For staying two or more nights at select luxury hotels, you can receive extra benefits through The Hotel Collection. Benefits include a $100 hotel credit and a room upgrade, if available. This is different than Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, which requires having the Amex Platinum Card.

Holding the Amex Gold Card entitles you to a complimentary upgrade to Hertz Five Star status (enrollment required). This gets you an upgrade to a higher car class on rentals when available as well as a 25% bonus on all Hertz rentals. If you already rent cars through Hertz, this is a nice extra. It’s one of the more recently added benefits on the Amex Gold Card, too, since it was introduced in celebration of the card’s 60th anniversary.

The Amex Gold Card comes with a handful of travel insurance benefits that can protect your trip when you pay with your card. Check the card’s benefits guide for exact exclusions and limits, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $300 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 12 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The Amex Gold Card is a great card for anyone who spends a lot of money on food (whether at restaurants or supermarkets), and who is looking to earn Membership Rewards points. Furthermore, the card potentially offers over $400 in annual credits, between the dining credit, Resy credit, Dunkin’ credit, and Uber Cash.

I’d argue that if you value earning Membership Rewards points, if you spend a lot on dining, and if you can use a decent number of the card’s credits, then picking up this card is a slam dunk. It’s hard to beat this kind of return on dining and supermarket spending, and it’s a great complement to some other Amex cards.

The great welcome offer that’s available is the icing on the cake, and makes applying for the card all the more tempting. I’d recommend confirming you’re eligible for a welcome bonus on the higher end of the spectrum with the current offer of as high as 100,000 points, especially because you can only get an Amex Gold Card welcome bonus once.

I will say, the Amex Gold Card might not be for you if you don’t spend a lot on dining, if you don’t live in a major city where you can easily use the credits, if you value airport lounge access as a card perk, or if you’d rather earn cash back than travel rewards, since those are all potential considerations with the card.

It’s also worth comparing the Amex Gold Card to other options. Here’s how the Amex Gold Card stacks up against some of the most popular alternatives.

The Amex Platinum Card (learn more) has a higher annual fee than the Amex Gold and comes with many more perks and annual credits. Here are the biggest differences to know about:

If you travel many times a year and want as many benefits as possible, the Amex Platinum Card is hard to beat. That said, the Amex Gold Card still offers a better return on spending when it comes to dining out and shopping at U.S. supermarkets. As I see it, the cards serve different purposes — one is about the perks, and the other is about the return on spending.

If you’re looking for a rewards card with a lower annual fee, the Chase Sapphire Preferred Card (learn more) is worth comparing against the Amex Gold Card as well. It has a much lower annual fee of $95 and fewer perks, but it still earns very strong rewards:

Between the Amex Gold Card and the Chase Sapphire Preferred, the best option for you could come down to whether you prefer Amex Membership Rewards points or Chase Ultimate Rewards points. Make sure to compare your welcome bonus offers between both cards before making a final decision as well.

The Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) is another great rewards card with useful bonus categories at the $95 annual fee level:

If you want just one rewards card in your wallet, the Citi Strata Premier makes a strong case for itself with its bonus categories. I value both Amex points and Citi ThankYou points at 1.7 cents apiece, but some travelers might prefer one rewards program over the other depending on their favorite airline and hotel partners.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is one of my favorite cards for those looking for a simple strategy, and who don’t want to focus on a bunch of credits, maximizing bonus categories, etc.

The card has a $95 annual fee, and offers a minimum of 2x miles per dollar spent, making this one of the best cards for everyday spending. The reasonable annual fee plus the flat 2x miles is ideal for someone who doesn’t maybe spend a huge amount in categories that are otherwise eligible for bonus points.

The Amex Gold Card is one of American Express’ best rewards cards for earning points. With 4x points on dining and supermarkets, earning Membership Rewards points is easy.

The card also offers some credits that are potentially useful, which for many will help offset the annual fee. The card offers up to $120 dining credits, up to $120 in Uber Cash annually, up to $100 in Resy credits annually, and up to $84 in Dunkin’ credits annually — a total of $424 in annual credits if you take advantage of all of them. If you don’t yet have the card, it’s seriously worth considering.

Over the past year, I've redeemed 1.3 million IHG One Rewards points for 62 hotel nights. I got 0.88 cents per point on these redemptions, so while TPG's November 2026 valuations peg the value of IHG points at 0.6 cents each, it's certainly possible to get more value when redeeming IHG points.

All these redemptions mean I also have to earn a sizable amount of IHG points each year. There are many ways to earn IHG points, so you have options, whether you need to top off your account or substantially boost your balance. In this article, I'll describe how to earn IHG points.

As you might expect, you can earn IHG points when you stay at participating IHG hotels. However, the exact number of points you'll earn on stays depends on a few factors:

You'll only earn IHG points and get access to elite benefits when you book a qualifying rate through a qualifying method. Qualifying methods include IHG Customer Care, IHG websites, the IHG One Rewards app, directly at the hotel and through authorized travel agents. Authorized travel agents exclude online travel agents and are defined in the IHG terms and conditions as "travel booking platforms operating under direct distribution agreements with IHG which specifically provide for nights booked through their platforms to be qualifying stays."

Related: The best IHG hotels in the world

Your earning rate for qualifying stays will vary by IHG hotel brand. Specifically, you'll earn points as follows:

You'll generally earn points on qualifying room rates and additional purchases charged to your room, including food and beverages. However, at some properties, you may not earn points on other purchases charged to your room.

Except at InterContinental Alliance Resorts, you can earn points on up to nine hotel rooms. Your IHG One Rewards account number must be associated with each room reservation, and you must stay at the property.

Members with IHG elite status earn additional points on stays. As you'd expect, the higher your elite status tier, the more points you'll earn on your stay. Here's how many bonus points IHG elite members will earn:

Here's an example of how these bonus points can add up. If you're a Diamond Elite member staying at a Kimpton hotel for three nights at $200 per night, you'll earn the following:

As a result, you'd take home 12,000 IHG points from your three-night stay — and potentially more if you made any qualifying charges to your room or paid for your stay with a rewards card. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, 12,000 IHG One Rewards points are worth $72.

You can often buy up to 5,000 elite qualifying points per night when booking a qualifying paid stay. Look for the option on the "Add Extras" page while booking.

There's no cap on the number of points you can buy each calendar year via these packages. As such, doing so can be a good option if you have already reached the maximum number of points you can outright purchase in a calendar year.

Starting at just 20 nights a year, IHG members earn a choice of Milestone Rewards for every 10 nights (up to 100 nights per year). IHG offers its members various rewards at each milestone, and some may be more valuable than points.

But if you're primarily interested in earning IHG points, you can choose points at each milestone. Specifically, you can earn points through Milestone Rewards each calendar year as follows:

I rarely choose points as Milestone Rewards, as I usually find food-and-beverage rewards, confirmable suite upgrade awards or an annual lounge membership provides more value.

IHG One Rewards frequently offers promotions that let you earn additional points on your hotel stays over the standard earning rates. However, you usually need to register for IHG bonus points promotions before completing your stay.

For IHG promotions that offer multipliers (such as double points), the multiplier typically applies only to the stay's base earnings. So, if you are an IHG elite member, your elite bonus usually won't be multiplied.

Related: How to get more out of every all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards

One of the easiest ways to earn IHG points is by spending on a cobranded IHG credit card. Here's how the four currently available IHG credit cards earn points, including their updated earning categories beginning Jan. 1, 2027 (see the paragraph below the table for some additional earning rates that end Dec. 31):

Through Dec. 31, IHG Premier and Business cardholders will also earn 5 points per dollar spent on all other travel, while no-annual-fee IHG cardholders will also earn 3 points per dollar spent on utilities, internet, cable, phone services and select streaming services.

Cardholders of the Premier, Premier Select and Business cards get automatic access to the valuable IHG fourth-night-free reward perk. But cardholders of the no-annual-fee IHG card will need to spend $5,000 or more with their card within a calendar year to unlock access to the fourth-night-free reward perk through the end of the next calendar year starting in 2027. I've used the fourth-night-free reward perk 13 times during the last year, so it provides a ton of value to me.

Related: The best IHG hotel stays you can book with 200,000 points

You can transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points and Bilt Points to the IHG One Rewards program. Points transfer at a 1:1 ratio from both programs.

However, I don't recommend transferring points from either program to IHG. Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, you'd need to redeem IHG points for at least 2.05 cents each to justify transferring Chase points or 2.2 cents each to justify transferring Bilt points.

As such, you'll generally only want to transfer points to IHG if you need to top off your account for a specific award. Otherwise, saving transferable points for higher-value redemptions is generally better.

Related: Why transferable rewards are worth more than airline miles and hotel points

The IHG One Rewards Dine & Earn program allows you to earn points when you dine at participating restaurants and bars. To use the program, you must sign up for an account online and link at least one credit or debit card to your account. Then, you'll automatically earn IHG points when you use a linked card to pay at participating restaurants and bars.

The points you'll earn vary depending on how frequently you use the program and whether you opt in for email notifications. You can earn between 1 and 8 IHG points per dollar spent on eligible purchases. These points are in addition to the rewards earned on your credit card, so consider linking and using one of the best cards for dining purchases.

Related: How to double-, triple- or even quadruple-dip on dining rewards

You can also earn IHG points through the IHG Business Rewards program. This program allows you to earn points when you plan a meeting or event — including a wedding — at select IHG properties.

Once you register for IHG Business Rewards, you can earn 3 points per dollar when you book rooms, meetings and events for others. Qualifying spending includes:

Some properties don't participate in IHG Business Rewards. And you usually can't earn more than 60,000 points on a meeting or event. Plus, qualifying spending usually excludes taxes, gratuities, service fees and the organizer's room.

Another option for earning IHG points is to purchase them. Buying IHG points can be a good deal, especially when the program offers a 100% bonus and you have a high-value redemption in mind.

The standard price to buy IHG points is 1 cent per point if you purchase at least 26,000 points. However, IHG One Rewards offers promotions several times a year during which you can purchase points with up to a 100% bonus. If you buy during a 100% bonus, you can earn IHG points for as little as 0.5 cents each.

TPG values IHG points at 0.6 cents each. Since it's easy for me to get more than 0.5 cents of value per IHG point, I usually consider purchasing IHG points whenever there's a 100% bonus sale. However, you usually can't purchase more than 200,000 IHG points per calendar year.

IHG members can transfer points to another member by paying a $5 fee per 1,000 points transferred. Each member can transfer up to 100,000 points per calendar year and receive up to 500,000 points per calendar year.

IHG members who hold Diamond Elite status — or belong to the IHG Business Rewards program and have "consumed a Business Rewards event in the current or previous calendar year" — can transfer points to other members without paying transfer fees.

So, if you have a colleague or family member who has Diamond Elite status (or is an active member of the IHG Business Rewards program) and wants to transfer IHG points to you, this could be a way to earn IHG points.

Related: Earn even more rewards when dining out with OpenTable

Throughout this guide, we've discussed how to earn IHG points that you can redeem for hotel stays. However, travelers looking to earn IHG elite status should also consider which points qualify for elite status.

Generally, the following activities earn IHG points that are redeemable and elite qualifying:

On the other hand, the following activities usually earn points that are redeemable but not elite qualifying (unless otherwise indicated):

Related: How to maximize award redemptions with the IHG One Rewards program

There are plenty of ways to earn IHG One Rewards points, from staying at IHG hotels and using cobranded credit cards to dining out and booking rental cars. You can also buy points when IHG offers a good promotion.

I frequently get significantly more than TPG's valuation of 0.6 cents per IHG point when redeeming for hotel stays, so I find it worthwhile to keep a decent balance. However, I'd generally avoid transferring valuable Chase Ultimate Rewards points or Bilt points to IHG unless you need to top off your account for a specific redemption.

#6262. Defiant Ritz-Carlton Singapore Joining Marriott Bonvoy… Finally!

The world’s only Ritz-Carlton that doesn’t participate in the Marriott Bonvoy program will finally be joining, which seems long overdue. I can’t imagine the hotel will be particularly generous, but we’ll see!

The 608-key Ritz-Carlton Millenia Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program as of December 1, 2026. So as of that date, Bonvoy members will be able to earn and redeem points, and take advantage of Bonvoy elite perks, when staying at the hotel (admittedly Bonvoy elite perks at Ritz-Carlton properties are fairly limited, as breakfast isn’t a benefit for any elite tier).

As I covered in late 2025, this property is the only Ritz-Carlton in the world that doesn’t participate in the Bonvoy program. The backstory here is that the hotel opened back in 1996, and at the time, Ritz-Carlton didn’t have any sort of a loyalty program that awarded points.

In 2010, the Ritz-Carlton Rewards program started awarding points for hotel stays, as a parallel program to Marriott Rewards. The ability to earn and redeem points came at a cost to individual hotels, but it was intended to boost occupancy and average daily rates.

Initially, hotels had the option of whether they wanted to opt in or out of the program. Most hotels bought into the concept, though the Ritz-Carlton Osaka and Ritz-Carlton Singapore were the two hotels that opted out. The Ritz-Carlton Osaka eventually decided to participate, leaving the Ritz-Carlton Singapore as the only hotel that’s not participating.

Ultimately when the Marriott Bonvoy program formed as the combination of Marriott Rewards and Starwood Preferred Guest, the hotel could still stick to its legacy contract of not having to participate in the program. Clearly the owners of the hotel have now had a change of heart… or something!

Obviously we don’t have any sort of an official explanation for the reason that this Ritz-Carlton property is finally backtracking. I can’t imagine that Marriott gave the owners an ultimatum, given that Marriott is known for letting hotel owners get away with anything, as long as they get paid.

My guess is that the competitive realities just finally caught up with this hotel — Singapore is an increasingly competitive hotel market, this is a massive hotel with 600+ rooms to fill every night, and the hotel is also a bit past its prime.

The truth is that loyalty programs exist for a reason, as they’re a great tool for getting heads into beds. Obviously the hotel will be on the hook for some additional loyalty fees, but I imagine this will make the hotel more appealing to people who otherwise wouldn’t have considered it.

I also have to imagine that even though the hotel did a decent job communicating its lack of participation in Marriott Bonvoy, I still suspect many guests didn’t realize this, and ended up being disappointed.

As of December 1, 2026, the Ritz-Carlton Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program. This is the only Ritz-Carlton hotel in the world that hasn’t participated in Bonvoy, so this is great to see.

The backstory is that the hotel opened before Ritz-Carlton had a loyalty program, and then when a program was finally formed, participation was optional. Literally every other Ritz-Carlton in the world saw value in this… except this one, apparently.

Fortunately they’ve now come to their senses, or something, so it’s great to see that this will be changing.

What do you make of the Ritz-Carlton Singapore joining Bonvoy?

#6261. KLM Plans 1,000 More Job Cuts

KLM expects to eliminate approximately 1,000 positions through productivity improvements as part of a restructuring announced Thursday.

The Dutch carrier said it would seek to limit the impact through natural attrition, voluntary arrangements and transfers. Other changes include moving about 800 ground services positions to outside providers and transferring 2,000 positions to Air France-KLM, including 1,500 at customer contact center Cygnific.

“But KLM’s future is not guaranteed,” CEO Marjan Rintel said in a statement, citing global instability, high fuel prices, and pressure on the industry.

KLM is targeting a structural productivity increase of at least 8% by 2028, alongside restrained wage growth. It said an additional €1 billion in annual earnings improvement is needed to fund investments.

The changes also affect its European fleet. KLM will replace planned Airbus A320s with Embraer E195-E2s, giving regional subsidiary Cityhopper a larger role. The A321neo will remain, while Boeing 737s and Embraer E190s will be phased out.

The announcement came as KLM reported a third-quarter operating profit of €458 million, up from €352 million a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, operating profit reached €526 million on revenue of €10.9 billion.

Despite the improvement, KLM said profitability remains insufficient to support its investment needs. Higher fuel costs and Middle East flight cancellations weighed on its passenger business, while Transavia faced competition and operational challenges.

“We need to increase it to more than 8% to secure a financially healthy future for KLM,” Chief Financial Officer Bas Brouns said of the airline’s profit margin.

#6260. American Airlines Quietly Removes Trump From West Palm Beach Gate Monitors

American Airlines has updated the gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach, and they no longer mention President Trump. This seems like a sensible change (unrelated to politics), and the timing sure is… interesting.

Over the summer, we saw Palm Beach International Airport (PBI) renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport. We knew that Trump wanted an airport named after him, and some conservative politicians in Florida came together to make it happen.

It’s interesting to see how airlines handled this. At the time, American updated its gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach. The monitors initially read “West Palm Beach, FL.” American then updated the monitors to say “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach.” Now JonNYC reports that as of this week, the airport name listed on the monitors has been changed again, and is back to the original name, with no mention of Trump.

so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ? https://t.co/IG2mPA3zgG

JonNYC specifically emphasizes that he’s not claiming there’s any connection between this and the election results, though the timing of it happening this week sure is interesting.

Personally I’m not a fan of airports being named after even semi-controversial figures, and particularly politicians. It’s something I’ve said over and over, regardless of the party affiliation of the person. Unless a city has multiple airports, I think it’s also stupid to identify the airport based on the name rather than the place.

Like, it makes sense to clarify London Heathrow (LHR) vs. London Gatwick (LGW), but it’s not like there are multiple airports in West Palm Beach. For that matter, saying you’re “flying to President Trump” just sounds a little weird, in my opinion.

JonNYC notes that he’s not suggesting that this had anything to do with the recent election, though everything about the timing here is interesting:

American Airlines CEO Robert Isom: "From a commercial aviation perspective, the eyes of the world have been on us, and we've certainly delivered… No doubt, it's a result of the economy and the job market." https://t.co/28JzoEf4Z3 pic.twitter.com/BcgYJbChNz

American Airlines seems to have quietly reversed course on how it refers to West Palm Beach’s airport on its gate monitors. In recent months, the airline has referred to the airport as “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach,” while now it seems to be back to “West Palm Beach, FL.”

This change comes the same week as the midterm elections, though everyone can decide for themselves to what extent these points are related…

What do you make of this American gate monitor change?

#6259. How This Airline Packs 39 Business Class Seats Into A 17-Hour Flight Nobody Talks About

EVA Air's routes from Taipei Taoyuan International Airport (TPE) to John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), lasting 17 hours, make use of the carrier's Boeing 777-300ERs. These aircraft have 38 or 39 of EVA's Royal Laurel business class seats onboard. They are configured in a 1-2-1 reverse herringbone layout, ensuring each passenger has direct access to the aisle.

Most of the long-haul premium aviation industry looks to firms like Singapore Airlines and Qantas. They offer business class seats on routes exceeding 19 hours. Meanwhile, EVA has quietly built a market for routes of almost this length and a higher premium density.

There are three flagship ultra-long-haul routes that make use of the premium-dense 777-300ER. It is also common for these routes to use the Boeing 787-9. The first is from TPE to JFK. This route has a flight time of 17 hours and 15 minutes. Around an hour shorter is the route from TPE to Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ), Canada's largest and busiest aviation hub.

At 15 hours and 30 minutes is the route from TPE to Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD). There are a number of additional destinations that EVA flies its premium dense 777-300ERs to, all of which are in North America. Examples in the US include Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH), and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

The latter was introduced this summer. 777-300ERs also fly to Vancouver International Airport (YVR) north of the border. The high business aviation market between Taiwan and North America is driven by the close geopolitical and economic relationship shared by the USA and Taiwan.

Taiwan is currently the USA's ninth-largest trading partner, while the US is Taiwan's second-largest trading partner. The linchpin of this relationship is Taiwan's position in the microchip and superconductor industries, and the research & development partnerships that the two countries share.

The 777-300ER entered EVA's fleet due to its first major long-haul fleet renewal, which began in 2000. The airline purchased four firm commitments for the aircraft, with an additional eight options, giving it a position as one of the jet's launch customers. It converted the eight options into firm orders in 2004, and the airline's first 777-300ER came into service in July 2005.

The carrier now has 41 Boeing 777s in its fleet, according to Planespotters.net, making it EVA's most numerous family of aircraft within its fleet of 89 jets (including 72 widebody planes). The table below shows the number of seats available in each class for each of EVA's 777-300ER layouts. It makes use of data from EVA's seat map. While the Royal Laurel offering is consistent, there is more variation in what is available for premium economy and economy passengers.

In 2007, the carrier introduced a major ultra-long-haul 777-300ER route for which premium dense 777-300ERs would be essential. The flight was from Taipei to Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). EVA is now looking to move away from this aircraft in its passenger fleet. It has begun work to convert three 777-300ERs into freighters. The airline has also placed orders for 24 Airbus A350-1000s to replace its outgoing 777-300ER and notably has made no Boeing 777X orders.

Some of the sectors flown by the type exceed 8,000 miles in length.

Also available on EVA's premium dense 777-300ERs is premium economy, which is unsurprising given that the airline was the first to introduce premium economy to the long-haul market. It was introduced on a Boeing 747-400 flight from Taipei to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) under the name Evergreen Deluxe Class.

The title is sometimes given to Virgin Atlantic, but EVA was the first to have a true premium economy product with unique catering, seating, and amenities. These passengers also had personal television screens available. EVA's product was quickly successful, showing that passengers without the means or desire to fly in business class could be motivated to pay an additional 20% to 30% for an increase in comfort and service quality.

EVA is now on its fourth generation of premium economy products. The table below shows what is available for EVA premium economy passengers flying on the carrier's 787-9s. All the figures represent a substantial improvement from what has been available in each previous generation.

The fourth-generation premium economy is only available on EVA's Dreamliners. Passengers using the product aboard its 777-300ER will be sitting in its previous-generation premium economy. This has a 2-4-2 layout, meaning that more passengers per row don't have direct aisle access.

EVA is able to offer its passengers such a premium dense layout aboard its 777-300ERs because of the aircraft's unique capabilities. This plane expanded on the Boeing 777-200ER, which had added fuel capacity and maximum takeoff weight to allow carriers to fly the jet further.

The 777-300ER featured an upgraded General Electric GE90 engine, without Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce options, a strengthened landing gear, and raked wingtips for better efficiency. This aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of over 700,000 lb (318 tons). It has now become the best-selling 777-300ER variant, with 833 delivered.

The 777 is the widest operational commercial aircraft in production. The vertical sidewalls also create the impression of more room. This width allows carriers like EVA to cram more seats into the cabin without high-paying premium passengers feeling claustrophobic. EVA is committed to giving passengers space across all classes. Alongside Singapore Airlines, Japan Airlines, and Air India, EVA is one of the few airlines that doesn't force economy class 777 passengers into ten-abreast seating.

EVA's 777-300ER business class seats are in a 1-2-1 reverse herringbone configuration. Each seat is set 60 inches (152 cm) back from the seat in front, with the pitch growing substantially when the seat is converted into lie-flat. Things are more cramped if you fly in Royal Laurel aboard EVA's A330s. These seats are in a 2-2-2 layout. Superb amenities are available to all Royal Laurel passengers.

This includes an amenity kit with premium skincare products, loungewear, and noise-canceling headphones, along with plush bedding. Adjustable light settings also help you to get comfortable when it's time to sleep. EVA's business class cabin crew are known for providing attentive and efficient service, which is sensitive to the cultural needs of each passenger.

They'll be particularly helpful during meal times. The exact food available will depend on the route you are flying on and when. EVA has built a menu working with famous Taiwanese restaurants like Kanpai Classic, the nation's first restaurant specializing in Australian Wagyu, and Kanpai Yakiniku Restaurant. An example of delicacies commonly available includes the braised beef noodle soup and the lychee and strawberry bread.

On the ground, Royal Laurel passengers have access to exclusive lounges to enjoy a relaxing pre-flight meal or show, or get some work done. EVA operates lounges at TPE, Kaohsiung International Airport (KHH), and Bangkok Suvarnabhumi Airport (BKK), and you'll be able to use Star Alliance member lounges when flying from other airports.

Creating a large business class cabin is meaningless if passengers are not being offered a high-quality product. Last summer, Simple Flying flew from London to Taiwan, via Bangkok, aboard EVA's 777-300ER in business class. We began the experience by making use of the United lounge at London Heathrow Airport's (LHR's) Terminal 2. Lounges like this are available to EVA's business class passengers due to its position in Star Alliance.

We were impressed by the roomy 26 inches (66 cm) of width and 82 inches (208 cm) of pitch available. He was able to get comfortable easily when fully reclined, aided by the cushion, designer pajamas, mattress, and duvet. We also enjoyed the food and wine available during the meal service, particularly given his gluten intolerance.

We concluded the review by writing that "Europe to Southeast Asia is always a long-haul stretch, no matter the route, but there aren't many better ways to sit back and enjoy the ride than EVA Air's Royal Laurel Class." Simple Flying reader Cloudswimmer agreed with our sentiments, commenting that "I flew that same route from LHR to TPE a few years ago and it was definitely the best business class experience of my 2.5 million miles of worldwide air travel."

#6258. KLM Plans 15% Workforce Reduction And Simpler Fleet: “Future Not Guaranteed”

It’s obviously a tough time for aviation in general, given the impact of high jet fuel prices. For that matter, Dutch national carrier KLM has faced its own unique challenges, given increasing limits placed on the carrier’s Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS) hub, plus all the competitive challenges (increased competition from regional low cost carriers, Gulf carriers, etc.).

In recent years, we’ve seen KLM introduce initiatives intended to improve economics. The airline is now taking that to the next level, and has just announced an absolutely massive project intended to improve economics by €1 billion per year.

KLM has unveiled the details of a project that it expects will contribute to annual earnings improvements of €1 billion per year, which it hopes will allow the company to invest in fleet, customer experience, and people.

KLM’s plan is to focus on its core strengths, which it describes as a global network of 160 destinations served nonstop from Schiphol, and reliable operations supported by a modern fleet. The company wants to become a smaller, simpler, and more agile organization, through restructuring, outsourcing, and closer collaboration with Air France-KLM.

Here’s how KLM CEO Marjan Rintel describes this initiative:

“Every day, we all work with incredible dedication, commitment, and pride. But KLM’s future is not guaranteed. The environment we operate in is becoming increasingly complex, with global instability, high fuel prices, and growing pressure on the aviation industry. That’s why, at this pivotal moment for KLM, we’re taking far-reaching, sometimes painful measures. Every department and every division will be asked to contribute.”

“We’re doing this with a clear vision for the future: one where KLM remains a great airline that connects customers to the world, a company people want to work for, and one the Netherlands can be proud of.”

How does KLM plan on improving economics by so much over the coming years? For one, the airline will simplify its fleet.

The long term plan is to have a fleet of 185 Airbus, Boeing, and Embraer aircraft. The latest changes particularly center around the European network, where just about all network carriers in Europe struggle to make money, given the costs and competitive landscape.

KLM plans to change the balance between larger and smaller aircraft on European routes. In the long run, the airline will fly a mix of 227-seat Airbus A321neos and 132-seat Embraer E195-E2s. The company no longer plans to acquire Airbus A320neos, which were part of a larger Air France-KLM order, as those planes are instead going to Transavia. Furthermore, in the coming years, we’ll see Boeing 737s and Embraer E190s retired.

Next, the airline hopes to achieve greater flexibility, higher productive, and lower costs, with its labor agreements. As you’d expect, this will be the most painful change. For one, KLM plans to reduce its workforce by around 15%, meaning that around 5,000 positions will be “reorganized.”

This follows the company’s number of staff already declining in recent years. The good news is that there aren’t expected to be mass layoffs — KLM expects to limit the impact on employees through natural attrition, voluntary arrangements, and transfers to other positions.

The airline also emphasizes that employment terms and conditions need to become simpler and more competitive, noting that “continuing on the current path is not sustainable.” KLM wants to work with unions to establish new collective labor agreements, and the company aims to achieve a structural productivity increase of at least 8% by 2028.

This decrease in headcount will come through a combination of Air France and KLM cooperating more closely, outsourcing catering and maintenance, and reducing planned growth of the fleet.

The airline industry is tough in the first place, and among the major network carriers, KLM is perhaps in the toughest spot, when you consider the overall industry dynamics:

KLM is planning to majorly cut costs and simplify things, which is probably necessary in light of how the situation has evolved.

As part of this, the carrier’s short haul fleet will eventually consist of just Airbus A321neos and Embraer E195-E2s. On top of that, we’ll see the airline reduce its workforce by around 15%, through a combination of increasing efficiency, outsourcing jobs, and more. The company will also be looking for some concessions from existing employees.

In total, the company hopes that these changes will contribute €1 billion per year. While aviation is tough across the board, it’s especially tough to be KLM, where you’re reliant on one hub (which regulators keep trying to shrink) with very high costs, and that hub isn’t a market that’s as lucrative as somewhere like London, Paris, etc. I’m a fan of KLM, and I hope these changes don’t do too much to change the quirky spirit of the airline.

What do you make of these major KLM changes?

#6257. Emirates Profits Plunge Due To War… But The Airline Still Made Money?!

It goes without saying that it has been a tough year for airlines, due to the United States getting into a war with Iran. All airlines have been dealing with higher jet fuel prices, but airlines in the Gulf region have of course been dealing with additional issues, as all kinds of airports in the region have been attacked, making some people reconsider traveling through the region.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note that Emirates has just released its financial results for the first half of the fiscal year (April 1 through September 30, 2026). Yes, Emirates’ profits decreased massively, but surprisingly, the airline still turned a healthy profit, and the numbers look much better than I would’ve guessed.

Prior to this year, Emirates was the world’s most profitable airline for two years in a row, as the carrier really is incredibly well run.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note how the airline performed over the first six months of the current fiscal year, which coincides entirely with the current Iran conflict. While there are results for the overall Emirates Group (which also includes dnata, etc.), I’m focusing on the airline specifically, since I find that to be most telling.

Emirates reported a half-year profit of $1 billion, down 68% compared to the previous year. Interestingly, revenue was $15.5 billion, down “only” 13% compared to the same period the previous year. The airline didn’t actually cut back its total capacity that much — available seat kilometers (ASKM) decreased by 17% compared to the previous year, while the passenger load factor decreased to 72%, from 79.5% the previous year. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers over the six months, down 22% from the same period last year.

As of September 30, 2026, Emirates is operating 91% of its pre-disruption network, with the passenger and cargo network spanning 150 airports in 78 countries. However, that reflects the number of destinations, rather than the total actual capacity (in other words, many destinations are being operated with reduced frequencies).

Emirates CEO Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum reflected on this as “a demanding six months,” and said that “once again our business model and our people stood up to the test.” He explained that the company is entering the second half of the fiscal year “with measured optimism,” “while keeping a close watch on costs and geopolitical developments.”

One would think that Gulf carriers are in the toughest spot of any airline, given that they’ve been so reliant on connecting people traveling between other regions, and at least among some people, their willingness to travel through the region has decreased, assuming it can be avoided.

Admittedly many people also just live in this region, so it’s not like there are endless options. But when you consider all factors, I’d say these are very encouraging results, much better than I would’ve expected.

I know there’s often a lot of skepticism when it comes to the reported financials of Gulf carriers. I do think at some Gulf carriers, there’s reason to be skeptical about the math, based on what is and isn’t reported.

In the case of Emirates, though, the airline is legitimately very profitable and well run. The airline has managed to efficiently scale its operation in a way that no other airline really has, and that’s where credit goes for the carrier’s success.

Of course we have to acknowledge that there’s a difference in underlying economics. Dubai (DXB) is much lower cost to operate out of than somewhere like London Heathrow (LHR) or New York Kennedy (JFK), and Emirates Group owns both the airline and the ground handling company. Furthermore, the cost of jet fuel is lower in Dubai than it is in somewhere like London, and I imagine the airline also has access to more attractive financing opportunities, given that it’s owned by the government.

However, that’s hardly anything that’s super hidden or secret. I mean, economics in US aviation are also sort of lopsided. Airline profits are largely reliant on everything except actually flying, which is a privilege and upside that most foreign carriers can’t fully unlock.

I think it’s also interesting to note how well Emirates’ yields have held up during this time. For example, just based on looking at fares through Google Flights, it seems like Etihad’s strategy has just been to publish incredibly low fares to fill seats, including in premium cabins. I haven’t found that to be the case with Emirates, though, as the airline has managed to maintain pricing power despite reduced demand.

Emirates has reported its financial results for the first half of the 2026-2027 fiscal year. As you’d expect, this was a generally tough time for a Gulf carrier, given the current war with Iran. While Emirates’ profits were cut by around two-thirds, the airline still turned a healthy profit of around $1 billion.

Honestly, the actual operating figures don’t at all reflect what you’d expect during a crisis, so it seems like the airline is weathering this story pretty well, all things considered. I do feel like Emirates is uniquely positioned among its competitive set, and I’d be shocked if the story is similar at Etihad or Qatar Airways.

What do you make of Emirates’ financial results?

#6256. Bizarre: Lufthansa Group Now Requires Travel ID For Online Check-In

Most airlines encourage travelers to check-in online, given that it’s mutually beneficial — it saves time for the traveler, and saves resources for the airline. Well, Lufthansa Group is implementing a new policy that makes it more difficult to check-in online, as flagged by aeroTELEGRAPH, and that strikes me as rather backwards.

Lufthansa Group has the concept of a Travel ID, whereby customers have an account they can use to log-in across digital platforms belonging to all carriers, including Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian, Brussels Airlines, Edelweiss, Discover Airlines, etc. This is separate from the Miles & More program, as the idea is that it simply creates a unified log-in for digital services across the airlines.

So along those lines, Lufthansa Group is progressively rolling out an initiative whereby customers need to have a Travel ID account in order to check-in online via the website or app.

Lufthansa Group is rolling out this requirement gradually. The Travel ID is required to check-in online as follows:

There are a limited number of exceptions for the Travel ID requirement. Specifically, you don’t need a Travel ID if you’re a traveler checking in at the airport counter or machine, if you’re traveling on a ticket issued by another airline, or if you’re on a flight operated by another airline with a ticket issued by Lufthansa Group.

Airlines love data and being able to market to customers. It’s one of the reasons that airlines create such strong incentives to sign-up for their loyalty programs (or in this case, a log-in that allows the airline to market to you). We’ve seen countless airlines roll out free Wi-Fi for those who are loyalty program members, and the logic is easy enough to follow.

However, in this case we’re talking about online check-in, which is something that arguably helps the airline more than it helps the customer. I can understand an airline wanting to add a step for something that entirely benefits the customer (like free Wi-Fi), but doing it for a basic function that saves the airline money? Well, that’s quite the approach to take.

In fairness to Lufthansa, I’m not sure this is actually a bad idea, or will backfire that much. Yes, it’s a minor annoyance, but:

Now, it’s still rather customer unfriendly, in my opinion, but that’s not exactly the first time we’ve seen something like that in the airline industry…

Lufthansa Group will start requiring passengers to sign-up for a Travel ID in order to check-in online. This is progressively being rolled out through November 30, 2026. Making it more complicated to check-in online seems counterproductive.

At the same time, clearly this is intended to encourage travelers to register for a Travel ID, so that Lufthansa can better track customer data and market to travelers. Usually we see incentives created to encourage this kind of registration, but in the case of Lufthansa Group, the airline is instead threatening to take something away if you don’t register.

What do you make of Lufthansa Group’s new online check-in requirement?

#6255. Qantas Launches Historic New 15-Hour Nonstop Route From Sydney: See Map Now

In an unexpected and highly intriguing network development, Qantas has announced a brand-new long-haul route. The oneworld member will begin flying from Sydney to the increasingly popular Cape Town.

It'll be historical in various ways. For example, it'll become Qantas' record third route to South Africa, while being the first time that Australia has had flights to Cape Town. It'll also be Cape Town's new longest route within the Southern Hemisphere. However, it will be far from Qantas' longest nonstop service on the Boeing 787.

On October 19, 2027, during the spring in the Southern Hemisphere, Qantas will lift off from its busiest and critical hub of Sydney Kingsford Smith Airport (SYD) to Cape Town International Airport (CPT). On a great circle basis, the brand-new route will cover 5,945 nautical miles (11,010 km) each way.

As this represents the shortest distance between two airports, real-world operations will increase that distance. There won't be any payload restriction, which means a full load of passengers and belly freight.

QF89: 10:15 AM-3:55 PM (same-day arrival; 14 hours and 40 minutes)

QF90: 5:55 PM-2:50 PM+1 (12 hours and 55 minutes)

Like so many new routes, SYD-CPT will be flown three times weekly. Given the block time and stage length of the airport pair, this means that one Boeing 787-9 will be able to operate it.

All of Qantas' 787-9s have 236 seats, which is not many. That's mainly because they're quite premium, with 42 seats in business (1-2-1), 28 in premium economy (2-3-2; 38" pitch), and 166 in economy (3-3-3; 32"). Around 18% of the capacity is in business.

Booking data shows that 87,000 round-trip passengers flew between Australia and CPT in 2025, with traffic up by nearly a fifth compared to 2024. While many South Africans live in Australia, it is unclear how many come from the CPT area. Many of the passengers would have been Australians visiting the increasingly popular city for tourism.

Unsurprisingly, SYD was the largest market to/from CPT. With around 23,000 passengers, the local traffic was not overly high, although the new nonstop flights may grow that by around 40%. The airline will also target passengers connecting to Auckland Airport (AKL), Brisbane, and Melbourne, in particular, with those places having around 42,000 passengers.

Significantly, SYD-CPT is relatively high-yielding, with the average fare across all airlines, cabins, and passengers being US$1,335 one way (excluding taxes but including a fuel surcharge). Reflecting higher premium demand, the average fare for SYD-CPT is around 12% higher than for SYD to Johannesburg's O. R. Tambo International Airport (JNB).

Interestingly, SYD-CPT flights will cover marginally less distance than SYD-JNB. As such, the fare difference is particularly notable, especially when coupled with similar operating expenses. Commenting on the new route, senior airline network planner, African specialist, and industry commentator Behramjee Ghadially said that:

"This new service will perform very well for Qantas, seeing how the Aussies love to visit new exotic places, especially where a combination of beach, wine and safari can be experienced in an upscale manner [although most safari-related activities are in eastern South Africa].

Qantas will also target tour operators selling South Africa packages from Australia and New Zealand as they can now offer an open-jaw itinerary for their clientele, such as flying into JNB and flying back from CPT using the same airline."

The carrier has just grown its footprint to this continent considerably. Find out more here!

As the above map shows, Qantas will now fly from SYD to CPT and JNB, along with from Perth International Airport (PER) to JNB. The latter route is the only one on which the airline has head-to-head competition, as it competes directly with the troubled South African Airways. It is also the one on which Qantas deploys an Airbus twinjet.

OAG data shows that Qantas flew between PER and JNB until 2023, with the route, which is nearly entirely overwater, returning 11 months ago, in December 2025. The operating A330-200 flies AKL-PER-JNB-PER-AKL. At some point, it then operates to SYD, where the specific airframe is switched.

#6254. British Airways Kept Losing Consumer Complaints—So They Found A New Arbitrator

British Airways is dropping the independent complaints service through which passengers won £5 million in a year. Its replacement has a record of much lower passenger success rates. They appear to be shopping for a more accommodating referee, putting their thumb on the scales by choosing who hears complaints against them. On August 24, 2016, I asked this exact question: Will the Centre for Effective Dispute Resolution get to keep the British Airways contract if they rule against BA too frequently? Ten years later, British Airways isn’t renewing that contract. They’re moving to AviationADR, the other major U.K. provider. And Head for Points reports that losing its biggest airline customer means CEDR is leaving aviation altogether. British Airways confirmed the switch, describing it as a contract renewal decision and saying: British Airways has selected AviationADR as the independent alternative dispute resolution body to resolve disputes between customers and the airline. British Airways Wasn’t Winning Enough Cases The Civil Aviation Authority’s figures for April 2025 through March 2026 show: British Airways settled 4,414 complaints before a decision. CEDR ruled for passengers in 1,619 cases and for British Airways in 2,234. Settlements and decisions together produced £5,001,728 in passenger awards. That’s a 73% passenger success rate including settlements. Passengers had already gone through the airline’s complaint process, then had to escalate to an outside body before getting an offer which means that BA was improperly rejecting complaints. Most passengers just give up at that point. EasyJet Already Made This Switch easyJet made the move from CEDR to AviationADR after CEDR upheld passenger complaints 79% of the time over its final six quarters with with the airline, and just 29% in the following six quarters with AviationADR. AviationADR’s explanation was that airlines had improved their handling of claims, including using major law firms to filter cases before escalation. Valid claims were being paid earlier, leaving weaker ones for adjudication. And that just happened to coincide with the switch. Ok sure. Airlines Get Advance Access To Decisions Against Them A February 2026 review commissioned by the Civil Aviation Authority described AviationADR giving airlines decisions in passengers’ favor one week before the passengers received them, ostensibly to ‘prepare payment’. During that time, airlines could raise legal challenges, although AviationADR said its legal review panel hadn’t needed to convene for years. The reviewer warned this advance access “may create an impression of bias in favour of the aviation body” and recommended ending it, along with airline challenges to individual binding decisions. CEDR generally uses legally qualified adjudicators. AviationADR doesn’t require legal qualifications and provides more extensive initial training. The commercial pressure to retain the contract paid for by one side is huge, and the fact that BA made this switch underscores what the new adjudicator has to do to keep its revenue stream. Relatedly, Ryanair left AviationADR in 2018 after adverse decisions over staff strikes, then rejoined in 2021 after rules changes. AviationADR says its decisions are independent and based on the evidence and law. Its service is free to the consumer, and passengers who reject a decision can still go to court. Head for Points reports that CEDR will stop accepting new aviation cases on December 31. The Civil Aviation Authority says it’s working with AviationADR on the capacity needed to handle the additional caseload. On August 24, 2016, I asked this exact question:

Will the Centre for Effective Dispute Resolution get to keep the British Airways contract if they rule against BA too frequently?

Ten years later, British Airways isn’t renewing that contract. They’re moving to AviationADR, the other major U.K. provider. And Head for Points reports that losing its biggest airline customer means CEDR is leaving aviation altogether.

British Airways confirmed the switch, describing it as a contract renewal decision and saying:

British Airways has selected AviationADR as the independent alternative dispute resolution body to resolve disputes between customers and the airline.

The Civil Aviation Authority’s figures for April 2025 through March 2026 show: British Airways settled 4,414 complaints before a decision. CEDR ruled for passengers in 1,619 cases and for British Airways in 2,234. Settlements and decisions together produced £5,001,728 in passenger awards. That’s a 73% passenger success rate including settlements. Passengers had already gone through the airline’s complaint process, then had to escalate to an outside body before getting an offer which means that BA was improperly rejecting complaints. Most passengers just give up at that point. EasyJet Already Made This Switch easyJet made the move from CEDR to AviationADR after CEDR upheld passenger complaints 79% of the time over its final six quarters with with the airline, and just 29% in the following six quarters with AviationADR. AviationADR’s explanation was that airlines had improved their handling of claims, including using major law firms to filter cases before escalation. Valid claims were being paid earlier, leaving weaker ones for adjudication. And that just happened to coincide with the switch. Ok sure. Airlines Get Advance Access To Decisions Against Them A February 2026 review commissioned by the Civil Aviation Authority described AviationADR giving airlines decisions in passengers’ favor one week before the passengers received them, ostensibly to ‘prepare payment’. During that time, airlines could raise legal challenges, although AviationADR said its legal review panel hadn’t needed to convene for years. The reviewer warned this advance access “may create an impression of bias in favour of the aviation body” and recommended ending it, along with airline challenges to individual binding decisions. CEDR generally uses legally qualified adjudicators. AviationADR doesn’t require legal qualifications and provides more extensive initial training. The commercial pressure to retain the contract paid for by one side is huge, and the fact that BA made this switch underscores what the new adjudicator has to do to keep its revenue stream. Relatedly, Ryanair left AviationADR in 2018 after adverse decisions over staff strikes, then rejoined in 2021 after rules changes. AviationADR says its decisions are independent and based on the evidence and law. Its service is free to the consumer, and passengers who reject a decision can still go to court. Head for Points reports that CEDR will stop accepting new aviation cases on December 31. The Civil Aviation Authority says it’s working with AviationADR on the capacity needed to handle the additional caseload. More About Gary »

While some at View from the Right Wing will clutch pearls over businesses having to pay fines to consumers when they fail, the rest of us, who actually fly, and have to deal with the inconvenience, real costs, and disruption caused by airlines that excessively delay and cancel flights under their control.

We’re overdue for meaningful air passenger rights legislation in the US, akin to UK and EU laws like 261 with a real, enforceable duty of care and compensation where appropriate, not mere partial refunds and silly games. So, no, it’s not a third party processor issue here. It’s the incentive structure; thankfully, their laws have teeth.

BA is just being cheap, like usual; operate a reliable airline, or pay up.

Exhibit A for why arbitration needs to be controlled. Looks good on the surface, fails badly when one side gets to choose whoever gives the most favorable results.

So basically BA doesn’t want customers to have fair arbitration. I’m a bit surprised that whatever body governs UK aviation is fine with this.

This is just so typical of BA and the Walsh legacy: rather than make badly needed improvements that would keep the airline from losing arbitration cases they dump the company that recognizes that BA is frequently wrong.

The credit card companies in the US set up a phony baloney arb service, the National Arbitration Forum, to resolve the problem of fair arbiters; the newly elected Senator from MN when AG uncovered the scheme.

This is the reason why “mandatory arbitration” is absolute BS that should be nuked from orbit and everyone fake “arbiter” exiled to Vostok Station in Antarctica for life.

There’s nothing remotely fair about a system where one side gets to pick the judge.

#6253. Lufthansa Realizes 28 Business Class Seats Isn’t Enough For Boeing 787

In recent times, Lufthansa has started taking delivery of factory fresh Boeing 787s, featuring the carrier’s all-new Allegris cabins. Management at the airline has reportedly decided that the configuration of these planes isn’t quite right for many routes, so now it’s planning some updates.

That’s a sensible change, but it always just feels like Lufthansa is a step behind when it comes to acting logically and catching onto trends, no?

Lufthansa currently has a fleet of 20 Boeing 787-9s. Four of these were acquired secondhand (they were former Hainan Airlines jets), while 16 are brand new, and feature Allegris interiors. Not only that, but Lufthansa has at least another 22 of these planes on order, which will be delivered in the coming years.

In the long run, the Dreamliner is supposed to be the carrier’s primary long haul aircraft based in Frankfurt, complementing the Boeing 747-8s and Boeing 777-9s. Meanwhile Munich (MUC) is primarily getting Airbus A350s (including the A350-900 and A350-1000).

Lufthansa’s 787s are configured with 287 seats, including 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats, and 231 economy seats. Keep in mind that three of those seats aren’t even certified yet (but should be certified before the end of 2026), so actual business class capacity is currently just 25 seats.

Anyway, even with all seats certified, Lufthansa Group management has decided that the capacity doesn’t actually match demand on many routes, with CEO Carsten Spohr indicating that the airline is working on installing more business class and premium economy seats on upcoming Dreamliners.

Reportedly nothing has been finalized yet, as this is still in negotiations with suppliers, but the idea remains that the current configuration doesn’t offer enough premium seats.

Given the eventual size of Lufthansa’s Dreamliner fleet, it would also be reasonable to think the airline may have two configurations in the long run, to reflect the demand of different destinations. For example, one would assume that the potential customer demand profile would be different to New York (JFK) than to Columbus (CMH), both of which are going to be Dreamliner routes in the coming months.

I know ragging on Lufthansa is just too easy, from its challenging labor relations, to its botched Allegris rollout, and more. However, I can’t help but feel like the airline is a little behind on trends.

I mean, for how long have we been talking about the surge in premium travel demand? American is taking delivery of 787-9s with 51 business class seats, United is taking delivery of 787-9s with 64 business class seats, and British Airways is reconfiguring 787-9s with eight first class seats and 38 business class seats.

So Lufthansa just taking delivery of dozens of factory fresh 787s with just 28 business class seats seems a little off, especially since Lufthansa only recently started adding these planes to its fleet.

I get that demand differs between markets, and the 787 is actually supposed to be the less premium plane in the fleet, in the long run (with the Boeing 747s and 777Xs being the most premium Frankfurt-based planes), but still, 28 seats just doesn’t seem like a lot by any metric. Heck, the Airbus A330s that are slowly being retired have 42 business class seats, and that’s an overall smaller plane.

Of course the whole Lufthansa Allegris and SWISS Senses situation is just sort of messy, from the 3.5-seat first class cabin that makes no sense, to the need to install a weight on SWISS A330s to balance out the weight of first class, to the new Allegris seats delaying entry into service for planes by years, despite it not actually being that cutting edge at this point.

Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr has indicated that the airline is considering a new configuration for many upcoming Boeing 787s. Management has decided that 28 business class seats and 28 premium economy seats isn’t sufficient, which strikes me as a rather obvious, when you look at trends. Heck, these Dreamliners are partly replacing planes with 50% more business class seats.

I’m curious to see what Lufthansa eventually settles on for a premium Dreamliner configuration, because I agree, 28 business class seats isn’t a lot!

What do you make of Lufthansa reconsidering its 787 layout?
