Your statement that ‘ragging on Lufthansa is almost too easy’ sums up the situation nicely. Can anyone really remember a time when this airline, and LH group in general, wasn’t a joke? Remember when Lufthansa itself could seriously claim to be among the most premium and reliable brands on earth? It’s long been a trope that British Airways is the airline that most severely shredded its premium image, especially under Cruz. But he lasted less than 5 years running BA, and they’ve spent the last 6 years doing (just) enough to recover some of that, and are arguably about halfway there at best in terms of repairing the damage. Spohr has had a dozen years to wreck Lufthansa, with no end in sight, and they clearly cannot start repairing the damage until he goes. The fact they continue to get the most basic planning wrong, misreading or ignoring clear industry trends, just underlines this. Among the flagship European carriers, LH is just so far behind Air France, and even BA as things stand, it’s hard to imagine when they can actually try to catch up, saddled with their current leadership.

How Sophr is still CEO just shows you how the LH board and management is clueless. Its one bad decision after another and they keep the guy on...

Nah they just knew all the premium travelers were going to spend their money elsewhere. Smart. :D

......yet still there is no accountability. Now that AA seem to have finally seen the light, LH must be out on their own as the most incompetant managemnt for a major airline

The whole Allegris philosophy was a gamble on one very specific aspect: segmenting customers with different seat types. The allegris business class seat is a very inefficient seat. It is essentially the same concept as united’s Polaris, except with more seat pitch, and every second row, just one middle seat instead of two. Lufthansa thought they could segment their business class customers, upsell certain seats (especially the throne seats, the long bed and the mini-first class at the bulkhead) and make up for the lost revenue of having such an inefficient layout and shrinking the size of the cabin (to maintain a large economy class cabin). But this gamble failed, because Lufthansa didn’t realise that by upcharging so many business class passengers even to simply select a window seat put a bad taste in many people’s mouths. Look at BA, AF and KL. all business class seats in their cabins are created more or less equal with the exception of the bulkheads. Furthermore, Frankfurt is a business heavy market, but has less point-to-point business traffic, and a lot of connecting traffic. It is easy for travellers who are not star-alliance loyal to simply connect elsewhere, or fly united across the Atlantic. Lufthansa wanted to create a segmented business class cabin, but instead created a business class “lite” and charged for extras after that. And now they’re stuck with a VERY expensive, delayed seat, which occupies way too much space on their aircraft, and as such they have had to make huge compromises like shrinking the first and business class cabins. They will seriously lose out in the long term.

Atmos Rewards is the joint loyalty program that serves both Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. It launched in 2025, a year after Alaska acquired Hawaiian.

The program is gaining popularity among frequent flyers thanks to its valuable points and robust network of partners. Plus, it won a TPG Award in 2026 thanks to some unique new features we haven't seen with any other airline.

Atmos Rewards has four elite status tiers that each come with exclusive benefits and can improve your overall travel experience. Those are perks you'll be able to tap into whether you're flying on Alaska, Hawaiian, or one of their partners in the Oneworld alliance.

Benefits range from complimentary first-class upgrades to lounge access and extra-legroom seats.

And top-tier Atmos status includes one of the U.S. airline industry's most alluring perks: unlimited, space-available upgrades into lie-flat seats on long-haul routes.

In this guide, we’ll explain the different Atmos Rewards elite status tiers, how to qualify for them, the benefits they offer and how to decide if pursuing status is worth the effort.

Atmos Rewards offers four elite status tiers, which members reach by accruing enough "status points" in a calendar year.

You can earn status points through Alaska, Hawaiian and eligible partner flights, as well as through spending on cobranded credit cards and select non-air partners.

Anyone can join the Atmos Rewards program for free online.

Once you do, you'll be able to start earning both Atmos Rewards points (which you can redeem on flights) and status points (which count toward the elite tiers).

Atmos Rewards' elite status tiers, from lowest to highest, are: Silver, Gold, Platinum and Titanium.

Like with most airline loyalty programs, the perks become more lucrative as you climb the status ladder.

As you remain loyal to these airlines and reach higher tiers, the perks become more lucrative.

Plus, because Alaska and Hawaiian are part of the Oneworld global airline alliance, you'll enjoy reciprocal benefits when you enter your Atmos number while flying on other alliance members — including top partner American Airlines.

Pro tip: Your Atmos Rewards points can also be really valuable when booking flights on American

For flights in 2026, Atmos Rewards members generally earn status points based on the distance flown, with the earning rate varying by fare class and airline.

For example, a first-class ticket on Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines in the J fare class earns status points equal to 200% of the distance flown, while many economy fares earn status points equal to 100% of the distance flown.

Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, Atmos Rewards members will have more flexibility in how they earn. Members can choose to earn points and status points based on distance traveled, price paid or segments flown:

You can change your selection once per year. Current members who do not make a selection will continue earning based on distance traveled. New members who don't make a selection will earn based on the dollars they pay.

It is possible to earn Atmos Rewards elite status entirely through credit card spending.

The Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card earns 1 status point for every $3 spent on purchases, while the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card earns 1 status point for every $2 spent. There is no cap on the number of status points you can earn through purchases on either card.

Additionally, Atmos Rewards Summit cardholders receive 10,000 status points each account anniversary. That means a cardholder who receives the anniversary bonus could earn Atmos Silver status simply by spending an additional $20,000 on the card.

If you have elite status with another eligible airline, you may be able to match it to Atmos Rewards Silver, Gold or Platinum status for 90 days.

Atmos Rewards currently offers status matches to eligible elite members of Aeromexico, Air Canada, Delta Air Lines, Frontier Airlines, JetBlue, Southwest Airlines and United Airlines. The Atmos Rewards tier you receive depends on your status with the other airline.

To keep your matched status beyond the initial 90 days, you must earn a certain number of base points on qualifying Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines flights during that period.

The status match is available only once per Atmos Rewards account, and your existing airline status must have been earned through flight activity rather than credit card spending or a promotional offer.

Alaska has a full list of its status match partners on its website.

You can also earn status points through a variety of Atmos Rewards' non-airline partners, including hotel, cruise, car rental and everyday partners. These include brands such as Marriott, IHG, Choice Hotels, Avis, Budget and Lyft, as well as Atmos Rewards Shopping and Atmos Rewards Dining. Earning rates vary by partner.

Additionally, members can earn status points on award flights booked with Atmos Rewards points, meaning even flights you don't pay for with cash can help you work toward elite status.

The perks are great for all members with Atmos elite status, but as you move up the tiers, the benefits become even more worthwhile.

This is the lowest elite tier in the Atmos Rewards program, where you will receive benefits when flying on Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines, such as:

As you level up within Atmos, you will receive all the same perks as Silver, plus:

Upon reaching Platinum, you will receive all the same perks as Gold, as well as:

This is the top tier in the Atmos program for its most frequent travelers. You will receive all the same perks as Platinum, plus:

In addition to the standard status perks, Alaska also lets you pick from a menu of optional perks each time you hit a new milestone. These start before you actually reach elite status.

Alaska continues to offer milestone perks beyond the 135,000 status points threshold for Titanium status. You can select from additional perk menus at the 150,000; 200,000 and 250,000 status points milestones.

Atmos Rewards offers multiple cobranded credit cards issued by Bank of America, including personal and business cards. They offer the following benefits. (Terms apply.)

In addition to the valuable redeemable points earned, Atmos cards come with perks like free checked bags, discounts on inflight purchases and the ability to earn points toward elite status.

Out of the three options above, the Summit card offers the quickest path toward elite status because it earns 1 point for every $2 spent, versus the others that earn 1 point for every $3 spent. If your main goal is elite status, that would be the card to prioritize.

Yes — especially if you regularly fly Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines, or expect to do so in the future.

Atmos Rewards elite status offers many of the perks frequent flyers have come to expect, including priority services, complimentary upgrades, bonus points and other travel benefits. But the program's value goes beyond the standard elite-status perks.

One of this program's biggest draws is the ability to earn milestone rewards as you accumulate status-qualifying points. These rewards can include valuable extras like upgrade certificates, lounge access and bonus points, giving members more opportunities to get something out of their loyalty beyond simply reaching the next status tier.

At the very top of the elite status tiers, Atmos Titanium members receive access to a particularly unusual perk: complimentary, space-available upgrades on the day of departure to international business-class suites on eligible long-haul flights. It's a benefit no other U.S. airline loyalty program currently offers, and it gives top-tier members another reason to stick with Alaska and Hawaiian when flying internationally.

Atmos Rewards can also offer value beyond Alaska and Hawaiian flights. Through its Oneworld alliance membership and close partnership with American Airlines, Atmos elite members can enjoy reciprocal benefits when flying American, too. These include preferred seating, priority services and eligibility for complimentary upgrades on qualifying flights, subject to availability and upgrade priority. In other words, earning status with Atmos Rewards can make flying on multiple airlines more rewarding.

Ultimately, if Alaska or Hawaiian is already part of your regular travel routine, Atmos Rewards elite status could be worth pursuing. And if you're able to earn enough status points to unlock milestone rewards along the way, the program becomes even more compelling.

Related: Alaska Airlines baggage fees and how to avoid paying them

Atmos Rewards stands out among U.S. airline loyalty programs, combining Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines under one program while offering valuable points, flexible ways to earn status and unique elite perks. Top-tier Titanium members, for example, can receive space-available upgrades to lie-flat business class on Alaska and Hawaiian flights.

When considering whether Atmos elite status is worth pursuing, think about where and how often you expect to travel and whether you will fly Alaska, Hawaiian and their partners enough to take advantage of the benefits.

Overall, Atmos elite status can make an Alaska or Hawaiian flying experience even more rewarding, particularly for frequent travelers who can maximize its upgrade, earning and partner benefits.

And remember, having Atmos Rewards status can help you out on American Airlines flights, too.

#6251. Teamsters Sue Horizon Air Over Pilot Rest Rules

The Teamsters have sued Horizon Air, alleging the Alaska Air Group subsidiary violated federal labor law by changing how it handles pilots who report fatigue.

The Teamsters Airline Division and Local 1224 filed the lawsuit Oct. 23 in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington. The union alleges Horizon requires pilots who report fatigue at their home base to travel to another city as passengers before taking the rest provided under their contract.

The union alleges the practice violates the Railway Labor Act and is asking the court to order Horizon to stop it and restore the negotiated rest protections.

“Management cannot pick and choose which parts of our contract it wants to follow,” said Sean Lenney, a Horizon pilot and member of Local 1224, in a news release.

The Teamsters also said Thursday that 99% of pilots who voted backed a no-confidence measure against Carlos Zendejas, Horizon’s senior vice president of operations. The union’s Horizon Air Pilots Executive Council called for his removal following the vote.

Horizon and its pilots have been negotiating a new collective bargaining agreement for more than three and a half years, according to the union. Pilots held informational pickets in Seattle and Boise, Idaho, on Oct. 15 over issues including pay, staffing, and training.

#6250. Lyft Launches 8% Ride Rewards—Free With Chase DashPass, But Airport Discounts And Priority Pickup Perk Go Away

Lyft’s new membership program earns 8% back in credits on eligible rides, and customers who get DoorDash DashPass through an eligible Chase card can claim it without paying. But they’re also losing benefits like a 10% discount on scheduled airport rides and free Priority Pickup upgrades. Lyft Go launched today, replacing ordinary Lyft Pink and the old DashPass ride benefits. Existing DashPass customers have to activate it even if their Lyft and DoorDash accounts are already linked. And anyone still holding Lyft Pink All Access through Chase: you can’t keep that membership and add Go alongside it. Lyft is selling two versions of Go: Benefit   Lyft Go With DashPass   Lyft Go Core Price   $9.99/month or $96/year   $4.99/month Credits earned   8% of eligible spending   5% of eligible spending Monthly earning limit   $40   $20 Where credits can be used   Eligible Lyft rides or DoorDash orders   Eligible Lyft rides DashPass membership   Included after activation   Not included Relaxed cancellations   3 per month   3 per month Lost-item return fee waiver   Unlimited   Not included Round Up & Donate matching   100%   100% The full plan works in both directions. Pay for Go and get DashPass, which waives delivery fees and reduces service fees on eligible orders, and DashPass members claim full Go at no added cost. DoorDash purchases don’t earn the new 8% rebate but you can spend credits earned with Lyft there. Chase may now get you both complimentary memberships: Make sure your Chase DashPass benefit is activated. Go to DoorDash’s Lyft benefit page, or claim Lyft Go in the DoorDash app. Complete activation, including the confirmation in Lyft. Previously linking the accounts isn’t enough. The complimentary membership lasts while you retain the qualifying membership and keep the accounts linked. And an eligible ride can now earn four layers of rewards: Lyft Go credits: 8% of eligible spending, up to $40 per month. Linked loyalty program points: for example, 2 Bilt points per eligible dollar when Bilt is your selected partner. Credit card rewards: for example, 5 Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar when you pay with an eligible Sapphire card. Card-linked offers: an activated offer for Lyft on the card you use, such as a targeted Chase Offer or SimplyMiles offer when available. You choose one linked loyalty points partner such as Bilt, Alaska Airlines or United. $100 of fare eligible for all three programs, paid with an eligible Sapphire card and credited to Bilt, can earn $8 in Go credits, 200 Bilt points and 500 Chase points – plus whatever card-linked offer applies. Sapphire Reserve and J.P. Morgan Reserve also have their separate $10 monthly Lyft ride credit. Sadly though existing DashPass discounts are going away. I’ve written about combining those discounts with Lyft’s other rewards. The old arrangement gave linked DashPass members: 5% off eligible on-demand rides. 10% off scheduled airport rides. A combined limit of four discounted rides per month. Two free Priority Pickup upgrades monthly. Under DoorDash’s transition terms, those benefits end at 11:59 p.m. Pacific on November 11, or when you activate Go, whichever comes first. So a frequent ordinary ride customer can gain – 8% back instead of 5% off, with earning continuing beyond four rides. A customer using the scheduled airport discount gets a lower percentage, has to spend the savings later, and loses the pickup upgrades. Here’s how the 8% works: Base fare only. Taxes, fees, tolls, tips, donations and amounts covered by coupons, discounts or earned credits don’t earn. 60-day expiration. You have to select credits to use them; they aren’t automatically applied. A monthly cap. Full Go stops earning after $500 in eligible spending. Core stops after $400. Membership dependence. Pausing blocks redemption while expiration continues. Once your membership ends, unused credits become unavailable and can be forfeited. No conversion of old balances. Purchased Lyft Cash, gift cards and unrelated promotional credits don’t become usable on DoorDash. Business profile rides and shared rides don’t earn. Eligible bike and scooter rides do, but Boston and Washington, D.C. bike and scooter rides are excluded. Lyft includes Wait & Save in its announcement, although DoorDash’s launch FAQ contradicts that. DoorDash redemption has exclusions: non-DashPass-eligible orders, DoubleDash, prescriptions, gift cards and group orders. Then there’s the cancellation benefit: Lyft requires you to rebook within 15 minutes and complete the replacement ride. They charge the cancellation fee, then give it back as a ride credit. These aren’t three unconditional free cancellations. Pink All Access members can continue but that’s now closed to new members, you can only hold one membership at a time, and once you leave All Access, you can’t rejoin. Switching to Go requires contacting support. If there’s anyone with Chase DashPass actually paying separately for ordinary Pink that’s a win. DoorDash says to cancel the paid Lyft subscription, then claim complimentary Go through DashPass. The companies won’t automatically consolidate those subscriptions For Chase DashPass customers who weren’t paying for Lyft, this is a modest improvement for frequent ordinary rides and a downgrade for occasional scheduled airport trips. Lyft gets more than a subscription payment out of this change – an immediate discount saves you money even if you never ride again while a credit gets brings you back for another transaction (or costs them nothing if you don’t). Under DoorDash’s transition terms, those benefits end at 11:59 p.m. Pacific on November 11, or when you activate Go, whichever comes first.

#6249. United’s Premium Boeing 787s With New Cabins: Which Routes Do They Fly?

We recently saw United Airlines introduce its long awaited new Boeing 787-9s, featuring all-new cabins, which are being branded as United Elevate. This represents the evolution of the carrier’s long haul experience, including all-new Polaris business class seats.

Of course one common question is which routes actually feature these new planes. So in this post, I’d like to go over that — which planes have the new cabins, and which routes do they fly? The airline is flying these planes on an increasing number of routes out of two hubs, so there are more opportunities to try this product.

Prior to 2026, United already had over 80 Boeing 787 Dreamliners in its fleet, split between the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 variants. However, United is now taking delivery of another 71 Boeing 787-9s, which recently started to be delivered (in addition to 56 Boeing 787-10s, which will be delivered as of 2028).

What’s exciting about these planes is that they feature an all-new passenger experience, and are in an ultra premium configuration. The planes feature just 222 seats, compared to the 257 seats you’ll find on all the previous 787-9s.

If you want to actually fly a United Boeing 787-9 with the new United Elevate interiors, what are your best odds of getting on one of these? The good news is that they’re consistently scheduled on certain routes.

As it currently stands, United has 16 of these 787s in its fleet, with several more expected to be delivered in the coming months. United plans to have 33 of these jets by 2028, so the airline is taking delivery of an average of around one of these per month (though the pace has been even faster in the first several months).

When you go to book a ticket, the best way to tell if a flight is operated by the new plane is whether you see “Polaris Studio available” listed under the United Polaris fare options (assuming those seats are for sale). Otherwise there are no obvious indicators, other than looking at the seat map.

We recently saw the IATA winter season kick off, and with that, we’re seeing the plane based out of both Houston (IAH) and San Francisco (SFO).

You’ll currently find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of San Francisco:

You’ll then find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of Houston:

Let me emphasize that schedules are always subject to change (especially when Boeing delivery delays are a potential factor), and the above is just how things currently stand. I’m also not including flights between San Francisco and Houston, which sometimes see the plane so that it can be rotated between hubs, but obviously that route doesn’t feature the true Polaris soft product.

In recent months, we’ve seen United start to take delivery of its brand new Boeing 787-9s, featuring a more premium layout, plus new cabins. These are exciting planes for passengers, as they feature a much improved onboard experience. They’re also great in terms of upgrade and award availability, given the number of premium seats.

If you want to fly United’s new 787s, you’ll currently find them flying out of Houston and San Francisco. Out of Houston, they’re primarily flying to London, Sao Paulo, Sydney, and Tokyo, while out of San Francisco, they’re primarily flying to London and Singapore. It’s great to see the pace at which United is taking delivery of these planes.

I look forward to trying the new interiors, though I’m hoping to wait until these planes have Starlink installed, since I think that really completes the experience.

What do you make of United’s new Boeing 787-9s, and the routes they’re flying?

#6248. Former American Airlines CEO Explains How Carriers Use Wall Street Analysts To Pressure Rivals To Stop Growing

Doug Parker says airline executives don’t collude by signaling to competitors. However, the former American Airlines CEO explains how executives use Wall Street analysts to pressure other airlines over decisions they don’t like or to back off from competition. On this week’s Airlines Confidential, Parker rejects suggestions of signaling: it “absolutely, positively does not happen.” Yet earlier, describing how airlines enlist analysts, he says they’ll put it to an analyst: “ask them why they’re doing this.” Airlines don’t need a secret meeting where everyone agrees to raise fares. They have fare filings that competitors watch, earnings calls that competitors listen to, and analysts who cover several airlines and can make life uncomfortable for the one that’s adding seats. Whether it violates antitrust law depends on the particulars, but executives certainly do try to send signals to other airlines. American Paid $45 Million To Settle A Capacity Collusion Case While Parker was CEO, American agreed in 2018 to pay $45 million to settle a private antitrust class action. Passengers alleged that major airlines coordinated capacity restraint to increase fares. American also agreed to cooperate with plaintiffs pursuing the remaining defendants. American denied wrongdoing, but paid a very real amount to resolve exactly the sort of allegation he suggests is almost unimaginable. Parker Even Emailed Delta’s CEO Directly To Collude The Justice Department’s 2013 complaint challenging the American–US Airways merger described a 2010 email exchange about a Delta’s aggressive promotion and expansion. Parker, then running US Airways, complained internally about the effect on everyone’s profitability, portrayed Delta as foolish to Wall Street, and forwarded the chain to CEO Richard Anderson. Anderson sent it on to his general counsel. I’ve written about this before. It’s particularly striking because the old email chain and the new podcast describe the same intermediary: Wall Street. Airlines Can Send A Message Without Sending An Email Airlines publish fares through the Airline Tariff Publishing Company. That lets travel sellers distribute prices, and lets competing airlines see and respond to them. Matching a competitor’s fare isn’t, by itself, evidence of an agreement. But pricing departments know how to use the system to get each other’s attention. Fare basis codes. These combinations of letters and numbers identify fares and their rules. I’ve covered the less subtle examples, including discount fares in a competitor’s home market with codes ending in “FU.” That isn’t information a passenger needs to choose a ticket. Economist Severin Borenstein’s account of the government’s earlier fare-filing case explains how codes and footnotes could connect retaliatory fares across markets. Retaliation somewhere else. In the American–JetBlue litigation, the government’s trial filing described JetBlue responding to an American $139 Boston–Los Angeles fare with $139 fares on five routes involving American hubs. The matching amount helped make the connection obvious. Flash fares. The same filing, citing testimony and internal records, described JetBlue planning to flash American over $44 Boston–Philadelphia pricing in February 2020. A fare filing could be used to draw the other airline’s attention to a pricing dispute. Scott Kirby Has Been Doing This In Chicago I laid out the strategy in January when United CEO Scott Kirby used his earnings call to promise a response to American’s growth at Chicago O’Hare. He wanted analysts asking American why it would expand into a fight that United was promising to make expensive. The intended pressure has two audiences. American hears that United will respond. Analysts hear that American’s investment may produce losses, and can press management to stop. If that deters American, United protects its position without having to operate all the additional flights it threatened. An analyst can legitimately believe American is making a bad investment. But American also has to consider the value of a competitive Chicago network to corporate customers, connecting traffic and AAdvantage credit card spending. United’s preferred accounting of the market isn’t necessarily the right one for American or its customers. Bob Crandall Was Less Subtle American’s former chief Bob Crandall famously called Braniff’s Howard Putnam in 1982 and proposed: Raise your goddamn fares twenty percent. I’ll raise mine the next morning. Putnam recorded the conversation and gave it to the government. He didn’t accept the proposal. The Fifth Circuit nevertheless reinstated the government’s attempted-monopolization case, rejecting the idea that an agreement had to be completed for that claim to proceed. Parker’s underlying point about hubs is sensible. An airline with connecting traffic, corporate contracts and loyal local customers has advantages a new entrant doesn’t. You don’t need a secret agreement to explain why a competing hub is hard to build. But natural advantages and efforts to discourage competition can both be true at the same time (and even true without running afoul of the law). That’s why Parker’s narrative about using analysts to send messages is useful. The executive who wants a rival to stop growing doesn’t have to call up directly and ask. It can be enough to make that the next question on its earnings call. But natural advantages and efforts to discourage competition can both be true at the same time (and even true without running afoul of the law). That’s why Parker’s narrative about using analysts to send messages is useful. The executive who wants a rival to stop growing doesn’t have to call up directly and ask. It can be enough to make that the next question on its earnings call. While Parker was CEO, American agreed in 2018 to pay $45 million to settle a private antitrust class action. Passengers alleged that major airlines coordinated capacity restraint to increase fares. American also agreed to cooperate with plaintiffs pursuing the remaining defendants.

American denied wrongdoing, but paid a very real amount to resolve exactly the sort of allegation he suggests is almost unimaginable.

Economist Severin Borenstein’s account of the government’s earlier fare-filing case explains how codes and footnotes could connect retaliatory fares across markets. Retaliation somewhere else. In the American–JetBlue litigation, the government’s trial filing described JetBlue responding to an American $139 Boston–Los Angeles fare with $139 fares on five routes involving American hubs. I laid out the strategy in January when United CEO Scott Kirby used his earnings call to promise a response to American’s growth at Chicago O’Hare. He wanted analysts asking American why it would expand into a fight that United was promising to make expensive.

The intended pressure has two audiences. American hears that United will respond. Analysts hear that American’s investment may produce losses, and can press management to stop. If that deters American, United protects its position without having to operate all the additional flights it threatened.

An analyst can legitimately believe American is making a bad investment. But American also has to consider the value of a competitive Chicago network to corporate customers, connecting traffic and AAdvantage credit card spending. United’s preferred accounting of the market isn’t necessarily the right one for American or its customers.

American’s former chief Bob Crandall famously called Braniff’s Howard Putnam in 1982 and proposed:

Raise your goddamn fares twenty percent. I’ll raise mine the next morning.

Putnam recorded the conversation and gave it to the government. He didn’t accept the proposal. The Fifth Circuit nevertheless reinstated the government’s attempted-monopolization case, rejecting the idea that an agreement had to be completed for that claim to proceed.

Parker’s underlying point about hubs is sensible. An airline with connecting traffic, corporate contracts and loyal local customers has advantages a new entrant doesn’t. You don’t need a secret agreement to explain why a competing hub is hard to build. But natural advantages and efforts to discourage competition can both be true at the same time (and even true without running afoul of the law).

That’s why Parker’s narrative about using analysts to send messages is useful. The executive who wants a rival to stop growing doesn’t have to call up directly and ask. It can be enough to make that the next question on its earnings call.

The $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card is currently offering its best-ever publicly available welcome bonus, which can earn you 100,000 Atmos Rewards points plus a 25K-point Global Companion Award (which I consider to be worth face value).

We only saw this bonus return a couple of weeks ago, and I’d like to provide an update, as I’ve received word that this offer is ending soon (though I don’t have an exact date to share). Obviously this was a very short term limited time offer, so you’ll want to apply ASAP, if interested.

This is one of the most lucrative airline credit cards on the market — it’s a card that I have, and it’s also one that I spend a lot of money on. If you don’t yet have the card, you really can’t go wrong with this, and this is the time to apply.

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card is currently offering a limited time welcome bonus that consists of 100,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award. To qualify, you need to spend $6,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Atmos Rewards points are worth 1.5 cents each. I consider the offer to be worth 125,000 points, putting the value of this at a staggering $1,875. Even if you’re not convinced on the long term value proposition of the card, I absolutely think it’s worth giving a try, given all the uses of Atmos Rewards points.

If you’re interested in applying for the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, the good news is that the application restrictions are pretty limited. Specifically, you are eligible for this card if you have any of the other Atmos Rewards cards, whether personal or business. So you’re eligible for this card even if you have the Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card (learn more) or Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card (learn more).

Personally, I find Bank of America to be one of the most straightforward and easier card issuers to get approvals from, though that’s anecdotal, and I’ve had good luck with these cards.

This card is worth getting for the offer alone, given the huge value for travel on partner airlines, even if it’s “just” for domestic flights on American. But I think the card also offers good long term value, from the annual Global Companion Award, to all the other perks. For that matter, there’s an argument to be made for spending on the card to earn oneworld status.

This is a card that I and everyone else in my family have, so I would seriously recommend considering it, if you haven’t applied already.

#6246. Lockheed Built The Constellation’s Famous Triple Tail For One Key Reason - To Fit Inside An Airline’s Existing Hangars

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

The Lockheed Constellation is one of the most recognizable aircraft ever built, and its most distinctive feature, the triple tail, was not an aesthetic choice. It was a solution to a hangar door. When TWA asked Lockheed to design a long-range pressurized airliner in 1939, one of the requirements was that the aircraft had to fit inside TWA's existing maintenance facilities. A single vertical stabilizer large enough to provide directional stability on a four-engine aircraft of the Constellation's size and speed would have made the tail too tall to clear the hangar doors.

Lockheed's engineers split the required fin area across three shorter vertical stabilizers, keeping the aircraft's overall height to 23 feet 8 inches (7.2 meters). The solution worked; TWA got an aircraft that fit its infrastructure, and Lockheed produced 856 Constellations across all variants before the jet age ended the propeller airliner era. Here is why the triple tail was necessary, how it worked aerodynamically, and what the aircraft contributed to commercial aviation beyond its silhouette.

In 1939, Trans World Airlines owner Howard Hughes approached Lockheed with a set of requirements for a new long-range airliner. Hughes wanted an aircraft that could carry a 6,000-lb (2,720 kg) payload, fly 3,500 miles (5,630 km) without payload, and cruise at more than 250 mph (402 km/h) at 20,000 feet (6,096 meters). Those were aggressive specifications for the era and would have produced a large, heavy, four-engine aircraft substantially bigger than anything TWA was operating. Hughes added one additional requirement: the aircraft had to fit inside TWA's existing maintenance hangars.

That constraint created a specific engineering problem. The Constellation's four Wright R-3350 engines drove large-diameter propellers that required tall landing gear to maintain ground clearance. The tall gear raised the fuselage, which in turn raised the tail. A conventional single vertical stabilizer providing enough area for directional stability on an aircraft of this size and speed would have pushed the total height well beyond what TWA's hangar doors could accommodate. Lockheed's engineers, led by chief engineer Hall Hibbard and chief aerodynamicist Kelly Johnson, needed to provide the required vertical stabilizer area without exceeding the hangar height limit.

The solution was to split the vertical stabilizer into three shorter fins mounted across the horizontal tailplane. Three fins provided the same total surface area as a single large fin while keeping each individual surface short enough to hold the aircraft's overall height to 23 feet 8 inches (7.2 meters). The design fit inside TWA's hangars.

The aerodynamic function of a vertical stabilizer is to provide directional stability by resisting unwanted yaw, keeping the tail of the aircraft tracking behind the nose in straight flight and during turns. The size of the fin determines how much yaw resistance it generates. A larger fin produces more stability. The total area required depends on the aircraft's size, weight, speed range, and the distance between the center of gravity and the tail surfaces. On the Constellation, splitting that area across three fins rather than concentrating it in one did not reduce the total stabilizer area. It redistributed it across three shorter surfaces.

The three-fin arrangement also produced a secondary aerodynamic benefit that a single center fin would not have provided. The two outboard fins sit in the slipstream of the inboard propellers, which means they receive accelerated airflow from the engines at all flight speeds. At low speeds, where a conventional vertical stabilizer is least effective because the airflow over it is slowest, the propeller wash over the outboard fins maintains a higher local airspeed across those surfaces. The result is improved directional stability during takeoff, landing, and low-speed flight, and better yaw authority during single-engine operations when the aircraft needs to counteract the asymmetric thrust of three operating engines against one failed engine.

The triple-tail configuration came with trade-offs. The horizontal stabilizer had to be structurally reinforced to support three fins and the associated loads, which added weight. The flight control system required three rudders instead of one, with corresponding control cables, hinges, and actuators that added mechanical complexity and maintenance requirements. The Douglas DC-6, which competed directly with the Constellation on the same routes, used a conventional single-fin tail and did not pay those weight and complexity penalties.

A nostalgic journey awaits as Lufthansa's iconic aircraft nears completion.

The Constellation was designed at Lockheed's Burbank, California facility under the leadership of two engineers whose careers extended well beyond the program. Hall Hibbard served as chief engineer and Kelly Johnson as chief aerodynamicist during the initial design phase, with project engineer Don Palmer managing the detailed engineering as the program progressed. Johnson, who was 29 when the Constellation project began, would later found Lockheed's Advanced Development Programs division, better known as Skunk Works, where he led the design of the P-80, U-2, and SR-71.

The Constellation's wing was derived from the Lockheed P-38 Lightning fighter, scaled up from a 52-foot (15.8 meters) span to 123 feet (37.5 meters). The structural approach and airfoil design carried over from the fighter program, which gave Lockheed's team a tested aerodynamic foundation to build on rather than starting from a clean sheet. The fuselage was a pressurized aluminum semi-monocoque structure with the distinctive curved dolphin shape that rose at the nose, dipped at the midsection, and rose again toward the tail. The pressurization system maintained a cabin altitude of approximately 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) while cruising at 20,000 feet (6,096 meters), making it one of the first large commercial airliners to offer pressurized flight as a standard feature.

Power came from four Wright R-3350 Duplex-Cyclone 18-cylinder radial engines, the same engine family that powered the Boeing B-29 Superfortress. Each engine produced approximately 2,200 horsepower in early variants, later increased to 2,700 and beyond in the Super Constellation series. The R-3350 was powerful but temperamental, prone to overheating issues that contributed to several incidents during the Constellation's early service years. The aircraft also introduced hydraulically boosted flight controls and a thermal deicing system on the wing and tail leading edges, features that were not standard on contemporary airliners.

The Constellation first flew on January 9, 1943, from Lockheed's Burbank field. It flew not as a TWA airliner but as a military transport designated C-69, requisitioned by the US Army Air Forces after the attack on Pearl Harbor redirected Lockheed's production priorities toward the war effort. The nine L-049 airframes originally ordered by TWA were purchased by the War Department, and 22 C-69s were built between 1943 and 1945. The aircraft spent the war years stateside, used primarily for long-range personnel transport while the Douglas C-54 Skymaster handled the higher-priority overseas airlift missions.

On April 17, 1944, Howard Hughes and TWA president Jack Frye flew the second production C-69 from Burbank to Washington National Airport in 6 hours and 57 minutes, averaging 331 mph (533 km/h) at 65% engine power. The aircraft was painted in full TWA livery despite carrying a military serial number, and the flight was a publicity exercise as much as a delivery. Hughes was required to hand the aircraft over to the Army Air Forces upon landing in Washington. On the return trip, the aircraft stopped at Wright Field in Ohio, where Orville Wright boarded for what would be his last flight, more than 40 years after his first at Kitty Hawk. Wright commented that the Constellation's wingspan was greater than the distance of that first flight.

When the war ended, TWA bought back every C-69 it could from the government and converted them to civilian configuration. Commercial Constellation service began in February 1946, and the aircraft immediately outperformed the Douglas DC-4, the airliner most carriers were using on long-haul domestic and early transatlantic routes. The DC-4 was unpressurized and cruised at approximately 227 mph (365 km/h). The pressurized Constellation cruised at 340 mph (547 km/h) at 20,000 feet (6,096 meters), above most weather. Douglas responded with the pressurized DC-6 in 1947, and later the DC-7, and the resulting competition between Lockheed and Douglas through the 1950s produced the most intensive period of propeller airliner development in aviation history. Lockheed built 856 Constellations across all variants before production ended in 1958, the same year the Boeing 707 entered service and rendered the entire category obsolete.

From the TriStar Stargazer to Buffalo’s Electras and Australia’s Connie — meet the oldest Lockheed commercial aircraft still flying today.

The Constellation introduced several technologies that became standard across commercial aviation. Cabin pressurization at the scale Lockheed implemented allowed airline passengers to fly above weather for the first time on a production airliner, establishing the principle that commercial aircraft should cruise at altitudes where turbulence and storms are below rather than around the aircraft.

Hydraulically boosted flight controls addressed the increasing force required to move control surfaces on larger, faster aircraft, a problem that would only grow as airliners became heavier through the 1950s and into the jet age. The thermal deicing system on wing and tail leading edges replaced the rubber boot deicing used on earlier aircraft with a more reliable heated-air approach. Triple tails disappeared from commercial aviation when jet airliners arrived.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

The Boeing 707, Douglas DC-8, and every subsequent commercial jet used a single vertical stabilizer. The hangars that had constrained the Constellation's designers were replaced or expanded to accommodate the new generation of aircraft, removing the height limitation that had created the three-fin design in the first place. By the time airports were building hangars for the 747 in the late 1960s, no vertical stabilizer height was too tall to accommodate. The engineering problem the triple tail solved ceased to exist.

Of the 856 Constellations built between 1943 and 1958, approximately 55 survive. As of 2026, only two are airworthy. VH-EAG, a C-121C Super Constellation operated by Australia's Historical Aircraft Restoration Society, flies from Illawarra Regional Airport in a restored Qantas livery and carries passengers on demonstration flights. N422NA, a VC-121A named Bataan that served as General Douglas MacArthur's personal transport and later flew for NASA during the Apollo program, is maintained by the Air Legends Foundation and appears at US airshows.

United Airlines is connecting its two West Coast hubs to northern Michigan.

Next summer, the carrier will launch nonstop service to Traverse City, Michigan, from both Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

The two routes will launch on June 19 and run through the peak summer season, according to details shared Thursday by Cherry Capital Airport (TVC). The airport touted the service as something that would give TVC its "first-ever coast-to-coast nonstop footprint."

Traverse City is a popular summer destination, situated on the banks of Grand Traverse Bay, an arm of Lake Michigan.

The region is also home to the famous National Cherry Festival each summer. That century-old extravaganza — which includes an air show — will feature the U.S. Navy's Blue Angels in 2027.

United will operate its California service to Traverse City on Saturdays through the summer.

However, the carrier will also offer flights on select Wednesdays — including before and after the cherry festival.

United will operate a Boeing 737-800 on the route, according to the airport.

That aircraft features 16 domestic first-class recliners across four rows up front, and 150 seats in the main cabin (the number of extra-legroom Economy Plus seats vary from one jet to another)

While United’s Los Angeles and San Francisco routes to TVC are new, the carrier is no stranger to the region.

United already offers service to the airport from each of its other mainland U.S. hubs — including Chicago, Denver, Houston, and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

On top of the two Traverse City routes, United announced additional new service from San Francisco.

The carrier will launch flights to Jacksonville International Airport (JAX) on March 29. That route will operate twice per week, year-round.

Traverse City and Jacksonville give United a total of seven new routes from its Bay Area hub in just the last couple of weeks.

Several of those flights are new transcontinental service, including routes to Hartford, Conn.; Richmond and Norfolk, Va; and Charleston, S.C.

#6244. Amex Platinum Card Review: Benefits & Credits That Easily Justify The Fee

While premium cards are incredibly popular nowadays, this is really a market that Amex started, with the American Express Platinum Card®. It takes some effort to maximize the card’s perks, but if you’re willing to put in the time, the value is potentially incredible.

This is my in-depth Amex Platinum Card review, so let me talk about the card’s value proposition, and the perks that make the Amex Platinum worthwhile. This is a card you should get for the rich benefits that it offers, including the lounge access, credits, and elite status, and not necessarily a card you should spend a lot of money on under normal circumstances, since there are more rewarding cards for that.

Link: Learn more about the American Express Platinum Card®

Before I get into my full Amex Platinum Card review, I want to go over the card’s key details at a glance. The card has such a long list of statement credits that it’s impossible to cover those briefly, so keep reading below to see those, as they could be worth up to thousands of dollars annually. To keep the list to non-statement credit details, here’s what you can expect:

I also put together my pros and cons of the Amex Platinum Card:

The Amex Platinum Card potentially has a huge welcome offer, though the card also has a high annual fee. So let’s cover all those details first, including card eligibility, since these are major factors cardmembers consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Platinum Card currently has the following lucrative welcome bonus offer: You may be eligible for as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $12,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer, so you’ll want to start the application, and then you’ll see what kind of an offer is available to you.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each, so depending on the offer you’re eligible for, this could be worth almost $3,000 in value. That’s pretty stellar, especially for a card that offers so much ongoing value after your first year.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Platinum Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card in the past (so the card has a “once in a lifetime” rule). If you’ve had the card in the past you’re still eligible to be approved, you just won’t get the bonus.

Note that this is a hybrid card and not a credit card, meaning that having this card won’t count toward Amex’s limit of five credit cards per person. Make sure you consider all of Amex’s standard application restrictions before applying.

Eligibility for this card is otherwise unrelated to having any other type of card that’s not an Amex Platinum, so lots of people should be eligible for the offer.

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee. Even among premium cards, this is among the highest annual fees out there, though for many people, the perks will more than offset the fee.

If you want to add authorized users to the card, you’ll pay $195 each (Rates & Fees). Fortunately there are some solid perks for authorized users, including lounge access, so some people might find that adding them is worthwhile.

As you’d expect of a premium travel card, the Amex Platinum has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees). This means you can use it abroad without racking up fees, though it’s not usually the best card for maximizing everyday spending on categories like dining.

Personally, I think the Amex Platinum Card is worth having for the benefits it offers, though it’s not a card that I think is worth spending much money on, with limited exceptions.

Some other Amex cards offer big bonus categories. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x Membership Rewards points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, and then 1x points) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 of spending per calendar year, and then 1x points), which is extremely lucrative.

Unfortunately, the Amex Platinum Card isn’t as generous in that regard. However, there are still some useful bonus categories…

The best bonus category on the Amex Platinum Card is 5x points on airfare purchased directly from airlines or through American Express Travel® (on up to $500,000 of flight purchases per calendar year, and then 1x points). This is spectacular, and it makes it the best card for airfare purchases, in my opinion.

Officially booking through online travel agencies (except amextravel.com) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice it may still sometimes code for 5x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them.

I value Membership Rewards points at 1.7 cents each, so to me, that’s the equivalent of an 8.5% return on airfare spending, which is incredible.

The Amex Platinum Card also offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

The exception is Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, where prepaid reservations earn 5x points. That can be a good deal because of the perks you get, and also because you still earn points with your preferred hotel loyalty program. You can also combine this with the card’s annual hotel credit to really maximize value. I’ll talk more about that in a bit.

The above are the only bonus categories — otherwise, the Amex Platinum Card offers 1x points per dollar spent, which isn’t especially good. There are other cards offering 1.5x-2x points per dollar spent, so I would much rather put my spending on those cards, or on another card that’s best for everyday spending.

The Amex Platinum Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many. While I love Membership Rewards, I’d say that not everyone should be earning these points.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to the below airline partners and hotel partners.

The reason this represents such a good option is that you can get outsized value toward premium airfare, especially for travel in first and business class. These tickets are often super expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal with points.

For example, I frequently transfer my Amex Membership Rewards points to Air France-KLM, and then redeem 60,000 points for business class across the Atlantic. Best of all, there are sometimes transfer bonuses of up to 25-30%, which lowers my real “out of pocket” in terms of Amex points even further.

I’d note that while you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than one cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Platinum Card really shines when it comes to its credits, as the card potentially offers thousands of dollars in annual credits. As you can imagine, for some people this alone will more than justify the annual fee. The catch is that there are some hurdles to using all of these, so don’t consider most of these credits to be worth face value.

However, I’d argue that it’s quite easy to recoup your entire annual fee on these credits alone. So let’s take a look at what you need to know about these credits, and how you can maximize them. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $600 per year in hotel credits. This is a semi-annual credit, so you get a $300 credit in January through June, and a $300 credit in July through December.

This is actually a pretty easy perk to use — just book a prepaid hotel through Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts® (no minimum stay) or The Hotel Collection (two night minimum stay) through American Express Travel®, and you can receive up to a $300 credit semi-annually. Effective January 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts® bookings will require a minimum two-night stay to be eligible for the Hotel Credit.

If you ask me, this perk alone can help recoup most of the card’s annual fee. So a major point in deciding whether this card makes sense is crunching the numbers as to whether you can get full value from this.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $400 per year in Resy credits, and enrollment is required. This is a quarterly credit, so the idea is that you receive up to $100 worth of statement credits each calendar quarter toward dining at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants.

There are no hoops you have to jump through, so as long as you dine at an eligible Resy restaurant and pay with your card, you can receive the statement credit. Personally, I’d consider this benefit to be worth close to face value.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in digital entertainment credits, with enrollment being required. This comes in the form of a $25 monthly statement credit on eligible purchases or subscriptions with any of the following:

I’d consider this to be quite valuable, since there’s an impressive variety of partners with which you can maximize this perk.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in Lululemon credits, with enrollment being required. This is a quarterly credit, so the idea is that you receive up to $75 worth of statement credits each calendar quarter toward purchases at Lululemon stores in the U.S. If you’re in the market for some athleisure wear, this is a great option.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in Equinox credits, and enrollment is required. This comes in the form of up to $300 in statement credits each year on a digital or club membership at Equinox. If you’d otherwise pay for an Equinox membership, this is a great perk, while otherwise, it’s probably of limited value.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a $300 credit when purchasing a SoulCycle bike. This credit can be used toward the purchase of a SoulCycle at-home bike, and it can be used for the purchase of up to 15 bikes per year.

You need to make the entire purchase of a bike in one transaction on your Amex Platinum Card in order to qualify for these savings. Suffice to say that this will be of limited value to most cardmembers.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $219 per year in CLEAR credits. When using your card to pay for a CLEAR membership, you’ll receive statement credits of up to $219 per calendar year. For those not familiar with CLEAR, this company can save you time at security, by allowing you to use your biometric data to skip the ID check.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in airline fee credits, which can be used toward airline incidentals and fees. The credit is offered every calendar year, so it follows a strict January 1 through December 31 calendar.

Every year you can designate on which airline you want to receive the credit, of the following:

You can change your airline selection in January of each year. If you don’t change your selection, then you automatically keep the same airline choice as the previous year.

Unfortunately, you can’t use your credit toward the following:

Airline tickets, upgrades, mileage points purchases, mileage points transfer fees, gift cards, duty free purchases, and award tickets are not deemed to be incidental fees.

This is particularly useful for airline ticket change fees (of which there are few nowadays), baggage fees, and other costs you may incur with an airline. Personally, this is something I have no trouble maxing out.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in Oura Ring credits. This is valid if you use your card to purchase an Oura Ring through ouraring.com, and enrollment is required. I’d say this is very niche, but if you’re in the market for this product, it has the potential to be valuable.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in Uber credits. The way this is broken up, you get a $15 credit per month, and then in December, you get a total of $35 in credits. You can use this either for rides with Uber in the US, or for food with Uber Eats in the US.

To activate this benefit, you need to enter your Amex Platinum Card card number on your Uber account, and then you should see the benefit unlocked. You’ll see an amount added to your Uber Cash balance every month, and the discount will automatically be applied to the first eligible ride or food delivery.

An Amex Card must be selected as the payment method for your Uber or Uber Eats transaction to redeem the Amex Uber Cash benefit

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $120 in statement credits each calendar year after purchasing an auto-renewing Uber One membership with the card. This is separate from the card’s $200 annual Uber Cash benefit.

An Uber One membership offers all kinds of benefits for rides with Uber and deliveries with Uber Eats, so if you use the platform with any frequency, this is pretty valuable.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $12.95 per month in credits toward a Walmart+ membership, which covers the full membership cost. Enrollment is required. (Up to $12.95 plus applicable local sales tax. Plus Ups not eligible.) With Walmart+, you can receive free deliveries on groceries or get savings at gas stations or on video streaming.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck statement credit every four years. Simply charge the membership fee to your card, and it will be automatically reimbursed. It’s worth getting Global Entry, which has a $120 application fee compared to PreCheck’s $85, because it includes TSA PreCheck membership too.

It doesn’t matter who the fee is being paid for, as long as you charge it to your eligible card.

The Amex Platinum Card offers one of the most comprehensive lounge access benefits of any card. This is called the Global Lounge Collection, and it offers access to over 1,550 airport lounges across 140 countries for eligible cardmembers. This includes proprietary Amex lounges, as well as access to lounges run by other airlines and companies.

Before I go through the details, let me mention that Lufthansa lounge access has been cut as of October 1, 2026, which is why I’m not including it in the list, though that used to be a benefit.

Amex is well known for its Centurion Lounges, and the Amex Platinum Card can get you into these lounges. These are significantly better than what you’ll find in most U.S. airline lounges, with a solid selection of hot food and cocktails.

Currently, U.S. locations include Atlanta, Charlotte, Dallas, Denver, Houston, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Miami, New York JFK, New York LaGuardia, Philadelphia, Phoenix, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, with more to come. There are also Centurion Lounges in Amsterdam, Hong Kong, London, and Tokyo, among other international destinations.

You can access these lounges up to three hours before your flight’s departure (if you’re connecting, then the three-hour limit doesn’t apply). Please note that you’re only eligible to bring in guests on a complimentary basis if you spend at least $75,000 per calendar year on the card.

The Amex Platinum Card also offers access to the Delta Sky Club, with some limitations. Card members can receive access within three hours of a departing or arriving flight, and must present their card, a boarding pass showing a confirmed reservation for an eligible Delta flight, and a government-issued ID.

Eligible cards issued in the United States receive 10 visits to the Delta Sky Club each year, to be used from February 1 until January 31 of the next calendar year, with all visits within a 24-hour period counting as a single visit. It’s also possible to earn an unlimited number of visits by spending $75,000 in eligible purchases on a card account in a calendar year.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a Priority Pass™ membership, which gives you access to lounges around the world. You can bring up to two guests into these lounges. While these aren’t the most exciting and high quality lounges, there’s no denying that this gives you access to a comprehensive collection of lounges.

The Amex Platinum Card offers access to Plaza Premium Lounges. Just present your Amex Platinum Card, and you’ll be admitted, and you can even bring one guest with you at no additional cost. This is hugely valuable, as Plaza Premium has dozens of lounges around the world, which are among the highest quality contract lounges you’ll find.

The Amex Platinum Card offers access to the growing network of Escape Lounges. Just present your Amex Platinum Card and you’ll be admitted, and you can even bring in guests.

Beyond the annual credits that potentially more than justify the annual fee, as well as an incredible lounge access program, the Amex Platinum Card also offers status with three hotel loyalty programs, status with three rental car loyalty programs, access to a program that gets you valuable hotel perks, and discounts on many premium cabin airline tickets. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive complimentary Hilton Gold elite status for as long as they have the card. This status is useful, and offers the following perks:

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive complimentary Marriott Gold status for as long as they have the card, which offers the following perks, among other things:

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive Leaders Club Sterling status from Leading Hotels of the World. Leading Hotels of the World is a collection of independent, luxury properties, so this offers perks at some properties that don’t otherwise participate in major global hotel groups.

This status typically requires $5,000 in annual spending at these hotels and offers perks such as five pre-arrival upgrades per year.

The Amex Platinum Card offers Hertz President’s Circle elite status, which is Hertz’s top-tier status. Your status is valid as long as you remain a cardmember; you just need to enroll. This should take the pain out of renting cars and offers the following perks:

The Amex Platinum Card offers National Emerald Club Executive status. You have to enroll to take advantage of this, and it’s valid for as long as you have your card. National is my favorite rental car company, and Executive status lets you pick out your car from the lot, and skip the counter altogether.

The Amex Platinum also offers Avis Preferred Plus status. Once you enroll, you’ll get this mid-tier status level with the rental car company and qualify for complimentary upgrades when available, a 25% points bonus, and a dedicated reservation and customer service line. You also get access to a discount code that can save you up to 25% off qualifying rentals.

With the Platinum Member Airfares program (formerly known as the International Airline Program), you can save on the cost of international first class, business class, and premium economy airfare, on around two dozen airlines. This typically provides discounts even on already discounted tickets, so is a spectacular value.

If you book paid international premium cabin travel with any frequency, this could cover the card’s annual fee over and over.

With the Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts® program, you can receive extra perks for stays at over 1,900 luxury hotels around the world. These benefits include the following:

Best of all, the rate is typically in line with the best available rate. Having the Amex Platinum Card gets you access to this, and if you prepay your reservation, you even earn 5x points. You can even stack this with the card’s up to $600 annual hotel credit.

The Amex Platinum Card offers several travel insurance benefits that can add extra peace of mind. You’ll want to consult the card’s benefits guide for the exact terms and any caps and exclusions, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $500 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 6 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company. Baggage insurance plan: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

The card also offers an extended warranty protection benefit as well as purchase, return, and cell phone protection.

Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

What benefits do authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card get? They receive most of the same perks as primary cardmembers.

This includes all the lounge access perks, access to Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, Hilton and Marriott Gold status, Leading Hotels of the World Sterling status, access to the Amex International Airline Program, additional Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credits, and more.

The main thing that authorized users aren’t getting is incremental credits, so they’re not receiving extra airline fee credits, digital entertainment credits, Uber credits, etc.

Of course there’s never going to be any “one size fits all” answer as to whether a card makes sense, since we all value perks differently. However, speaking only for myself, I’d argue that the Amex Platinum Card is rather easy to justify.

To start, let’s just take a look at the credits. Personally, I’m able to get full value out of the $600 annual hotel credit, $400 annual Resy credit, $300 annual digital entertainment credit, $200 annual airline fee credit, and $200 annual Uber credit. That’s $1,700 in value right there, and it actually doesn’t take much effort for me to maximize that.

That also says nothing of all the other perks offered by the card, from the bonus points on airfare, to the lounge access, and more. So yeah, I’m really finding this card to be pretty great. Let me emphasize that in 2027 the hotel credit will be harder to maximize, so I’ll need to assess how much value I get out of that. But even if you drop that benefit entirely, I’m still getting $1,100 in value from the other credits.

Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves, but I think the math works out very nicely on this product. But that’s not the case for everyone. So who should skip the Amex Platinum Card?

If it won’t be easy for you to get full value out of the card’s many travel and statement credits — or even if you just don’t want to be troubled with keeping track of so many credits to prevent leaving value on the table — the Amex Platinum may not be the card for you. Credit card fatigue is a real problem!

It’s also not a great card for everyday spending, since it doesn’t earn bonus rewards on categories like dining. I’ve written a more detailed post specifically addressing the question of whether the Amex Platinum is worth it, so I recommend checking that out.

This also brings me to the next section, which is the best Amex Platinum alternatives.

There are several premium cards to choose from nowadays, so it always makes sense to look at what the competition is offering. Let’s look at a few popular alternatives to the Amex Platinum.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) is the other premium card heavy hitter, with a slightly lower annual fee of $795. I have a full post comparing the Amex Platinum and Chase Sapphire Reserve — my verdict is that both cards are worth having, but if you can only pick one, the Sapphire Reserve is better for lazy optimizers while the Amex Platinum is better for those willing to put some real work into optimizing all the card’s benefits.

Here’s an overview of the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s standout features. It’s no slouch when it comes to perks, but its list of benefits and statement credits is considerably shorter than the Amex Platinum Card’s. Specifically:

If you take full advantage of the Amex Platinum’s main statement credits for travel and dining, it has the potential to offer more value than the Chase Sapphire Reserve. But the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s earning rates are better for maximizing everyday purchases, and you might prefer having fewer “coupon book” style benefits to keep track of.

In my opinion, the Amex Gold Card (learn more) is one of the most rewarding cards out there. At $325 (Rates & Fees), its annual fee is significantly lower than the Amex Platinum Card’s, and while it doesn’t have as many benefits, it’s a better choice for everyday spending, especially if you eat out frequently.

Here are the highlights of the Amex Gold:

The Amex Gold Card can’t beat the Platinum when it comes to travel perks, but if your main goal is earning as many Amex points as possible on your spending, it could be a more useful everyday pick.

The Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another premium card with an annual fee that’s one step down from the Amex Platinum — in this case, it’s $395. I find this card to offer strong value, and it’s much simpler than the Amex Platinum Card:

The travel credit and anniversary bonus miles help justify the annual fee, and while 2x miles isn’t the highest everyday spending rate, it’s a better base than 1x points with the Amex Platinum. It’s also worth comparing Amex points with Capital One miles to see which currency you prefer before making a final decision.

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee and a much longer list of credits than it used to. This isn’t a card that you should get for the return on spending it offers, but instead, it’s a card to get for all of the perks and credits that it offers.

While the $895 annual fee is obviously steep, personally I’m able to get outsized value thanks to all the credits offered, which offer significant value. And that says nothing of the bonus points on airfare, the lounge access, and more.

So even if you haven’t been able to make the math on this card work in the past, it might be time to give it another look.

If you want to learn more about the Amex Platinum Card, follow this link.
