#6243. Wyndham Is Giving Members Free Hotel Status Upgrades—Some Can Claim 3,000 Points Instead

You have to register, and the gift depends on your current status, where you live, and whether you’re already enrolled in Wyndham’s Insider subscription.

I don’t get excited about Wyndham status, but free status and free points are good things. If you don’t have hotel status today, having something could be an avenue to match somewhere else. So it could be worth a couple of clicks, even more so if you have a Wyndham stay coming up.

Claim the status upgrade by December 30, 2026. It lasts through December 31, 2026, and Wyndham says to allow 24–48 hours for it to take effect. (Do it on December 30 and it may activate and expire simultaneously – yay!) New members can join and claim Gold. Note that you can’t use the promotional status to match to Caesars Rewards.

The upgraded earning rate is determined by your status at checkout. A stay ending January 1 won’t earn the holiday status bonus.

Wyndham normally requires 5 qualifying nights for Gold, 15 for Platinum, and 40 for Diamond. The benefits are modest:

Preferred room choice means a better location or view within the room category you booked. Early check-in and late checkout are subject to availability, generally up to two hours before or after the hotel’s stated time. Diamond suite upgrades depend on availability at check-in.

As I explained when I looked at Wyndham’s instructions to hotels, you should ask for the preferred room and checkout benefits. And there’s no program-wide elite breakfast or lounge benefit. At a hotel earning the usual 10 base points per dollar, moving from Platinum to Diamond adds just 50 points on $100 of eligible spending. That’s 35 cents at a valuation of 0.7 cents per point.

Eligible Diamonds need to claim their 3,000 points by December 31, 2026.

Members who become Diamond through this holiday upgrade don’t qualify for the points gift. Neither do members with a competitor status match unless they’ve completed the required 10 qualifying nights within 90 days of receiving that matched status.

Wyndham’s messaging on this says 3,000 points are enough for a discounted night at any participating hotel. That doesn’t actually match their current award chart.

Following the September 15 devaluation, standard free nights cost 5,000, 15,000, 30,000 or 45,000 points per bedroom. The points plus cash price at a 45,000-point hotel starts at 4,500 points plus the cash portion.

Ultimately Wyndham has lost much of what made it interesting to me: Vacasa redemptions are gone, the easy credit card route to Caesars Diamond ended, and the top award price rose 50%.

Wyndham Rewards Insider normally costs $95 per year and automatically renews. It offers hotel discounts, extra points, and access to deals on flights, cruises, rental cars, activities and entertainment, along with a concierge.

The advertised 50% increase in earning applies to the elite bonus. A Diamond’s bonus rises from 20% to 30%, so ordinary earning at a 10-point-per-dollar hotel goes from 12 to 13 points per dollar or 8.3% more points. And the hotel discount isn’t a promise of the lowest price. Wyndham acknowledges that another rate available to non-Insiders can be cheaper. Buying Platinum could make sense for someone who isn’t, can’t status match, but still plans a bunch of Wyndham stays upcoming.

The holiday upgrade can be combined with Wyndham’s current 4X points promotion. Register before booking, book direct by January 15, 2027, and complete eligible paid stays by January 19. The holiday status itself ends December 31. The multiplier applies to base points, with a cap of 15,000 promotional bonus points. At the normal 10-point base rate, a non-Insider Diamond earns 40 points per dollar from the base earning and promotion, plus 2 elite bonus points (not four times their usual 12). Insiders can earn another 5,000 points after two qualifying nights, either together or across two stays. That bonus doesn’t stack with the separate Wyndham cardholder bonus. Premier cardholders can earn 10,000 instead. For an upcoming stay, claim your status first and register for the points promotion before making the reservation since a booking made before promotion registration doesn’t qualify. #6242. The 6 Best Airplane Bathrooms On Any Airline: The A380 Reigns Supreme

When most people think of airplane bathrooms, it’s probably not a nice image that comes to mind. Airlines have largely shrunk bathrooms on newer aircraft significantly, and at times they’re also not very well maintained.

That’s not true across the board, though. In premium cabins, we’ve seen airlines introduce some pretty amazing amenities in recent years, and that even includes awesome bathrooms.

In this post, I’d like to share what I consider to be the airlines with the best first class bathrooms (somewhat overlapping with my list of the world’s best first class airlines).

Unsurprisingly, the Airbus A380 takes center stage on this flight, as it’s an aircraft that has ushered in the most bathroom innovation. That’s because the front of the upper deck has a bit of extra space that can’t be utilized for seats, making room for some cool amenities.

With that in mind, below are my six favorite airplane bathrooms, roughly ranked…

Emirates A380 first class is one of my all-around favorite first class products, and a large part of that is the amazing A380 first class shower suites.

Emirates’ A380s have two first class shower suites at the front of the upper deck, equipped with heated floors, enough amenities to start a toiletry resale business, and most importantly, a shower.

As a first class passenger, you can schedule a shower at the beginning of your flight, and while there’s no time limit to how long you can use the shower spa, you’re limited to five minutes of water. Fortunately you can turn the water on and off without the clock “running,” so that’s more than enough water for a nice shower.

Of all the excitement I’ve experienced in the air, I don’t think anything compares to the first time I took a shower on Emirates. The airline even has shower spa attendants, who make sure the shower spas are well maintained throughout the flight.

Etihad A380 first class consists of nine “First Class Apartments,” and these passengers have access to the shower suite at the front of the cabin. Much like on Emirates, each passenger gets five minutes of water, and the shower suite is refreshed between each use.

While this is a great and refreshing feature, the shower suite definitely isn’t as spacious as on Emirates. So if you’re used to showering on Emirates, you might find that it’s a bit tight, but otherwise you’ll no doubt be delighted. Also keep in mind that there’s still The Residence on Etihad, which is a three room suite that can be reserved as an upgrade over the standard first class. This comes with a private bathroom, including shower.

Singapore Airlines A380 Suites is an incredible first class product, with only six seats in the cabin. While you won’t find a shower on Singapore Airlines’ A380s, you will find some of the most spacious bathrooms in the sky. One of the lavatories has a huge vanity, and is probably the size of 10 typical Boeing 737 MAX bathrooms. Airplane bathrooms don’t get much more luxurious than this!

Qatar Airways A380 first class has two very nice lavatories at the front of the upper deck. While there aren’t any special amenities, you’ll find that they’re incredibly spacious, and nicely decorated.

Lufthansa A380 first class features two huge lavatories at the front of the upper deck, each equipped with a bench, and most excitingly, a urinal! Lufthansa is the only airline to offer urinals on planes, so that’s pretty special… or something.

While we’re speaking of Lufthansa, I have a soft spot for Lufthansa 747-8 first class, probably at least partly because the Boeing 747-8 is my favorite plane as an avgeek. While not quite as over the top as some of the other options, Lufthansa’s 747-8 lavatories are spacious, have a bench you can extend out over the toilet, and most importantly, have a window. It’s so nice to be able to look out the window while in the lavatory.

Lastly on the topic of Lufthansa and lavatories, I do have to bring up how cool the economy lavatories on the carrier’s A340-600s were (these planes were just recently retired). They were located on the “lower deck” (in a cargo compartment), so they were probably the most unusual lavatories you could’ve recently found in commercial service. By comparison, the Lufthansa A340 first class lavatories weren’t much to get excited about at all.

All Nippon Airways A380 first class has two large, identical lavatories at the front of the upper deck. They’re huge, but there are also a couple of thoughtful design touches that I appreciate about them.

For one, ANA has a bidet function for its toilets, which is always a nice feature to have. I also appreciate how there’s a “plank” of sorts that you can extend on the ground, for situations where you want to change into pajamas without touching the regular floor of the bathroom.

On top of that, ANA does an amazing job with keeping its lavatories clean between each use, down to folding the toilet paper into perfect triangles.

Now, in fairness, there are a decent number of products with a bidet function in service, from Japan Airlines A350 first class, to Gulf Air 787 business class, to Oman Air 787 business class.

There are some pretty incredible airplane bathrooms out there. While nothing can compete with Emirates’ amazing shower suites, there are plenty of other impressive airplane bathrooms out there as well, with everything from vanities, to bidets, to urinals. As A380s increasingly get retired, unfortunately going to the bathroom on a plane is getting less pleasant!

What’s your favorite bathroom on a commercial aircraft?

#6241. Passenger Forced To Pay ‘Employee Retention Fee’ For JFK Airport Self-Checkout Machines

A traveler buying a $21.99 book at New York JFK used self-checkout but was still forced to pay an employee retention surcharge. Hudson’s Bryant Park Market in terminal 5 added the mandatory 3% fee, then sales tax on the fee. Does the machine’s employee wellness program cover maintenance on the cooling fan, or maybe paid time off to install Windows updates? The passenger bought John U. Bacon’s The Gales of November: The Untold Story of the Edmund Fitzgerald, and shared the self-checkout receipt. A 3% surcharge has been applied to your purchase. This charge is for employee and retention programs and is not a gratuity. Mandatory employee fee at bookstore when I used self checkout.by u/alternativo- in EndTipping The tax on the surcharge annoyed the shopper, too. But New York calculates sales tax on the full taxable purchase price. And the surcharge is just a hidden part of the price. I’ve written about airports allowing surcharges as an end-run around their own pricing rules. The Port Authority of New York New Jersey is clear on this. Its regulation generally caps prices at 15% above comparable street prices, but expressly allows an additional employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%. The regulation also excludes the employee fee from gross receipts under agreements where the Port Authority collects a share of concession revenue. I covered the same 3% employee benefit and retention charge at a Newark self-checkout last year. The Port Authority tells merchants to add the fee, and incentivize them to do it – moving part of the price into fees means they get to keep more of the money. Philadelphia authorized a similar 3% add-on while retaining its street price cap. There it was expressly a way to let merchants charge passengers more and circumvent the cap. Minneapolis prefers a 4.5% hospitality charge with signage explaining it wasn’t a tip and didn’t go to the people providing the hospitality. The employee fee on this book isn’t a tip, but airport machines have been demanding those, too. In Austin, I couldn’t pay for a bottle of water without entering a tip. The terminal rejected $0.00. Staff confirmed it, and the transaction only went through when I entered a penny. Earlier this year I also flagged an Austin airport self-checkout that defaulted to an 18% tip while adding a card processing surcharge. One commenter asked about the JFK airport charge, “Since I would be paying the employee retention fee, do i get a say which employees stay or go?” I’d retain the scanner, but put whomever programmed the surcharge on a performance improvement plan. #6240. The Airlines Offering Premium Economy On Airbus A380 Flights

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Six of the 10 airlines still flying the Airbus A380 offer a premium economy cabin on the type. British Airways will shortly have the largest at 84 seats, following the retrofit announced on October 5, 2026, which also gives its aircraft the highest premium ratio of any A380 at roughly 48%. All Nippon Airways (ANA) follows at 73 seats, then Qantas at 60, Emirates at 56, Lufthansa at 52, and Singapore Airlines at 44.

The four without it are Qatar Airways, Etihad, Korean Air and Asiana. Qatar's layout of 8 first, 48 business and 461 economy produces a premium ratio of around 11%, the lowest among A380 operators. Where the cabin exists, the experience varies considerably. Emirates won the Skytrax award for best premium economy seat in 2026 and is adding the cabin to 68 A380 routes. ANA fits 73 premium economy seats against only 56 in business and flies them on a single route between Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT) and Honolulu (HNL).

British Airways announced a full retrofit of its Airbus A380 fleet on October 5, 2026, and the new layout puts World Traveller Plus at 84 seats. That is the largest premium economy cabin on any A380 operating anywhere. The refurbished configuration runs 12 First, 106 Club Suites, 84 World Traveller Plus and 215 World Traveller for a total of 417 seats, down from 469 in the current layout. Economy absorbs the entire reduction, falling by 88 seats, while premium economy grows by more than half.

The proportions are what make the aircraft unusual. Head for Points calculated that the new layout gives British Airways 202 premium seats, roughly 48% of the aircraft, which is the highest premium ratio of any A380 operator by a wide margin. Emirates and Qantas are the next closest at around 30%, and both carry at least 56 fewer premium seats than the refurbished BA aircraft will. Since the A380 is the largest passenger aircraft ever built, that also gives British Airways the highest absolute number of premium seats on any single aircraft in service.

The timing matters for anyone trying to book. The first refurbished aircraft is expected in service within months, with the program running into 2027 and 2028, which means the 84-seat cabin will exist alongside the older 55-seat World Traveller Plus layout across the fleet for an extended period. British Airways operates 12 A380s to a small number of destinations from London Heathrow Airport (LHR), so the chance of drawing a refurbished aircraft on any given booking depends on how far along the program the fleet has progressed.

Emirates won the Skytrax award for the best premium economy seat in 2026, finishing ahead of Cathay Pacific and EVA Air, and The Points Guy named it Best International Premium Economy for a second consecutive year. AirlineRatings.com's passenger-voted Flyers' Choice Awards also named Emirates the preferred premium economy. The airline ranks second overall for premium economy with Skytrax and first for both the seats and the catering.

The A380 cabin seats 56 passengers within a four-class layout of 14 first, 76 business, 56 premium economy and 341 economy, giving the aircraft 146 premium seats and a premium ratio of around 30%. The seats are leather with adjustable headrests, calf rests, and footrests, and Emirates serves multicourse meals on china tableware with stainless steel cutlery, which is closer to a business class service pattern than most premium economy products attempt.

Scale is the other factor. Emirates operates roughly half the world's A380 fleet, with 116 aircraft, about 100 of which are active, and premium economy is arriving through the carrier's retrofit program rather than on new deliveries. The cabin joined Dubai to Milan on A380 services from November 10, 2025, alongside New York routes, and Emirates confirmed plans to offer premium economy on 68 routes by March 2026. Given the size of the fleet receiving it, a passenger searching for premium economy on a superjumbo will find more Emirates departures than from any other operator.

The cost of the world's longest A380 premium economy fares typically range within the $2,000-2,500, although this varies by discounts and season.

Qantas carries 60 premium economy seats on its A380s within a four-class layout of 14 first, 70 business, 60 premium economy and 341 economy, totaling 485 seats. That gives the aircraft 144 premium seats and a premium ratio of around 30%, effectively matching Emirates. The seats offer more width and legroom than economy, with adjustable headrests, footrests, storage and charging ports, and the fare includes priority check-in, priority boarding, upgraded meals, noise-canceling headphones and an amenity kit. Qantas operates 10 A380s, with around eight active, on routes from Sydney and Melbourne to London, Los Angeles, Dallas and Singapore.

Lufthansa fits 52 premium economy seats into a 509-seat A380 alongside 8 first, 78 business and 371 economy. The carrier operates eight aircraft and has committed to the type while retiring other quadjets, with summer 2026 routes including Los Angeles, Boston, Denver, Washington and Delhi, plus a new Munich to Mumbai service from July 2026. Lufthansa's premium economy ranks seventh overall in Skytrax's 2026 assessment and fifth for the seat specifically, though its highest-rated version is the Allegris cabin on the A350 and 787-9 rather than the A380.

Singapore Airlines has the smallest premium economy cabin on the type at 44 seats, in a 471-seat aircraft carrying 6 suites, 78 business and 343 economy. That is a premium ratio of around 27%, the lowest of the three. The product itself rates highly, placing third overall with Skytrax for premium economy and fourth for the seat, with calf and footrests, personal storage, charging ports and large entertainment screens. Premium economy passengers also get the Book the Cook service, allowing a main course to be reserved before departure, alongside priority check-in, boarding and baggage handling. The carrier operates 12 A380s across eight major routes from Changi for summer 2026.

All Nippon Airways carries 73 premium economy seats on its A380s, which ANA's own fleet material confirms in a 520-seat layout of 8 first, 56 business, 73 premium economy and 383 economy. That makes it the second-largest premium economy cabin on any A380, and Simple Flying reported it as the largest premium economy cabin across ANA's entire fleet. The seats sit at the rear of the upper deck behind first and business, arranged 2-3-2.

The aircraft itself is unlike any other A380 operation. ANA has three, each painted in a different sea turtle livery, and every scheduled A380 flight operates between Narita and Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) in Honolulu. No other operator confines the type to a single route. The aircraft entered service in May 2019 and continues to fly Narita to Honolulu year-round, with ANA adjusting frequencies seasonally. The third airframe only entered commercial service in late 2023 after an extended period in storage during the pandemic.

The configuration reflects who the aircraft carries. ANA built it around the Hawaii leisure market, and the cabin mix shows it, with 73 premium economy seats against 56 in business. The economy deck includes ANA COUCHii, where groups of three or four seats convert into a sofa-style space with raisable leg rests for an additional fee, which Airport Spotting described as aimed at families traveling with young children. For a passenger wanting premium economy on an A380, ANA offers one of the largest cabins available and the only route where you can find it.

A pro-Russian Serbian politician has allegedly caused a jet to return to Belgrade after dodging security

Four airlines fly the A380 with no premium economy cabin. Qatar Airways configures its aircraft with 8 first, 48 business and 461 economy seats across 517 total, giving it 56 premium seats and a premium ratio of around 11%, the lowest of any A380 operator by a substantial margin. Simple Flying excluded Qatar entirely from an earlier comparison of premium economy fares on the world's longest A380 routes, noting the airline does not offer the cabin on the type.

Etihad, Korean Air and Asiana complete the group. Etihad operates nine A380s and Asiana six, with Asiana running a three-class layout that includes 104 upper deck economy seats arranged 2-4-2. Those Asiana aircraft are also on borrowed time. Simple Flying reported that following the Korean Air merger, both carriers were expected to retire the type as part of fleet optimization.

The division is not a straightforward premium versus budget split. Qatar Airways has one of the most highly regarded business class products in the industry in Qsuite, yet its A380 carries the smallest proportion of premium seating of any operator of the type. A passenger wanting more than economy on a Qatar A380 has to buy business outright, with no intermediate option. Across the roughly 10 airlines still operating the A380, six offer premium economy and four do not, meaning the cabin is available on most superjumbo flights but not all of them.

#6239. Flagship Dining: American Expands A La Carte Lounge Dining To Business Class

Several weeks back, American announced plans to completely change the concept for its Flagship First Dining facilities, as the airline eliminates international first class. With this, we’re seeing Flagship First Dining simply rebranded as Flagship Dining, with business class passengers also getting access.

While these changes went “live” as of September 15, 2026, there’s now an additional update, as a third Flagship Dining facility has just opened, so you can now enjoy this experience in Dallas (DFW), Los Angeles (LAX), and Miami (MIA). Let’s cover all the details.

For years, American had Flagship First Dining, which are facilities inside select Flagship Lounges. The idea was that this offers an a la carte dining experience for those traveling in international or premium transcontinental first class.

American is currently in the process of eliminating “premium” first class — Boeing 777-300ERs are being reconfigured without first class, while Airbus A321XLRs (without first class) are replacing A321Ts. First class is no longer being sold on the wide bodies as of November 19, 2026, or on the narrow bodies as of March 28, 2027. So there has been a big question as to what American would do with these facilities in the future. Would they just close, or what? Well, it’s much better than that.

As of September 15, 2026, Flagship First Dining has simply become Flagship Dining, and the idea is that this is now open to all Flagship Business passengers traveling on qualifying long haul international, transcontinental, and Hawaii flights.

In other words, if you have access to a Flagship Lounge on account of your American business class ticket, you’re also eligible for Flagship Dining, on a space available basis. However, if you have Flagship Lounge access on account of elite status, or through traveling in a premium cabin on a partner airline, you wouldn’t have access to this facility.

American notes how guests interested in dining should check in with the host team inside the Flagship Lounge upon arrival. If a table is immediately available, guests will be seated at that time. If all tables are occupied, guests may be added to an electronic waitlist and will be notified when their table is ready. Tables will be offered on a first come, first served basis, and as I understand it, there’s no priority for first class passengers, Concierge Key members, etc.

I would expect that demand will greatly exceed supply, especially during peak hours. However, the same is true for the a la carte dining in United Polaris Lounges and (to a lesser extent) at some Delta One Lounges. This is really a great way for American to become more competitive with Delta and United. I’m really, really impressed, and this seems like a sincere effort to improve the premium experience.

Launching alongside the expanded dining facility access is an all-new four-course Flagship Dining menu. The airline promotes that “the seasonal offerings blend regional flavors, thoughtfully sourced ingredients and refined culinary techniques to create an elevated dining experience inspired by some of the world’s most celebrated restaurants.”

American is sharing some of the dishes that will be on offer, including a Texas pear and burrata salad…

In addition to that, American is introducing a wine and chocolate pairing, featuring KHK Wines and K+M Extravirgin Chocolate. Chef Thomas Keller, who co-founded K+M Extravirgin Chocolate with Italian olive oil producer Armando Manni, curated the pairing.

American has launched Flagship Dining, essentially a rebranding and repurposing of the Flagship First Dining facilities. This is being done because American is eliminating “premium” first class in the coming months.

This means American is now offering proper a la carte dining in its business class lounges, increasingly matching the competition. What an awesome change from American! You can find these facilities in Dallas, Los Angeles, and Miami.

What do you make of the evolved Flagship Dining concept? If you visit a Flagship Dining facility, please report back with your experience (food quality, wait times, etc.)!

#6238. American Airlines Has Reopened Its Exclusive LAX Dining Room After 6 Years—Here’s How To Get In

Last Wednesday I wrote exclusively American Airlines would reopen its Flagship Dining inside the business class lounge at LAX this week. Now it’s officially open. What was First Class Dining has been closed since March 2020, and when it returns, qualifying American business class passengers will be able to use it with their tickets, and there are other paths to entry too. That’s great news. When it was open previously it was fantastic. Flagship First Dining was a restaurant inside the Flagship Lounge. There were tables, booths, a bar and a window looking out toward the aircraft. The room had 59 seats, but when I visited there were never more than two other passengers at once. The food was excellent, too. I especially liked the miso black cod, and the pork belly came with cauliflower tempura that I still remember. American has since dropped “First” from the name. As the airline removes international first class from its Boeing 777-300ERs and replaces its three cabin Airbus A321Ts, they’ve opened the dining rooms to a much larger group instead of doing away with them. Since September 15, qualifying Flagship Business and Flagship Business Plus passengers have been able to use Flagship Dining in Dallas and Miami. Los Angeles is next. Access covers qualifying American Airlines long haul international, premium transcontinental and Flagship Hawaii itineraries. That includes eligible Flagship flights between Los Angeles and New York JFK, though an ordinary domestic first class ticket doesn’t get you in. The qualifying flight must be marketed and operated by American. Business class access doesn’t include a guest. Getting into the Flagship Lounge based on AAdvantage or oneworld status doesn’t get you into the separate dining room. Eligible partner first class access continues, and there’s also a way in with miles. AAdvantage Platinum Pro members can redeem 25,000 miles and Executive Platinum members can redeem 20,000 miles for a Flagship Dining pass. It includes the member and their immediate family or up to two guests on an eligible same day American or oneworld flight, even when flying coach. It includes the Flagship Lounge, too. I’ve thought this was one of the best uses of miles when traveling as a family. American has introduced a new dining menu and a wine and chocolate pairing featuring KHK Hillside Cabernet Sauvignon and K+M chocolate, co-founded by chef Thomas Keller. The cabernet retails for about $125 a bottle. Here’s American’s photo of the pairing. The new Dallas wine list also includes Bollinger La Grande Année, which retails for around $200 a bottle. American even listed it as an ingredient in a cranberry orange spritz. That seems like an expensive way to make it harder to taste the champagne. I’d ask for it in a separate glass. And the food has improved in the broader Flagship lounges, not just in the separate dining rooms. On a recent visit to the Dallas Flagship Lounge, I found a better buffet, a staffed charcuterie station and an improved chef station. I ordered from the lounge’s menu using a QR code, and the food arrived at my table in four minutes. It was a relatively quiet Tuesday evening, but I was impressed. That menu ordering is available in Los Angeles, too. When I last wrote about the rollout, the QR codes were in the theater seating and across from the secondary beverage station. Delta still offers the more ambitious food. It now has two Delta One lounges at LAX, with table service throughout, while United’s Polaris Lounge has a sit down restaurant. I’d still put the food in American’s main Flagship Lounge behind Delta, even though the gap has narrowed. But American makes the larger Flagship Lounge available to many more passengers, including eligible elites traveling in coach. And now a regular qualifying Flagship Business fare comes with the separate dining room. United’s base Polaris fares don’t include Polaris Lounge access. Delta’s Basic Business fares will lose Delta One lounge access for travel beginning January 19, 2027. At this point Americna’s three Flagship Dining locations really close a gap and even start to offer a competitive advantage for some. The tradeoff is that First Dining was so special because almost nobody was there. Opening it to business class is a big improvement for those passengers, but it also means many more people competing for a table. American uses an electronic waitlist when the dining room is full. If you’re traveling before a busy departure period, I’d check in with the host when you first arrive. July 22, 2018 I was flying back from Sacramento to Dallas via LAX. I was CK and either got it or burned a pass for dining. Went in and thought I was the only person in there. Heard some faint talking. Positioned myself to see who was talking because I thought I recognized the voice. He hung up his call, so I made my move once I realized who it was. Former VP Joe Biden. Literally all by himself and making calls to thank people for attending an event the day before. He was not a presidential candidate (until April 2019). He was so gracious and invited me to sit with him for a bit and asked me where I was coming from and where I was going. Shared I was heading home from a 40-man golf tournament of high school friends (g.1989). I asked if it would be okay for a picture I could share with friends, he said of course. Enjoyed a brief 1:1 with future President of the United States. Btw – there was no Secret Service, he was Joe-citizen and hadn’t declared.

So the Flagship Dining at LAX is a special place in my heart.

Wow, its a wow moment for me! I like the sound of all this new details and would love to dine here. Hopefully I have enough time to sit and relax. Great job AA. See you soon!!

#6237. Singapore Airlines Unveils New First & Business Class Cabins For A350, 777-9

The wait is finally over — Singapore Airlines has today unveiled its all-new cabins, which were first teased two years ago. Most significantly, this includes a brand new business class, plus the expansion of first class to more planes. This really represents the carrier’s next generation product offering, since these cabins will be installed on future Boeing 777-9s, as well as retrofitted on dozens of Airbus A350s.

Let’s first talk briefly about which planes will be getting this product, and then we’ll cover the details of the cabins. Keep in mind these changes will also include an updated soft product, including a new dining concept as well as new amenities across cabins.

Singapore Airlines’ new cabin products will be coming to all of the carrier’s upcoming Boeing 777-9s, as well as to select Airbus A350-900s. This includes a new first class, business class, premium economy, and economy, along with updated inflight entertainment and the installation of Starlink Wi-Fi.

Singapore Airlines has 31 Boeing 777-9s on order, which are expected to eventually be the carrier’s flagship aircraft. These will come delivered with the new cabins. As a matter of fact, Singapore Airlines had initially planned to debut the new cabins on these 777-9s all the way back in 2020. However, delivery of those planes has now been pushed back to late 2027 at the earliest.

More immediately, Singapore Airlines also plans to invest 1.1 billion SGD (~835 million USD) to update the interiors of its entire long haul Airbus A350-900 fleet. This consists of a total of 41 jets, and includes the carrier’s seven A350-900ULRs, with the “ULR” standing for “ultra long range,” as these planes operate the world’s longest flights.

The only A350-900s that won’t be reconfigured are the ones that are specifically designed for regional flights, featuring the same cabin products you’ll find onboard Boeing 787-10s.

How will the layouts of A350s change, once reconfigured? Singapore Airlines’ standard long haul A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines’ ultra long range A350-900s:

With the above out of the way, let’s take a look at Singapore Airlines’ new first class and business class seats. Let me say upfront that:

Below is a chart with the basics of Singapore Airlines’ new first class product.

Singapore Airlines’ new first class seat is designed by PriestmanGoode, and manufactured by Collins Aerospace, and it’ll be available exclusively on Boeing 777-9s and Airbus A350-900ULRS (so not on standard A350-900s, and it won’t be retrofitted on existing aircraft).

Entertainment will be available on a 32″ 4K monitor. As you’d expect, tech will be cutting edge beyond that, with bluetooth audio, wireless, AC, and USB-C charging, etc. There will also be a touchscreen handset that provides easy access to KrisWorld, plus a panel with seat controls and flight information.

One of the nice things is that the center suites have a retractable divider, potentially creating a large, expansive space, so that guests in the center seats can dine and relax together. Singapore Airlines claims that when combined, the double bed becomes the biggest bed in commercial aviation, as it measures 80″ long and 60″ wide.

There won’t be overhead bins in first class, so bags can be stored in a cabin baggage compartment underneath the seat. There will also be a personal wardrobe, and a leather-lined vanity drawer.

What’s my take on Singapore Airlines’ new first class? Quite honestly, this is almost exactly what I was expecting from the airline:

Below is a chart with the basics of Singapore Airlines’ new business class product.

Singapore Airlines’ new business class seat is designed by Designworks, and manufactured by RECARO, and it’ll be available exclusively on Boeing 777-9s and Airbus A350-900s (both long haul and ultra long haul).

Entertainment will be available on a 20-22″ 4K monitor. As you’d expect, tech will be cutting edge beyond that, with bluetooth audio, wireless, AC, and USB-C charging, etc. The airline also highlights how the seat has multiple storage options, which is appreciated.

Perhaps what’s most interesting is how in every other row, the center seats will be very close together, with the ability to form a double bed, which is a feature that customers always appreciate.

What’s my take on Singapore Airlines’ new business class? In some ways it’s what I expected, but there are some real surprises here:

Maybe it’ll look different in person, but am I the only one who is genuinely confused by the color choices? Those yellow accents just feel very… Spirit Airlines or Scoot, no?

When can we expect Singapore Airlines’ new premium products to debut? The expectation is that we’ll see a long haul Airbus A350-900 reconfigured first, and the first of those planes should now enter service in the second quarter of 2027. We don’t yet have any details beyond that.

The expectation is that the first retrofitted A350-900ULR (the ultra long range plane, operating the world’s longest flight) will debut at some point later in 2027, though that’s still up in the air. Meanwhile the 777-9s should start to join the fleet in late 2027 or early 2028 — only time will tell, given never-ending delays with Boeing.

Singapore Airlines should finish retrofitting its 41 A350s with the new cabins by either 2030 or 2031, though that timeline also remains subject to change. The delays with these new products reflects industry-wide supply chain constraints, as well as delays in the certification of the new seats (a common industry problem). The aircraft will be retrofitted by SIA Engineering Company in Singapore.

Which routes are likely to get the new cabins first? While we’ll see how this plays out, based on historical precedent, it’s likely that Sydney (SYD) and London (LHR) will be the first two destinations, since those are the first destinations where the airline has sent all of its new long haul products.

Singapore Airlines has just unveiled all-new cabins, which includes a new first class and business class. These cabins will be retrofitted on select Airbus A350-900s, and installed on all factory fresh Boeing 777-9s. These new products are long overdue, and I can’t wait to see them in service.

In first class, Singapore Airlines opted for a product that feels on brand, with warm colors, and a functional design that even allows for a double suite in the center seats. Meanwhile in business class, the airline chose a staggered product that looks solid, but I just can’t get over the cabin finishes… maybe it’s just me.

What do you make of Singapore Airlines’ new long haul cabins?

I get asked some version of the same question all the time: what’s the best travel credit card to actually keep in your wallet?

For me, the answer has changed over time. As my travel habits have evolved, so has the mix of cards I rely on. Some help me earn points quickly, others offset travel costs with built-in credits, and a few simply make traveling more comfortable.

While getting outsize value from a travel credit card often means paying an annual fee, I've found that the right perks can more than justify the cost. And one of the cards I'm looking to add to my wallet next doesn't charge an annual fee at all.

These are the travel credit cards I keep coming back to — and in some cases, the ones I'm planning to add next — based on their earning potential, flexibility and benefits I actually find useful.

I chose these cards based on the value they can provide travelers. In particular, I considered:

I've also included cards for different types of travelers, from beginners and those seeking premium perks to airline and hotel loyalists and travelers who don't want to pay an annual fee.

Purchases that qualify for the $300 annual travel credit will not earn points.

*Welcome offer value is an estimated value based on TPG's November 2026 valuations and is not provided by the issuer.

The newest premium travel card in my wallet is the Chase Sapphire Reserve, and after just a few months, it's already become one of my favorites.

While the $795 annual fee is steep, I've been getting plenty of use out of the card's travel perks. One of my favorite benefits so far has been the up to $500 in annual credits for The Edit, Chase’s curated hotel booking platform (issued as two credits of up to $250 per calendar year for stays of two nights or more).

I recently used one of those credits for a luxury stay at At Six in Stockholm, where I also enjoyed some of the other perks when you book with The Edit, such as complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit. The hotel's impressive breakfast spread was a particular highlight, and I was able to use the property credit to cover a couple of dine-in meals.

Lounge access has also been a major benefit. I frequently fly through Dulles International Airport (IAD) when visiting family on the East Coast, and the Etihad Lounge, which is part of the Chase Sapphire Lounge network, has become one of my go-to spots to relax before a flight.

I've also booked other hotel stays through Chase Travel, where the card earns 8 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases. Between the hotel benefits, lounge access and $300 annual travel credit, I've found plenty of ways to put the Reserve to work in a short period of time.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve: Earn 100,000 valuable points

The Sapphire Preferred was the first travel card in my wallet — and that goes for a lot of us here at TPG. It’s also the card I recommend most often to beginners or casual travelers who want flexible points without a sky-high annual fee.

With beginner-friendly perks like a $100 annual hotel credit and strong travel protections, it delivers real value without overwhelming complexity.

The card also makes it easy to get quick, upfront value. After earning the welcome offer and maximizing bonus categories — like 3 points per dollar spent on dining and 2 points per dollar spent on travel purchased outside the Chase Travel portal — I was able to build a sizable stash of points within a few months.

I ultimately redeemed those points for a trip through four European countries, which felt like a pretty great return for my first year with the card.

I'm also particularly excited about the card's newer earning category for vacation rentals. As someone who's stayed in more than 60 Airbnbs, I love that I can now earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible vacation home rentals, including Airbnb bookings.

It’s the travel card I recommend over and over again to friends and family because of its ease of use, strong earning potential and outsize value relative to its modest $95 annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Preferred.

Related: 6 ways to maximize the Chase Sapphire Preferred as a beginner

Best for: Straightforward premium rewards

Another top contender in the premium space — and one that’s firmly earned a place in my wallet — is the Capital One Venture X Rewards Card. For me, its biggest selling point is how easy it is to get value from the card without having to overthink my spending.

Part of the reason I added the card was to diversify my points and miles beyond Chase Ultimate Rewards. Up until recently, I’d been almost exclusively earning Chase points, but as I’ve gotten deeper into the points and miles world, I’ve realized how valuable it is to have access to multiple transferable currencies and transfer partners.

At the same time, the Venture X fits naturally into my everyday spending habits. Cardholders earn a flat 2 miles per dollar on nearly every purchase, which removes the need to track bonus categories or optimize every swipe. It’s become my go-to catch-all card and the one I reach for whenever a purchase doesn’t neatly fit into a bonus category on another card.

I've also gotten great use out of its travel benefits. I recently used the card's $300 annual Capital One Travel credit toward a three-night stay at the DoubleTree by Hilton London Marble Arch, bringing the cost down from $1,096 to $796. I also appreciate being able to relax in Capital One Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges when I travel.

For me, the Venture X works because it combines straightforward everyday earning with travel benefits I actually use, making its $395 annual fee easier to justify.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

Related: 5 reasons why I’m applying for the Capital One Venture X

For travelers who regularly fly a single airline — especially those based near one of that carrier’s hubs — a cobranded airline card can make a lot of sense.

That’s been true for me with United, but I think the same general strategy applies to frequent Delta and American Airlines flyers as well. If you consistently fly one carrier, the right airline card can make your travel experience cheaper, smoother and more comfortable through perks like travel credits, free checked bags and priority boarding.

Despite its $350 annual fee, the United Quest offers several easy-to-use benefits that help offset the cost. The $200 annual United travel credit, for instance, has helped offset flights home to visit family. And the two free checked bags for me and a travel companion have already saved me a significant amount in baggage fees.

The card also offers award flight discounts, anniversary bonus miles, priority boarding and improved award availability, which make the card feel like a keeper for the long term.

That said, I do wish it included lounge access — especially at this price point.

Still, the Quest has made flying United more affordable and convenient for me, which is exactly what I want from an airline credit card.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Quest.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

Not every worthwhile travel rewards card needs to charge an annual fee. The Freedom Unlimited is one I'm interested in adding to my wallet because it could fill an important gap in my Chase strategy without adding another annual fee.

On its own, the Freedom Unlimited earns cash-back rewards. But when you pair it with an eligible Ultimate Rewards-earning card like the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, you can combine your rewards and potentially get more value by redeeming them for travel or transferring them to Chase's airline and hotel partners.

That's particularly appealing to me because I'm working toward building the Chase Trifecta, a strategy that combines multiple Chase cards to maximize earnings across different types of purchases.

With no annual fee, the Freedom Unlimited could give me another way to earn rewards on everyday spending while letting my Sapphire cards handle travel purchases and unlock more valuable redemption options.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

Related: The best beginner Chase card combo for travel rewards

Best for: Hilton perks without the premium price tag

The Hilton Surpass is the newest addition to my wallet — and my first hotel credit card.

For years, I've prioritized flexible rewards over hotel-specific points because I didn't want to commit to a single hotel program. But as I've started traveling more and spending more nights in hotels, I realized I was leaving some valuable perks on the table.

After comparing several hotel cards, I ultimately chose the Hilton Surpass because it struck the right balance between cost and benefits. One of the biggest draws for me is automatic Hilton Honors Gold status, which gives me meaningful hotel perks without requiring me to earn status through stays.

I'm also a fan of the card's up to $200 in Hilton statement credits each calendar year, issued as up to $50 each quarter. And Hilton's large footprint means I'm much more likely to find a property where I can actually put those benefits to use when I travel.

For me, the Surpass is a relatively approachable way to test-drive hotel loyalty while getting useful benefits from the start. As I spend more nights with Hilton, I'll be able to see whether a hotel card deserves a permanent place in my travel strategy.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Surpass.

Related: How I chose my first hotel credit card — and the 4 cards I considered

Choosing the right travel credit card ultimately comes down to how you travel, where you spend your money and which perks you'll actually use.

For beginners, the Chase Sapphire Preferred remains one of the strongest entry points thanks to its balance of value, flexibility and simplicity. Frequent travelers looking for a more premium experience — especially when it comes to lounge access and travel perks — may get more value from the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Meanwhile, the Capital One Venture X is a great fit for travelers who want premium benefits without overcomplicating their rewards strategy, and the United Quest offers a strong value proposition for frequent United flyers who prioritize convenience and United-specific perks.

For travelers who don't want to add another annual fee, the Chase Freedom Unlimited can be a useful complement to a Sapphire card, particularly if you're building a Chase trifecta. And for travelers who want hotel-specific perks, the Hilton Surpass offers a relatively accessible entry point to hotel loyalty with automatic Hilton Gold status and useful Hilton credits.

You certainly don't need all six cards on this list to get good value from travel rewards. But whether you're looking for your first travel card or considering adding another to your wallet, I'd start by thinking about which benefits you'd use most often — and whether they're worth the annual fee.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

#6234. World of Hyatt Card Limited Time Bonus Offer: Earn Four Free Night Awards

We’ve just seen a new limited time welcome offer rolled out on the World of Hyatt Credit Card, making it the ideal time to apply. I’d consider this to be one of the most lucrative hotel credit cards out there — it’s a product you don’t get just for the bonus, but instead, for the long term value that it offers.

Let’s take a look at the details of the card bonus and eligibility requirements, as well as the long term value.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card bonus offer

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is currently offering a limited time welcome bonus that consists of four Category 1-4 free night awards after spending $5,000 within the first three months.

World of Hyatt Category 4 properties retail for up to 25,000 points per night, so the absolute maximum value of this offer is 100,000 points. However, I of course wouldn’t value it that highly. That’s because these free night awards expire 12 months after they’re issued, and you also can’t top off these awards to redeem at more expensive properties. So actually maxing out the value of these isn’t easy.

One thing I should mention is that while I don’t love the lack of flexibility of this welcome offer, it’s significantly better than the standard bonus, which tends to be lackluster. Obviously Chase and Hyatt know that this is a card people will get for the long term value, rather than just for the bonus.

For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each.

If you’re interested in applying for the World of Hyatt Credit Card, the eligibility rules for the bonus are pretty straightforward. This product is available to you if you don’t have this exact card, and haven’t received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months.

So that means you could potentially earn the bonus if you’ve had the card in the past. Furthermore, eligibility is unrelated to whether you have the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more).

On top of that, Chase’s general application rules apply, including that you can typically be approved for at most two Chase cards every 30 days, and the Chase 5/24 rule is also worth considering (you may not be approved if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months).

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to be approved for this card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

The World of Hyatt Card is one that offers a lot of long term value, so only think of the welcome bonus as being part of the bigger picture. The World of Hyatt Card has a $95 annual fee, and offers the following perks, among other things:

This is a card I’ve had for years, and one that I spend at least $15,000 on annually, so that I earn the second free night award, plus six additional elite nights. If you stay at Hyatts with any frequency, having this card should be a no-brainer. For more details, read my full World of Hyatt Card review.

If you’re looking for a Hyatt co-branded credit card but want a business card instead, then the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card is for you. The card is currently offering a bonus of 70,000 points after spending $7,000 within the first three months.

At my valuation of 1.4 cents per point, that’s roughly $980 in value, which more than offsets the $199 annual fee in year one.

Eligibility is straightforward, as you can’t currently hold this specific card, and you can’t have received a welcome bonus on it within the past 24 months. Having the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card doesn’t affect your eligibility, as you can hold both cards and earn bonuses on each. Standard Chase application rules apply.

For more details, read my World of Hyatt Business Card review, as well as my World of Hyatt personal vs. business card comparison.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is currently offering a limited time welcome offer that can earn you four Category 1-4 free night awards upon completing minimum spending. Category 4 properties go for up to 25,000 points per night, so this is potentially quite a substantial welcome bonus.

However, the bonus isn’t the main reason you get this card. Instead, it’s about the long term value proposition, including elite nights toward status, an anniversary free night award, etc. Furthermore, it’s a card that’s worth spending $15,000 on per year, if you can swing it, so you can earn a second free night award and six more elite nights toward status.

If this card has been on your radar, this is a good time to apply…

#6232. New Hyatt Credit Card Offer: Earn 4 Free Nights—Why I Spend On The Card Towards Elite Status

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The World Of Hyatt Credit Card (See rates and fees) has a new initial bonus: earn 4 free nights at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. That’s an improved offer from a card whose bonuses have usually been more modest than competing travel cards.

I have this card, and I put actual spending on it. Hyatt points are still valuable, but what gets me to use the card is the credit toward elite status and the rewards earned along the way. Hyatt status does more to improve my hotel stays than status with other major chains.

These are four separate certificates, so you can use them for one trip or spread them across different stays. You’ll need standard room award availability, and the certificates expire 12 months after they’re issued. The terms require checkout before the expiration date. Under Hyatt’s current award chart, a Category 4 standard room can cost as much as 25,000 points per night. Four certificates could therefore cover nights that would otherwise require 100,000 points. Their category restrictions and expiration date make them less flexible than having those points in your account. The card has a $95 annual fee. Chase excludes current holders of this card and previous cardmembers who received its initial bonus within the past 24 months. The usual Chase restriction on applicants who’ve opened five or more personal cards in the past 24 months also generally applies. Why I Keep The Card And Spend On It The annual Category 1-4 free night after each cardmember anniversary makes the $95 fee easy to justify. There’s also a second Category 1-4 night after $15,000 in purchases during a calendar year which makes that spending more rewarding. And these nights are transferable to another World of Hyatt member. If I won’t use one, I can give it to someone who will. For spending, the card earns 4 Hyatt points per dollar on qualifying Hyatt purchases; 2 on restaurants, airline tickets bought directly from airlines, local transit and commuting, and fitness club and gym memberships; and 1 on other purchases. More significantly, it comes with 5 qualifying nights each year, plus 2 more qualifying nights for every $5,000 spent. Those nights count toward both status and Milestone Rewards. Put $15,000 of otherwise unbonused spending on the card during a calendar year and you earn: 15,000 Hyatt points. An additional Category 1-4 free night certificate. 6 qualifying nights from spending, giving you 11 including the card’s annual 5. That means 49 qualifying nights actually spent in hotels, plus the card’s 5 annual nights and 6 from spending, gets you to the 60 needed for Globalist. And the $5,000 spent earning the initial bonus counts toward the $15,000 free-night threshold in the calendar year when you spend it. Milestone Rewards start at 20 qualifying nights and continue every 10 nights through 150. Some of the rewards on the way to Globalist are: Qualifying Nights Notable Rewards 30 A Category 1-4 free night, plus a choice of additional reward. 40 A Guest of Honor Award, plus a choice that includes a Suite Upgrade Award. 50 A choice that includes 2 Suite Upgrade Awards. 60 Globalist status, a Category 1-7 free night, 2 Suite Upgrade Awards, 2 Guest of Honor Awards, and My Hyatt Concierge. The value of another $5,000 in spending depends on where those two nights get me. Crossing a threshold for suite upgrades or Globalist can be worth giving up a higher earning rate on another card. Hyatt Status Is Stronger Than At Other Major Chains The card itself comes with Discoverist status. That’s better than a hole in the head as my grandfather used to say. But reaching Globalist has real value – as well as the milestone choices along the way. The biggest benefit is confirming a suite at the time of booking with a Suite Upgrade Award for up to seven nights when an eligible standard suite is available for the stay. That’s a huge value on family trips. I also value having a My Hyatt Concierge I can email requests to, actual delivery of 4 p.m. late checkout at eligible properties, and a more generous breakfast benefit than I get from other chains. At participating hotels without an available club lounge, Globalist breakfast generally covers a full breakfast for up to two adults and two children registered in the room, including tax and gratuity. Late checkout has exceptions, including availability limits at resorts, but I’m usually proactively offered late checkout everywhere else (and personally find it honored more often than not at resorts). The Free Night Certificates Should Be More Flexible The current version of this card launched in 2018. Its annual certificate is still capped at Category 4, while category creep has taken away many of the hotels where I’d most want to use it. Just this year, 14 hotels moved from Category 4 to Category 5, including Hyatt Regency Seattle, Hyatt Regency Grand Cypress and Hyatt Regency Jersey City. Five moved the other way, bringing options like Hyatt Centric Congress Avenue Austin and Dream Nashville within reach, but the certificate lost more hotels than it gained. I’d like Hyatt to at least let members add points to a certificate to book a higher category. The certificate works at a Category 4 hotel charging 25,000 points, but won’t work at a Category 5 hotel when it’s charging 15,000 points. And I wish Hyatt would let us combine these free nights with Suite Upgrade Awards or Guest of Honor Awards. I value them most traveling with my family when I’m paying for rooms out of pocket. That’s always when I want to use my suite upgrades! I don’t need a suite on a business stay (paid by someone else, when it’s just me) or to use the free night award. That’s always when I want to use my suite upgrades! I don’t need a suite on a business stay (paid by someone else, when it’s just me) or to use the free night award.

#6230. How To Combine Hilton Honors Points Between Accounts For Free

Every hotel loyalty program has a different policy when it comes to being able to combine points among members. Arguably Hilton Honors has among the most generous policies of any program when it comes to letting members combine points, so I’d like to take a closer look at that in this post.

For what it’s worth, separately I’ve covered the policies of Marriott Bonvoy and World of Hyatt when it comes to combining points.

Hilton Honors offers a generous feature to allow members to combine and share points with others at no cost. First let’s go over the basics:

Technically Hilton Honors has two features by which you can combine points for free, and this can cause quite a bit of confusion. These two options are as follows:

The reality is that these two options are more similar than they may sound. The same limits exist on points transfers regardless of which method you choose:

The end result is the same, though, which is that points are being consolidated in one account. Given the similar restrictions on transfers, personally I think it’s easier to just use the points transfer feature over the points pooling feature, which just adds an unnecessary step.

Before we talk about how combining Hilton points works, why should you even care about this feature? There are a few reasons this could make a difference:

Long story short, being able to combine points just gives you a lot more flexibility.

The process of combining Hilton Honors points differs based on whether you’re just looking to make a simple transfer, or are looking to create a points pool with up to 11 accounts.

This is the most basic function, and also what I recommend. Visit the Hilton Honors points transfer page to start the process of transferring points from one Hilton Honors account to another.

You’ll be prompted to log into your Hilton Honors account, and then will be asked to enter the number of points you want to transfer (between 1,000 and 500,000), along with the name, email address, and Hilton Honors number of the person you want to transfer points to.

This is still facilitated by points.com (as points purchases usually are), except in this case you’re not paying anything. While the points are supposed to be available for redemption immediately, they may only show in your online account activity 24 hours after the transaction was processed.

This is the function to be aware of if you want to have up to 11 people combine points into one account. Visit the Hilton Honors points pooling page to start the process of creating a pooling account with multiple Hilton Honors members.

While the points transfer feature only requires the participation of the member who is transferring points, the process of pooling points requires participation of all members involved. One person can start sending invitations to pool points, which requires entering the names and email addresses of the people you want to invite.

That person will receive an email invitation to join your points pool, at which point they can transfer points to you.

The person will have to log into their Hilton Honors account, and then they’ll be brought to the same page for combining points as above.

If the member does choose to pool/transfer points, the person who invited them will be informed.

The reality is that this process is more or less the same as just combining points, with the difference being that someone is prompted to transfer points, rather than just doing so straight out of their account with no prompting.

Not only does Hilton Honors offer an excellent rate of return (in points) on hotel stays, but there are lots of other great ways to earn Hilton Honors points.

For one, there are four excellent co-branded Hilton Amex credit cards in the United States, including the following:

On top of that, Hilton Honors often sells points at a discount. In many cases there’s a 100% bonus on purchased points (or even more), which allows you to purchase points for just 0.5 cents each (or in some case even less). This can be a good deal, particularly for high-end redemptions (though Hilton Honors devaluations in recent times make these redemptions less exciting than in the past).

It’s always nice to easily be able to move points between loyalty program accounts in order to maximize them. As far as hotel loyalty programs go, Hilton Honors has what’s arguably the best option for combining points.

You can combine points at no cost, with some reasonable limits in place. You can either use the standard points transfer option, or you can go through the process of pooling points; personally I find the former option to be easier.

Have you ever used Hilton Honors’ points pooling feature? If so, what was your experience like?

#6228. American Airlines Adds New App Option When Flights Go Wrong—Try For An Earlier Flight Without Giving Up Your Confirmed Seat

American Airlines is making it easier to try for an earlier flight when your travel falls apart. Its app and website will now offer standby options when you’re dealing with a travel disruption while keeping your new confirmed flight. You don’t need an agent for this – it’s part of their self-service tool. The change to list yourself for free standby on an earlier flight went into effect this week. During a disruption, the flight you can confirm may be hours later than one you could actually get on if a seat opens up. You no longer need to deal with customer service to get on the standby list. . How The New Standby Option Works American calls its tool Dynamic Rebooking. Here’s the sequence described in an internal company memo: Open your disrupted trip on aa.com or in the American Airlines app. Start with Flight Options or Rebook Trip in the disruption banner. If your flight was canceled and you don’t have a replacement, confirm one first. Choose a flight with availability, then return to Flight Options to look for standby. Look for earlier nonstop flights. Up to three standby options may appear when American can’t confirm the earlier rebooking. Pick one. You can join one standby list at a time through this tool. You can remove yourself or switch to another option without contacting an employee. Keep your confirmed flight while you wait. Your itinerary changes only if you clear onto the standby flight. If you’re confirmed for an 8 p.m. flight and the app can’t confirm you on the 5 p.m., you can standby for it while remaining confirmed on that 8 p.m.. If you don’t clear, your confirmed itinerary remains intact. Employees are told, Do not cancel the customer’s confirmed flight because the customer joined standby If you do clear standby you lose the confirmation on your original flight so if you can’t make it you need to remove yourself from standby. What American Is Actually Adding For Passengers American has offered same day changes and standby through its app since 2017. And keeping your original booking while standing by for an earlier flight was already part of published policy. The improvement is putting standby inside the flight disruption rebooking process. Here’s one example of where this matters: an Executive Platinum member facing a seven hour Dallas–Charlotte delay could see confirmed alternatives in the disruption tool, but couldn’t find a way to request earlier standby. Even accepting a later confirmed flight didn’t solve it. An agent eventually added them to standby and they cleared. I covered American’s new disruption banners in January, alongside rebooking, baggage tracking, and digital hotel and meal vouchers. Standby was one of the additions they said was coming. American also described the feature in its October 26 iPhone app release notes. American is trying to offer more tools for managing disruptions. That’s both a cost savings and also empowering to the passenger. A customer who feels in control of their options is going to have a better view of the airline than one who feels at the mercy of broader forces. It’s about raising net promoter scores when things go wrong, which is part of customers being willing to be repeat purchasers, purchasers of premium products, and passengers willing to pay more to fly American. That’s the strategy anyway. In contrast, in 2024, American restricted most passengers to digital standby even when its systems couldn’t handle their requests. They restored agent assistance in July 2025. Improving digital tools and offering agent help is ultimately the right direction to be moving. The Limits Customers Should Know Nothing is being taken away here, but the new tool has limits: Three displayed choices means one standby request. You aren’t joining three lists at once, and the memo only describes nonstop options. That’s not every possible way to get where you’re going. This doesn’t fix ordinary same day confirmed changes. I’ve written about American’s restrictive availability and routing rules. This update is an improvement for recovery from disruptions, but ordinary standby and confirmed flight changes are still broken at American. United introduced a broader version of this in September: disrupted customers can select up to three eligible earlier flights, and United monitors for seats and texts when one opens. Customers choose whether to switch while retaining their confirmed reservation until they decide. American’s memo allows one standby listing and says the confirmed itinerary changes when standby clears. This isn’t going to change the need for me to work with an agent, but it’s going to be helpful to a lot of people. Plus, American’s Executive Platinum members and higher can have more than one flight in their itinerary confirmed at a time during irregular operations (for instance, I book a backup in case I misconnect when my first segment is delayed – rather than having to make the call early to make the switch and give up my shot at making it, I can lock in the option of flying later while still running for my connection). And bear in mind that you can still ask for a partner flight (such as on Alaska Airlines) if your confirmed option is the next day as well. #6227. Lol: Beond Airlines & Air Cairo Plan All-Business Class Carrier In Egypt

Guys, sometimes I wonder if I’m losing my mind, or if others are. All-business class carrier Beond Airlines has just announced that it’s partnering with all-economy class carrier Air Cairo to launch an all-business class airline flying to and from Egypt.

No disrespect to Egypt, but of all the business ideas in the world, is this really the one that makes the most sense? Maybe next we’ll see Beond partner with Ryanair to offer all-business class service between Leeds and Agadir?

Beond Airlines and Air Cairo have announced a partnership to bring Beond’s all-business class travel experience to Egypt. The two airlines signed a memorandum of understanding for the concept.

For the summer of 2027, Air Cairo will operate Beond-branded flights with all-business class configurations, connecting Egypt with Europe and the Gulf region. This is clearly targeted at inbound tourism to Egypt, so “travellers reach Egypt’s coast, its history and its cities rested and at ease.”

Routes and schedules will be announced in the coming months, with bookings expected to open in the first half of 2027. Just so we’re on the same page here, Air Cairo operates a fleet of planes exclusively in an all-economy configuration, so the airline hasn’t seen merit to offering even a small business class cabin. But now they’ve decided “hey, what we really need is a plane that exclusively has business class?”

Here’s what Beond CEO Tero Taskila had to say about this concept:

“Egypt has some of the most remarkable places on earth, and many travellers who want to reach them in comfort. Air Cairo knows this market better than anyone. Together we can start the holiday from home, not at the hotel. Our cabin gives us the luxurious surroundings. Our people give us the experience. Both have to match the places we fly to.”

Meanwhile here’s what Egypt’s Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, Sherif Fathy, had to say about this:

“Encouraging this partnership is an integral part of the Ministry’s strategy to promote Egypt’s unparalleled tourism diversity and expand its range of distinctive tourism products and experiences. We highly value the role of Air Cairo as one of the key supporters of the tourism industry, whose efforts contribute to enhancing connectivity, supporting tourism growth, and strengthening Egypt’s position as a leading global tourism destination. Such partnerships reflect our commitment to fostering closer cooperation with our partners in the aviation sector to achieve sustainable growth and further enhance the competitiveness of the Egyptian tourism destination.”

Beond Airlines was initially formed as an airline intended to transport people to and from the Maldives. I’ve flown the airline, and the onboard experience was actually quite lovely (with two caveats — the lack of Wi-Fi, plus the limited range of the planes requiring a refueling stop, which limits the ability to get rest).

This airline obviously has funding, and the company’s CEO is a really nice guy who has a fair bit of experience. But nothing about the past few years gives me any faith in the future of the company.

When Beond Airlines launched in 2023, management claimed the airline would have 32 planes and serve 60 destinations within five years, which would be by 2028. Currently, the airline still has two planes, with no additional firm orders, at least as far as I know.

It has just been announcement after announcement from Beond, with little substance to anything:

I have no clue what’s going on here anymore, though I’d assume it’s one of two things:

But I have to say, of everything we’ve seen from Beond, I find this to possibly be the most bizarre development yet. Egypt is generally a budget vacation destination, and not a premium vacation destination. So if an all-business class experience to the Maldives didn’t prove successful, I can’t imagine that Egypt is the key to unlocking prosperity for the airline.

Beond Airlines and Air Cairo are partnering to launch an all-business class airline that will serve Egypt. Egypt is generally a budget travel destination, and there’s an irony to an all-economy airline getting involved in an all-business class operation.

What can anyone really say at this point, though? Beond is all over the place in terms of its strategy. Initially it was going to fly to dozens of destinations out of the Maldives. Then it promised to set up subsidiaries all over the place, including partnering with an airline that liquidated just weeks later. Then the airline suspended commercial operations altogether. And now the airline is planning all-business class service in Egypt.

What do you make of Beond’s latest Egypt play?
