Delta Air Lines and American Express offer seven cobranded cards for everyone from occasional Delta flyers to frequent travelers.

Depending on the card and the offer you qualify for, you could earn up to 125,000 bonus SkyMiles.

Here’s how the current offers compare and what to consider before applying.

*Bonus value is based on TPG’s November 2026 valuations and is not provided or reviewed by the issuer.

American Express has a few eligibility rules to keep in mind before applying for one of these cards. For starters, Amex typically only allows a person to earn one welcome bonus per card in their lifetime. That means you'll want to prioritize applying when a card offers an elevated, limited-time offer, such as the ones all but one of these cards have right now.

You also may not be eligible for a welcome bonus on a personal Delta Amex card if you have or previously had a higher-tier Delta Amex card. For example, if you have or previously had the Delta Reserve Amex, you may not be eligible for the welcome offers on the Delta Blue, Delta Gold or Delta Platinum.

Delta's business Amex cards are not subject to this same "family rule."

Amex may consider other factors when determining your eligibility, including your income, credit score and history with the issuer. Fortunately, you'll generally find out whether you're eligible for a welcome offer before accepting the card.

Delta offers four personal cards. The card that is right for you depends on how frequently you fly with Delta and how much you’re willing to pay for an annual fee.

Let’s take a look at what differentiates each of the Delta SkyMiles personal cards.

Best for: Delta loyalists or those who want Sky Club access (subject to limitations)

The Delta SkyMiles Reserve is ideal for hardcore Delta fans and frequent flyers.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

This bonus is worth up to $1,500 per our valuations.

If you qualify for the full 125,000 miles, this is an excellent time to apply. It matches the highest mileage bonus we’ve seen on the card and requires $1,000 less spending than the previous 125,000-mile offer with the lowest spending requirement.

Key benefits: Delta’s premium consumer credit card offers a range of valuable perks. For loyal Delta flyers who enjoy visiting the Sky Club, this card can pay for itself through lounge access, spending boosts and other benefits.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline. Plus, you'll enjoy a slew of Delta-related perks, including:

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card

If you fly frequently with Delta but can’t justify the pricier Delta SkyMiles Reserve, the Delta SkyMiles Platinum is worth considering.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 90,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,080.

If you qualify for the full 90,000 miles, this is a strong offer for $3,000 in spending. We’ve seen offers with more miles or a statement credit, though they required more spending.

Key benefits: This card is a good option if you fly Delta regularly and want to earn miles on purchases and reach elite status. However, even if you aren’t pursuing status, the companion certificate alone can make the annual fee for this card worth it.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Platinum American Express Card

Best for: Occasional Delta flyers or those test-driving a Delta card

If you want to take advantage of a welcome bonus but don’t fly Delta frequently, the Delta SkyMiles Gold is a strong option.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 80,000 bonus miles after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

TPG's valuations place this bonus at up to $960.

If you qualify for the full 80,000 miles, now is a good time to apply. However, we have seen up to 90,000 miles — as well as up to 80,000 miles plus a statement credit — offered before.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150

Key benefits: This card is ideal for occasional Delta flyers seeking a few extra perks when flying with the airline.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Gold American Express Card

If you want an entry-level card to start earning SkyMiles and fly less frequently with Delta, then Delta SkyMiles Blue is the card for you.

Current welcome offer: Earn 10,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership.

According to TPG’s valuations, these miles are worth $120. The SkyMiles Blue typically doesn't receive an elevated offer, so we recommend applying whenever you're ready.

Key benefits: As a no-annual-fee card, it offers fewer benefits than the others. Still, there are some simple perks for cardmembers.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Blue.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Blue American Express Card

If you own a small business or have a side hustle through which you pay business expenses, one of these offers may be a great addition to your work wallet.

Best for: Business owners who fly Delta frequently and want lounge access

As the most expensive business card Delta offers, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business comes packed with great perks for Delta loyalists.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

Per TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,500.

If you qualify for the full 125,000 miles, this clears our usual threshold. The highest offer we’ve seen was 200,000 miles after $20,000 in spending, compared with $15,000 for this offer.

Key benefits: This card offers a range of useful perks for Delta-loyal small-business owners.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on purchases made directly with Delta.

Its suite of Delta-related benefits includes:

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business American Express Card

Best for: Business owners who fly frequently with Delta

Business owners who are looking for a good mid-tier airline business card should consider the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business for its earnings potential and benefits.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 100,000 bonus miles after spending $10,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

According to TPG's valuations, this offer is worth up to $1,200.

The full 100,000-mile bonus matches the highest mileage offer we’ve seen, though previous offers awarded the same bonus after $8,000 in purchases. If you already have $10,000 in eligible business spending planned and want the card now, this is a good offer. If you’re flexible on timing, we’d consider waiting for the same bonus with a lower spending requirement.

Key benefits: This is a solid mid-tier option for business owners who travel with Delta semi-frequently.

With this card, you’ll earn 3 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business American Express Card

Best for: Business owners who fly occasionally with Delta

The Delta SkyMiles Gold Business is ideal for smaller businesses or business owners who aren’t Delta loyalists.

Current welcome offer: Find out your offer and see if you are eligible for as high as 85,000 bonus miles after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers may vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.)

The bonus is worth up to $1,020 when factoring in TPG's valuations.

If you qualify for all 85,000 miles, this is a good time to apply. It’s just 5,000 miles shy of the highest offer we’ve seen, which also required $6,000 in purchases. If the card already fits your business, we’d take the full offer.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150

Key benefits: Even if they don't fly Delta often, small-business owners can still benefit from this card's perks.

With this card, you’ll earn 2 miles per dollar spent on Delta purchases made directly with the airline.

To learn more, read our full review of the Delta SkyMiles Gold Business.

Apply here: Delta SkyMiles Gold Business American Express Card

With a full lineup of Delta cards, you may wonder how to pick the best offer for your needs. While it might be tempting to go with the highest offer, you should also consider its long-term value to your wallet.

The good news is that many of these offers can be a great fit, depending on your travel habits. As a round-up:

Related: Why the Delta SkyMiles Reserve card is still one of the best cards I’ve added to my wallet

Delta and American Express offer a wide range of cobranded cards, whether you fly with the airline occasionally or are a frequent Delta loyalist.

Just remember that American Express has a once-per-card, per-lifetime rule for welcome offers. If you've had a particular Delta Amex before, or, in some cases, a higher-tier personal Delta card, you may not be eligible for that card's welcome offer.

Welcome offers vary, so check the bonus you’re offered and make sure you can meet the spending requirement with purchases you already plan to make.

#6224. Singapore Airlines Unveils New Suites With Double Beds—Rollout Slips Again, And Many Planes Miss Out

First class is coming to the ultra-long-range Airbus A350s that operate the world’s longest flights. Business class gets doors, a different sleeping position, and more foot space. We’re not going to see the first aircraft with the new cabins until the second half of 2027, and several fleets won’t ever get these seats at all.

I flew to Singapore in November 2017 for the unveiling of their last new A380 business class and Suites. Nine years later, plenty of their aircraft still have an older product. And even the 380 itself didn’t finish installation until late 2023. Long haul A350 and Boeing 777 seats date to 2013. I flew to Seattle for delivery of the first 777 that had them.

Singapore’s new business class was designed with BMW’s Designworks and built by Recaro. It’s a bespoke seat, with a forward-facing, staggered 1-2-1 layout with doors and direct aisle access throughout. The biggest improvement is being able to adjust the seat continuously from upright to flat, choose a comfortable lounging position, and sleep without angling my body across the seat.

The A350 seat goes from 28 inches wide to 22 inches. On the wider Boeing 777-9, it’ll be 24 inches. So that’s a real tradeoff in seat width. Singapore’s old seat was exceptionally wide, but short and you had to angle your feet. A350 business class gets a 22-inch OLED screen, while the new 777-9 gets a smaller 20-inch screen without OLED.

The new first class, designed by PriestmanGoode and manufactured by Collins Aerospace, will have four seats on the ultra-long-range A350 and six on the 777-9.

The center pair can remain two independent suites or open into one shared space. Each passenger still has their own entrance, screen and table. Those seats can form a sofa for two or an 80-by-60-inch double bed. That’s the size of a standard U.S. queen mattress. Singapore calls it the largest double bed in commercial aviation. Individually, the beds measure 80 by 30 inches. The seats are 23 inches wide with the armrests raised.

Curved sliding doors, warm colors, Poltrona Frau leather and batik details make this look much more like Singapore Airlines than the new business cabin.

Companion dining is available at every first class seat, using the ottoman, which restores something missing from the current A380 Suites experience. The joined center suites can accommodate four people dining together.

Other features include a personal wardrobe, an illuminated vanity drawer, carry-on storage beneath the ottoman, wireless charging and a 32-inch 4K screen. Bang & Olufsen wireless headphones are supplied, and you can pair your own headphones. A small information panel shows flight details and lavatory availability without requiring you to turn on the main screen. Seat and lighting preferences can be saved for future flights.

This isn’t the A380’s separate armchair-and-bed concept. The chair becomes the bed. It’s a massive improvement over today’s 777 first class, while the A380 retains its current expansive Suites layout. There is only one center pair on each aircraft. Six first class seats on the 777-9 means four window singles and one potential double suite, not three double beds.

The announced program covers 41 existing A350s and Singapore’s 31 ordered Boeing 777-9s. Only the 777-9 gets all four new seat designs.

The A380, existing 777-300ER, medium-haul A350, 787-10 and 737-8 aren’t included in this seat program. Those aircraft keep their current cabin products under the announced plan. The A380 is separately getting Starlink.

The rollout has already slipped twice: the first refurbished long-haul A350 was originally due in the second quarter of 2026, then the first quarter of 2027. Now it’s the second half of 2027. The airline still targets the end of 2030 to complete the A350 retrofits.

Boeing’s delays explain why seats originally intended for the 777-9 are going onto A350s. But seat certification is also holding things up: the 777-9 seats have been certified, while the airplane hasn’t. The A350 seats still need certification. The ultra-long range A350 doesn’t have a firm separate debut date or announced launch route for its new first class.

The new premium economy seat offers 40 inches of pitch, up from 38, and nine inches of recline instead of eight. It’s 19 inches wide, in a 2-4-2 cabin, with adjustable leg and footrests.

777-9 economy cabin goes to 3-4-3 and 31 to 32 inches of pitch. It’s a wider cabin, but Singapore’s current 777-300ERs are 3-3-3. There are redesigned cushions, adjustable headrests and a revised recline mechanism intended to improve knee and shin clearance, plus 13-inch 4K screens, Bluetooth and USB-C.

Meanwhile, an A350 retrofit won’t bring these new premium economy or economy seats. Those cabins get refreshed upholstery and an updated entertainment interface, while keeping their existing seat hardware.

There will even be two hardware versions within the 777-9 fleet. Premium economy and economy on the first 12 aircraft get conventional 4K screens. The later 19 get OLED screens but lose USB-A. Economy also loses universal power outlets on those 19 aircraft, retaining USB-C. Premium economy keeps universal power. On those later jets, coach will have OLED while first and business won’t.

The early reaction is much warmer toward first class than business. In the FlyerTalk discussion folks like the larger bed, the return of companion dining and the ability to separate the middle pair into two proper suites. That’s a better arrangement for unrelated passengers than Lufthansa’s shared center suite. The business class thread is much rougher. Gray surfaces and bright yellow trim draw comparisons to Scoot, car interiors and a loss of Singapore’s warmth. Reddit reactions echo the complaints about generic styling and lost identity. Still, folks like the doors, storage and companion beds. Several Other Changes Arrive Before The Seats Singapore’s broader announcement bundles together upgrades with different schedules: Sleepwear and amenity kits. New kits begin rolling out this month on flights over six hours: Sisley in Suites and first, Byredo in business, INK & WATER in premium economy, and travel essentials in a batik pouch in economy. Business class gets pajamas for the first time, on all long-haul flights and selected overnight medium-haul flights over six hours. First class and Suites get new cotton sleepwear. Dining. The package includes more than 100 new or refreshed dishes, expanded drinks and Christofle serviceware in Suites, first and business. Lounge and ground-service improvements are also part of the broader investment. Entertainment and internet. The next KrisWorld system adds easier navigation, personalization, a wellness planner and more than 2,500 entertainment options, with hardware varying by cabin. Starlink begins rolling out from early 2027 on the A380 and long-haul and ultra-long-range A350s. The announced Starlink list doesn’t include the 777-9. The Biggest Commercial Change Is At The Back Of The Longest Flights The ultra-long-range A350 goes from 67 business and 94 premium economy seats to four first, 70 business and 58 premium economy. That’s 36 fewer premium economy seats or a 38% cut. Total passenger capacity falls from 161 to 132, or 18%. Singapore is replacing a substantial portion of its lowest-priced cabin on these aircraft with space it expects to sell for more. First class provides a new way to monetize the nonstop flights. Net net I expect this to mean tougher award space overall (certainly in premium economy). Emirates posted a 66% drop in first-half net profit to AED 3.3 billion ($899 million), and the result rested on AED 7.1 billion ($1.93 billion) in fuel hedging gains. The airline said that without those gains, at open-market fuel prices, it would have lost money after the U.S.-Iran war closed regional airspace and sent jet fuel costs soaring. Revenue fell 13% to AED 56.9 billion ($15.5 billion). Passenger traffic dropped 22% to 21.8 million, capacity fell 17%, and seat factor slipped to 72% from 79.5%, as connecting traffic moved to Istanbul, Singapore, and other hubs. Pre-hedge fuel costs rose 60% year over year; hedging cut the net increase to 13%, with fuel still 34% of operating cost. Cargo was the bright spot: tonnage fell 1% but revenue rose 52% as conflict squeezed airfreight capacity and shipping disruption pushed volume to air. Emirates kept spending through the downturn, taking nine A350s, refitting 12 aircraft under a $7 billion-plus retrofit program, and adding Starlink to 36 more aircraft. Linus Benjamin Bauer of BAA & Partners said the core flying business was likely loss-making on an unhedged basis and that the second half will show whether the operating model has recovered. Emirates has not disclosed its hedging position for the fiscal second half.

#6220. Denver Airport Taco Bell Worker Sues For Pay While Waiting At Security — And They May Win

A former Taco Bell food preparer at Denver International Airport is suing the restaurant’s operator for pay for time spent going through security and getting to the restaurant before clocking in. According to Law360, the Colorado state court lawsuit also alleges that hourly employees weren’t provided paid rest breaks. I’d normally be skeptical of a claim for pay while passing through an airport checkpoint. Government-required screening looks like part of getting to work. However, Colorado law is unique and more generous here than even California. This Wouldn’t Fly In California In January, I wrote about a Delta Sky Club worker at Los Angeles International Airport seeking pay for time spent going through TSA. A similar claim by an Admirals Club employee had already lost. In Cazares v. Host International, the Ninth Circuit upheld dismissal because the employee hadn’t alleged facts showing employer control during federally mandated screening. Federal law is also favorable to employers here. The Supreme Court’s Integrity Staffing Solutions v. Busk decision held that warehouse workers didn’t have to be paid for certain employer-required security searches. Simply requiring an activity doesn’t automatically make it paid work under federal law. Colorado Specifically Includes Security Screening As Work Colorado’s wage rules list “security or safety screening”, including waiting for it, among activities that can count as paid work. The state’s labor department explains that screening required to work for an employer can qualify “whether discretionary with the employer or legally required.” Its example is federally required radiation screening for nuclear plant guards. In Rael v. Q3 Contracting in 2024, a federal judge dismissed claims involving vehicle inspections and commuting under federal law, while allowing claims for that same time under Colorado law. The Taco Bell concessionaire’s best argument is that a shared airport checkpoint remains part of the commute: it serves aviation security generally, outside the restaurant’s premises and supervision. The worker’s answer is that this is a required screening to reach the assigned workplace, exactly the sort of activity Colorado treats as work. It’s not a frivolous theory the way it was for California airport lounge employees. Interestingly, the time security to the restaurant could count as work, too. Colorado generally excludes ordinary commuting and the initial trip to a workstation. However, its travel rule includes an exception once compensable work has begun. If the security checkpoint is work, then travel from that work location to the next one can be work, too. The state’s travel time guidance even discusses walking from an entrance to a workstation after paid activity starts. I’ve written plenty about the time it takes to get around Denver airport. So this could be a lot of time. My bet is that this dispute is more likely to produce a negotiated payment than a clean employer win based on who runs the checkpoint. But that’s just going to encourage more similar suits. Colorado’s wage rules list “security or safety screening”, including waiting for it, among activities that can count as paid work.

The state’s labor department explains that screening required to work for an employer can qualify “whether discretionary with the employer or legally required.” Its example is federally required radiation screening for nuclear plant guards.

In Rael v. Q3 Contracting in 2024, a federal judge dismissed claims involving vehicle inspections and commuting under federal law, while allowing claims for that same time under Colorado law.

The Taco Bell concessionaire’s best argument is that a shared airport checkpoint remains part of the commute: it serves aviation security generally, outside the restaurant’s premises and supervision. The worker’s answer is that this is a required screening to reach the assigned workplace, exactly the sort of activity Colorado treats as work. It’s not a frivolous theory the way it was for California airport lounge employees.

Interestingly, the time security to the restaurant could count as work, too. Colorado generally excludes ordinary commuting and the initial trip to a workstation. However, its travel rule includes an exception once compensable work has begun. If the security checkpoint is work, then travel from that work location to the next one can be work, too. The state’s travel time guidance even discusses walking from an entrance to a workstation after paid activity starts.

I’ve written plenty about the time it takes to get around Denver airport. So this could be a lot of time.

My bet is that this dispute is more likely to produce a negotiated payment than a clean employer win based on who runs the checkpoint. But that’s just going to encourage more similar suits.

Tripadvisor said Thursday that CEO Matt Goldberg and the board agreed to his departure, effective February 16, and that Chief Financial Officer Michael Noonan resigned to pursue another opportunity. The exits come 16 months after Starboard Value took a 9% stake in Tripadvisor and eight months after the activist investor won four of 10 board seats. That campaign has coincided with Chairman Greg Maffei's exit, a 20% workforce cut, and the $700 million sale of TheFork to American Express. Tripadvisor did not announce a CEO search process, and the company has said no option is off the table for monetizing Viator, its experiences booking business, and its non-core hotel metasearch business. Kristen Dalton, chief strategy and operations officer, becomes interim CFO on January 1, 2027, after Noonan stays through December 31, 2026. The leadership vacancy arrives as the board entertains strategic alternatives, which leaves the structure of the company — and the ownership of Viator — unresolved.

#6217. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

The European Commission released its EU Sustainable Tourism Strategy on Wednesday, setting out a vision to spread visitors across lesser-known destinations and across the full year — without new funding, binding mandates, or numerical targets. The Commission said 42% of nights spent in a destination fall, on average, in its three busiest months, and the strategy arrives after a summer of extreme heat, wildfires, and continued overtourism backlash. Its sustainability pillar rests on three voluntary instruments: the EU Model for Tourism Management, a proposed Council Recommendation for Balanced Tourism, and an EU Toolbox for Balanced Tourism that will include shared approaches to short-term rentals. A Cruise Cooperation Dialogue was also proposed. The Commission said €18 billion in EU support is expected to have benefited tourism from 2021 to 2027 but committed no fresh money, pointing instead to the 2028–2034 budget still under negotiation and to combining private investment with financial instruments. Industry voices quoted by Skift welcomed the volume-to-value direction while pressing for measurable targets, simpler funding access, and practical fixes such as interoperable transport ticketing, which the Commission said it would only "explore" by 2028. The strategy also flags that AI trip-planning tools could reinforce existing tourism hubs if destinations stay passive.

#6214. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohenâs latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. âWho Is America?â The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of âDa Ali G Show.â His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

âAli Gâ and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and BrÃ¼no Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, âWho Is America?â is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, âthe most dangerous show in history.â At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our populationâs capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohenâs new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. âWho Is America?â A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

âWho Is America?â was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedianâs dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtimeâs part: âHope youâll tune in next week for an interview with me,â Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You canât blame âWho Is America?â for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palinâs wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same characterÂ â Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org â sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palinâs accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. âI did NOT say I was a War Vet,â Ruddickâs âofficialâ response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was ânot military, but United Parcelâ.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewerâs line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohenâs character replies that no, he is not. âThis here scooter is to preserve my bodyâs finite energy,â Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral âstrangers on a planeâ Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sandersâ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sandersâ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled Â âObamanoids â For Real!â?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled âAge of Reason,â said to feature âconversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on todayâs most important topics.â Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named Â Nira Cain-NâDegeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are Â âafflicted with white privilege.â But it soon becomes clear that his marksâ problem isnât close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohenâs interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to âfree bleedâ on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wifeâs ongoing affair with a dolphin, they donât have any questions like, say, whether what theyâre hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to âWho Is America?â: weâre so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohenâs third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, itâs entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

âWho knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?â she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about âWho Is America?â, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. Iâm not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that Iâm not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or sheâs a friend of Baron Cohenâs and in on the gag. I hope itâs option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of âWho Is America?â have pointed out that Baron Cohenâs sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohenâs tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but itâs one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. Itâs difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of âWho Is America?â guaranteed to dominate Mondayâs gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohenâs Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself âthe terrorist terminator.â

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his âKinderguardiansâ program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walshâs boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walshâs comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, âThe way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!â If he didnât want to say it, he wouldnât have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episodeâs biggest laughs by reading the âscienceâ behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesnât know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboardâs pop charts.

Yes, âWho Is America?â gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise arenât all that different than what theyâd say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next weekâs episode introduces one or two new characters, although I donât imagine they do anything more âdangerousâ than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohenâs schtick, that wonât matter.

To them âWho Is America?â is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, âWho Is America?â is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, thatâs for sure. But Iâm not sure itâs the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. Itâs not even really news.

It’s been two years since Singapore Airlines began teasing all-new business- and first-class cabins, and nearly 10 years since the last time the airline unveiled a new generation of flagship products.

But, after much anticipation and a flurry of recent announcements about upgrades and refreshes to everything from the airline’s dining program and inflight meals and serviceware to its KrisWorld entertainment system and amenity kits, today we finally got to see what the new Singapore Airlines business- and first-class seats are like along with a preview of the new economy and premium economy seats coming to its Boeing 777-9s.

We joined a slew of international media for two days of announcements and executive interviews culminating in the big reveal at Marina Bay Sands, the even included a newly composed theme song titled "Made of every world you can dream of," performed by flight crew.

“Today Singapore Airlines unveils the next chapter in our end-to-end travel experience,” began Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong in his remarks to the crowd. “This is an important milestone and it is also part of our continuous journey to…invest in a product we know our customer will love.”

The new products represent a multiyear investment of over 2 billion Singaporean dollars ($1.56 billion) in addition to the S$130 million ($102 million) the airline has spent renovating its SilverKris lounges around the world.

“This is our biggest investment in improving the customer travel experience,” said Siva Govindasamy, divisional vice president of public affairs, “because we’re not just talking about seat development. We’re talking about improvements in the customer service journey from end to end.”

The airline surveyed over 5,000 frequent flyers, incorporating their feedback on what they were looking for from the travel experience, what elements of Singapore Airlines’ current seats and service they liked, and what needed to evolve.

“Our development process has been shaped by extensive research and feedback to help us understand how our customers work, dine, relax, sleep and use technology in their journeys,” explained Lee Lik Hsin, Singapore Airlines’ chief commercial officer, to a small media gathering ahead of the event. “This launch represents a significant milestone, but not an end point,” he continued.

Here’s how, based on what we saw of the new seats and service elements, and all the fancy, industry-leading features in store for passengers.

Related: Singapore KrisFlyer: Ultimate guide to earning, redeeming and elite status

Perhaps the most exciting announcement of the bunch was the unveiling of Singapore Airlines’ new long-haul first-class seats.

Designed by PriestmanGoode and manufactured by Collins Aerospace, these fixtures were initially slated for the airline’s upcoming order of Boeing 777-9s, but given the delays on those aircraft deliveries, Singapore is also installing them on its ultra-long-range subfleet of seven Airbus A350-900ULRs starting in the second half of 2027. This will be the first time the airline’s A350s have sported a first-class cabin.

The A350s will have just four of these seats on board in a 1-2-1 configuration at the very front of the plane. The 777-9s will eventually have six of them on board — two running down either side of the cabin and two in the center. They have 89 1/2 inches of pitch, giving them a fairly large footprint, though not as big as the Suites aboard the airline’s Airbus A380s. Singapore Airlines does not have plans to update the first-class cabins on board its Boeing 777-300s or A380s.

In one of the lighter moments during the pre-reveal press conferences, one journalist asked Singapore’s Hsin how flight crew would address couples who might want to use the space inappropriately. Without missing a beat, Hsin replied, “We will address it,” prompting chuckles around the room. “We want every passenger to be able to enjoy the comfort that we have provided without disturbing the comfort and experience for any other customer.”

Back to the seat, though, it incorporates a cocktail tray for inflight aperitifs and wardrobe areas on the aisles where passengers can stow their clothes (after slipping into the airline’s new pajamas, of course…more on that below!). Those with a keen eye will also notice a subtle batik motif on the soft wall panels hearkening to the airline’s famous uniforms and branding.

The chairs are upholstered in Poltrona Frau leather, are 23 inches wide (30 with the armrests lowered) and recline to 80-inch lie-flat beds that flight attendants will make up with 100% cotton linens, a duvet and a selection of pillows, as well as a breathable new mattress topper from German luxury brand Paradies.

Passengers can adjust the various components of the seat including the arm and legrests, the ottoman and lumbar support as well as the lighting using the inflight entertainment system control and can create a profile so that their settings will carry over to their next flight.

Passengers can dine face to face thanks to large, sturdy tray tables and will find a wireless charging pad, USB-C ports and a universal AC power port to keep their devices charged. The 777-9 seats will have a USB-A port as well.

The storage areas include a slim personal wardrobe, a vanity drawer lined in leather and a small compartment for a cabin bag beneath the ottoman.

The inflight entertainment system is a 32-inch 4K touchscreen loaded with the airline’s KrisWorld content system. It will include an integrated touch panel display for flight information, destination weather, inflight Wi-Fi connectivity status and the availability of lavatories.

Passengers will be given Bang & Olufsen wireless headphones to use, but will also be able to connect to the entertainment system using their own Bluetooth headsets.

Overall, the new first-class seats are a big step forward from the first-class cabins you’ll find aboard the airline’s Boeing 777-300s and sit somewhere between those and the A380 Suites. Their look feels like an evolution of the palette and finishes of the Suites, with welcome tech updates that should keep travelers happy and connected.

Related: The ultimate guide to Singapore Suites

Lest you think first class is the biggest news, the airline also unveiled its all-new business-class seats, designed from the ground up in conjunction with seat manufacturer Recaro and BMW’s DesignWorks.

These seats will appear on the Boeing 777-9 and both the A350-900ULR and the long-haul A350-900 but not the airline’s medium-haul A350s. If you’re losing track, don’t worry, we have tables laying out the details below. We also got a few exclusive shots from a mockup cabin at Singapore Airlines' headquarters the day before the official unveiling, which you can see below. Just note that they don't have all the finishes and other details the final seats on board will have.

“We wanted to bring an automotive-inspired seat and our knowledge from experiential design into the cabin,” explained BMW DesignWorks CEO Julia de Bono. Thus the seats feel like a mix between seats in a luxury sedan and a racecar with mineral gray-toned leather and bright yellow trim, meant to convey balance and stability on the one hand and energy and creativity on the other, according to de Bono.

The seats are laid out in a front-facing 1-2-1 pattern — this was a direct result of customer feedback, with frequent flyers telling airline executives that they wanted to move past an angled orientation, which could feel constraining at times.

Passengers will also receive new padded seat covers with memory foam for cushioning and support.

The tray table placement and stowage — it pops out from under the entertainment screen and can be maneuvered flexibly — also allows the seat to have a larger ottoman, alleviating a common complaint about the airline’s current business-class seats.

Like the new first-class seats, these will allow passengers to create a profile via the inflight entertainment system so their preferred seat and lighting settings are saved from flight to flight.

They have 22-inch 4K touchscreen entertainment systems (20 inches on the 777-9) with Bluetooth pairing capability. Among the storage spaces are a small cubby that slides out from the chair-side seatback and a little cupboard next to the entertainment screen. Passengers will also find wireless charging pads, USB-C ports and universal power plugs.

Related: Which Singapore Airlines business class is better? A380 vs A350

Singapore Airlines worked with FactoryDesign and Collins Aerospace to create updated versions of its economy and premium economy seats specifically for the Boeing 777-9. There are currently no plans for these to be installed aboard the airline’s other jets.

The new premium economy seats have a swanky, contoured look with dark gray leather upholstery and vibrant orange accents. They will see their seat pitch increase from the 38 inches previous versions offer to 40 inches and they will get an extra inch of recline, rounding it up to nine instead of eight. They will be 19 inches wide and have adjustable leg and footrests plus adjustable headsets.

Their entertainment screens will be 16 inches wide with 4K resolution and Bluetooth pairing capability. The seats will also feature universal power plugs, USB-C ports and USB-A ports on some aircraft.

As for economy seating, these look a lot like current versions and are squeezed into a tight 3-4-3 layout, with just 17.6 inches of width per seat. Their screens get an upgrade to 13 inches and 4K resolution with Bluetooth pairing available. They will also have USB-C ports (and A versions on some aircraft) plus universal power plugs.

Related: Worth the upcharge? Flying Singapore Airlines premium economy

So how exactly are all these new seats going to get onto planes and when will passengers start seeing them? Here’s the plan.

Singapore Airlines currently has 58 Airbus A350s. Seventeen of those are configured for medium-haul and regional routes.

Of the remaining 41, 34 are long-range A350-900s with business class, premium economy and economy on board. These will be kitted out with new business class seats with the following adjusted seat numbers in each class. The process is expected to start in the second half of 2027 and to last through 2030.

The other seven A350s are the airline’s A350-900ULRs, which stands for Ultra-Long-Range, and which are deployed on the airline’s longest routes from Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) to New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). These ULR jets will get a full overhaul with the new first- and business-class seats. The changes will reduce the plane's overall seating capacity to 132, down from 161.

All the seats on this jet will be new, but here’s how it breaks down.

So the good news is that the majority of Singapore Airlines' long-haul fleet will have new first- and business-class seats on them once this retrofit is complete and the 777-9s are in service. The bad news is that we don't know how long that will take, exactly, and we don't know what routes will see the new seats first.

In the meantime, here are some of the other fun things the airline has cooking up. Quite literally, in some cases.

Related: A review of Singapore Suites first class from Frankfurt to New York

As if new seats weren’t enough, Singapore Airlines is making major updates to its meal service as well.

The airline is already well-known for offering a “Book the Cook” meal preorder service with dozens of dishes available to flyers in Suites, first, business and premium economy, but there are about to be a lot more options.

The airline is touting over 100 new and refreshed dishes on offer, including appetizers, mains and desserts, which will be introduced across all four classes of service under a new category titled “SIA Chefs’ Selection” developed by the airline’s partner guest chefs, who include Monica Galetti, Nandu Jubany, Sanjeev Kapoor, Sid Sahrawat, Yoshihiro Murata and Zhu Jun.

Among the new dishes you might spot are poached Maine lobster with champagne sauce in Suites and first class, a Japanese-inspired prawn cocktail in business class, beef short rib in coconut-based sambal percik with nasi kerabu rice in business class, tandoor-roasted paneer in tangy pasanda gravy in all classes and Irish lamb stew with buttered cabbage and caraway seeds in premium economy.

And take a closer look at what those dishes will be served on in business and first. The airline is introducing an all-new line of chinaware from French luxury brand Christofle, making it the first airline to partner with the longstanding luxury house.

The patterns are inspired by Christofle’s Malmaison Impériale collection and incorporate an interpretation of Singapore Airline’s floral batik patterns. There will also be new custom-designed Christofle glassware with tulip-shaped champagne flutes and wine glasses with long stems for more utility.

A new selection of spirits across the board and new wines for business and first class passengers is coming, too. First-class and Suites passengers will be treated to an expanded selection of champagnes including Krug Grande Cuvée, Louis Roederer Cristal, Taittinger Comtes de Champagne, Charles Heidsieck Blanc des Millénaires and Bollinger La Grande Année while those in business class will find Charles Heidsieck Brut Reserve N.V. and Piper-Heidsieck Vintage.

Among the new spirits to be carried on board, there will be a blended whiskey from Japan’s Komoro Distillery created exclusively for Singapore Airlines first class, Bowmore 19 Year Old Pinot Noir Cask Finish single-malt Scotch whisky and Roky Botanical Kasane Edition gin in business class and Whyte & Mackay blended Scotch whisky in premium economy and economy.

Related: Behind the scenes with Singapore Airlines' wine experts as they choose the Champagnes that will be on board soon

For a carrier with such a premium reputation, one thing that surprises some business-class passengers is the fact that Singapore Airlines has not traditionally handed out amenities in business class (first-class passengers do get them, though). That’s all about to change, starting this week.

In fact, Singapore Airlines is introducing all-new amenity kits available on flights over six hours. Here’s what’s in store for passengers.

When Singapore Airlines launched its second-generation A380 First Class Suites in 2017, it also formed a partnership with French luxury house Lalique to create onboard amenities including pajamas, linens and amenity kits with fragrances and skincare products.

Now, with the introduction of its third-generation suites, the airline is turning to French cosmetics brand Sisley to create all-new men’s and women’s kits for first class passengers featuring anti-aging Sisleÿa (for women) and Sisleÿum (for men) products.

Passengers will also find Sisley’s Eau de Campagne fragrance, moisturizing body lotion and floral spray mist along with dental kits in the first-class lavatories.

As for pajamas, customers will receive all-new sleeper suits in dark gray cotton with a subtle imprint of the airline’s batik pattern on the plackets and side seams, along with new, better padded slippers. They will be available in four sizes.

While visiting the airline’s fancy The Private Room lounge and the First Class SilverKris Lounge at Changi Terminals 2 and 3, passengers will also find Hair Rituel by Sisley fortifying densifying shampoo and restructuring conditioner in the shower suites, along with Sisley’s Eau de Campagne bath and shower gel, fragrance and moisturizing body lotion.

Singapore Airlines is also introducing new amenity kits and, for the first time, pajamas for business-class passengers.

The sleeping apparel will be navy-blue poly-cotton with a subtle batik print on the tops’ inner collars and the lining of the trousers’ pockets. They will be available in two sizes.

Business-class passengers will also receive new amenity kits from Swedish brand Byredo that include:

The business-class lavatories will have Blanche body lotion and vitamin E and chamomile facial toner.

Don’t worry, the airline hasn’t forgotten about premium economy passengers, who pay a pretty penny for that extra legroom. They will now receive new zip pouches made from recycled materials and decorated with the airline’s recognizable batik motif.

The pouches will contain Australian personal care brand Ink & Water’s white tea-scented lip balm as well as eye masks, socks and dental kits.

Related: Singapore Airlines premium economy review

Even the folks in the back will receive drawstring pouches with a batik motif containing eye masks, socks and a dental kit.

Long flights are tough on kids, so for travelers 12 years of age and under on flights that are over five hours long, the airline will offer collectible Beary soft toys — essentially airline-branded teddy bears. The airline also offers Pixar’s “Toy Story”-themed amenities on all flights including things like infant bibs, activity pads for kids and drawstring bags.

Related: I make my own amenity kit for long-haul flights: Here’s what’s inside

Singapore Airlines will also be updating the KrisWorld inflight entertainment systems on its A350s and offering new systems on its forthcoming 777-9s.

The new systems will have 4K resolution and Bluetooth pairing capability, but interface improvements that include better search functions, content shortcuts, a mini-player function so passengers can browse content while watching something, better personalization and wellness programming.

First-class passengers will receive Bang & Olufsen noise-cancelling Bluetooth headsets to use in flight while business-class and premium economy flyers will receive active noise-cancellation sets. Economy passengers get wired headphones, but all will be able to pair their own Bluetooth devices with the new systems.

The airline will also progressively roll out new Starlink Wi-Fi service starting in 2027 aboard its Airbus A380s, A350-900 long-haul fleet and its A350-900ULRs. Like the airline’s current Wi-Fi offerings, Starlink service will be free for business and first class passengers and passengers in all cabins who are members of KrisFlyer or PPS Club.

“For our customers, every touchpoint — from seats, meals, inflight entertainment, connectivity and amenities, to our lounges and other ground experiences — is part of one similar Singapore Airlines journey," remarked Phong in his speech at the unveiling event. "By continuing to invest and elevate this end-to-end customer experience, we offer greater comfort and convenience while reinforcing our commitment to earning their trust and loyalty at every single phase of their journey.”

New airline seats represent huge investments of time, money and research, let alone the costs of updating onboard services and amenities. That makes Singapore Airlines’ current slate of announcements all the more exciting.

Flyers have a lot to look forward to on board the airline’s long-haul A350s and forthcoming 777-9s. While the first-class seats are not as large as the Suites on board the airline’s A380s, they are still roomy with high-end finishes and up-to-date tech that passengers should welcome.

As for premium economy and economy, hopefully the airline will consider bringing its latest seats to the A350 as well in an attempt to standardize the experience across the fleet. Still, for 777-9 passengers, these updates will be a win.

If you're curious to see some of the elements unveiled today for yourself, there should be a special display at The Jewel at Changi in the coming weeks followed by one in the transit area of Terminal 3 in early 2027.

What do you think of Singapore Airlines’ new seats? Leave a comment with your impressions below!

#6211. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trumpâs trusted lawyerÂ and cable newsâs favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Boratâs ultimate get in 2006âs âBorat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,â the pranking of Americaâs mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: hisÂ corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ to succeed in theirÂ mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohenâs exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie.Â By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout âSubsequent Movefilmâ for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment weâre introduced to Bakalovaâs Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on parÂ with the sinking of the Titanic.Â Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, âthe happiest wife in the world,â emboldening her to join Boratâs latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Boratâs government, have not been kind to him since âCultural Learningsâ conquered America with great success â high five! â 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstanâs current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, heâs hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form â ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all â and given a new mission to smooth glorious leaderâs entry into the worldâs strongman club. How? By presenting toâVice Premier Mikhail Penceâ valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, âKazakhstanâs Minister of Culture and No.1Â porno star.â

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the filmâs release fails to ruin âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas, Â plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the filmâs full title: âBorat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstanâ merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series âWho Is America?â â which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American â enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit heâd pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. âTheyâre fun!â

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, âSubsequent Moviefilmâ makes Tutarâs empowerment the centerpiece of the movieâs second half. Â Baron Cohenâs signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Wolinerâs past TV work (which includesÂ series such as âNathan for Youâ) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that âBorat Subsequent Moviefilmâ and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

Thereâs the practical matter that the character ofÂ Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that âthe problem with success, although itâs fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I âgetâ with Borat again, so itâs a kind of self-defeating form, really.â

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today.Â However, heâs right about the problem of Boratâs fame. âSubsequent Moviefilmâ confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Boratâs relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant â except for when he revealshis subjectsâ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original âBoratâ donât involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Boratâs stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in âSubsequent Moviefilm.â Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctorâs office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohenâs infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama âwith the Wuhan flu.â

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business donât tell us anything we donât already know. Instead, itâs what the context implies about Americaâs psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isnât merely in the pastorâs misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutarâs stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutarâs father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesnât disturb the status quo.

Thereâs the Texas baker who uses icing toÂ pipe the wordsÂ âJews Will Not Replace Usâ on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. Thereâs theÂ shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the âno means yesâ dress section. Thereâs the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, âWhat color is best for racist family?â says without pause or reaction, âI wouldnât go any darker than a six or a seven.â

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; sheâs also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first âBoratâ and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, sheâs a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of âSubsequent Moviefilmâ relative to the first âBoratâ sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has arenât deadly, although itâs plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the filmâs ending in ways that donât feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the âBoratâ of 2006 and the 2020 âSubsequent Moviefilmâ is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trumpâs election in 2016, to say nothing of howÂ decline and fall of basic critical thoughtÂ has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, thereâs simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If thereâs a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called âlesserâ nations.

Now it doesnât allow the audience to be so sure of itself,Â implying in the final sceneÂ that we arenât merely ugly Americans. Weâre a once glorious nationÂ being led by goons who areÂ sliding us backwardÂ into diminishment, and dangerously so. ThatÂ is nothing to laugh about.Â

âBorat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstanâ is currently streaming on Amazon.

#6209. The GOP’s midterm plan: Make America hate Muslims again

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicans’ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who don’t know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOP’s anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurse’s office without parental consent.

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which has  been the central organizing principle of Trump’s decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as “no new wars” and “bringing prices down on day one,” but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, he’s even exceeded expectations.

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the party’s leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohio’s Republican nominee for governor.

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of “lone-wolf” terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding “and worse,” and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America “until we can figure out what the hell is going on,” he executed his infamous “Muslim ban” days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trump’s ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But she’s a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trump’s bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the state’s governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesota’s community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and that’s saying something.

Somalia, he said, is “garbage, a “sh*thouse country” that “stinks.” He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants don’t work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to “fight back” against the state’s Somali population, writing that they “view you as weak and stupid people.”

Another target of MAGA’s anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as “very, very evil,” a “psychopath” who pushes “anti-white racial hatred.” This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to “welfare” and “busing” to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, “law and order,” as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about “welfare queens” during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in states’ rights — another dog whistle — in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his “birther” campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the party’s burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name — Barack Hussein Obama — with a childish glee.

I don’t think claiming that a whole African country is a “sh*thouse” or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighbors’ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. It’s just a matter of time. And if he does, I’m sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGA’s staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.
